#6265. This Cruise Proves the Congo is No Heart of Darkness—Or Viral Fad

Occasionally, a place will take hold of our collective imagination in much the same way that an unsolved mathematical problem does, or a treasure hunt, or an ancient, coded message found moldering in an attic, beguiling with its mystery, difficulty, and promise of a reward. Few places exert quite this pull like the Congo Basin, a thick block of forest and rivers covering much of Central Africa, home to some 150 ethnic groups, and a raft of extraordinary biodiversity. Despite its size and its importance as a counterbalance to climate change, the region endures a dearth of scientific research funding and conservation efforts. Roughly the size of India, it has inspired and vexed many visitors (even those who might otherwise have claimed to have conquered it).

A floating village in the Congo River Basin

The idea could be said to originate in the late 19th century, as Europeans made their way into the great forests seeking fortune and glory. The Welsh explorer Henry Morton Stanley, the first to leave a detailed record of his journey across the Basin, claimed that even after a three-year trek (1874-77) it remained “a region of fable and mystery.” That was exactly the mix sought by Polish sailor Józef Korzeniowski, who, as a boy, looked at the map of Africa, then a white space, and “declared that some day I would go there.” Eventually, and not long after Stanley, he did, and with the captaincy of a steamboat on the Congo River, was tasked with collecting one Mr. Klein, an upcountry agent employed by the brutal Belgian trading company. Korzeniowski was horrified by what he saw along the river—colonization and resource extraction at its cruelest and bloodiest—calling it “the vilest scramble for loot that ever disfigured the history of human conscience and geographical exploration.” Later, Józef Korzeniowski became Joseph Conrad, Mr. Klein became Mr. Kurtz, and the rest is literary history.

Dzanga Baï, a protected area in the southwestern Central African Republic also known as “the village of elephants.”

The latest journeyman to apply themself to the region is another Welshman, Ash Dykes, whose TikTok videos of his journey paddling down the Sangha River (a tributary of the mighty Congo River) have received millions of views. By mid-October, Dykes, who calls himself an extreme athlete, was midway through the 400 miles he hoped to cover. His videos—the anxiety and speculation of his preparation; the amplification of the danger en route—are over-exaggerated, designed to amuse his audience; they are spectacle. Looking bewildered in his state-of-the-art inflatable boat, Dykes is most often met by competent, unaffected locals, paddling their wooden pirogues with balletic grace. And brave though Dykes certainly is, most of what he has accomplished—attending a hunt with the Ba’aka people, seeing the forest elephants in Dzanga Baï, or tracking Western lowland gorillas—can be done by just about anyone.

The Princesse Ngalessa, a multi-level riverboat operated by Ducret Expeditions, is the basin's only passenger cruise.

I, too, was one enchanted by the inscrutability of the Congo Basin, and I dreamt of one day traveling along its rivers and into its forests; in my mind’s eye, I envisioned dusk slipping into night, to the rhythm of a pounding drumbeat. Not long ago, I departed Brazzaville, the capital of the Republic of Congo, aboard the Princesse Ngalessa, a multi-level riverboat operated by Ducret Expeditions. As the only such passenger vessel in the Congo Basin, the crew of the Ngalessa is accustomed to receiving rarefied looks from the riverbank. But just as often, the ship’s approach was greeted with aplomb, for it was an event in the villages and brought goods, along with community support and news from away.

In comparison to the coarse and crowded daka-dakas—flat-topped river barges, stuffed with goods and spewing black, acrid smoke as they chunter between Kinshasa and Kisangani—those of us onboard the Ngalessa traveled in glorious comfort: air-conditioning, three square meals a day, and private bathrooms. We also had the benefit of our local guides and their familiarity with the languages, customs, and faces up and down the river. This included, in the riverside village of Ngabe, the appearance of an Ejengi, a forest spirit made of palm fronds that danced and spun as a crowd of onlookers sang, drummed, and screamed in delight.

“Don’t worry,” our guide said. “Look at his dusty bare feet!” Elsewhere, we watched an Indigenous Luma woman cut, strip, and chew twigs into a pulp that could be used as medicinal pain relief. On other days, we kayaked through the flooded forests of the Alima River, and traded with fishermen who brought their slim pirogues against our mammoth ship to hand over smoked fish and fruit.

Kayaking through the flooded forests of the Alima River.

Eight days and 600 miles after leaving Brazzaville, we arrived at the outpost of Ouesso on the Sangha River. I journeyed further upon that water by launch boat, into the Central African Republic, and spent days at Sangha Lodge, drinking gin and tonics with local legend Rod Cassidy, an eco-tourism pioneer who has spent years living and working with the local Ba’aka people. It was through him I had the good luck to attend a hunt with those same Ba’aka, and to look on while they divvied up the duiker they snagged in their homemade nets. Afterwards, they whooped and hollered as they carried the meat out and into their village—a feast!

In the heightened state of travel, there comes occasionally a moment like falling into an empty space and, as two glancing stones can spark a blaze, a light of comprehension is illuminated. Sometimes this moment manifests itself as love, other times as admiration, or confusion. Conrad left the Congo in spiritual, psychological, and physical shock. “Before the Congo, I was a mere animal,” he wrote after his consequential journey. He was changed, as travelers who go forward with their ears and eyes open (to say nothing of their hearts) are changed. Watching the Ba’aka poised in their hunt, ears tilted to the slightest sound, I felt myself see humanity as it had existed since time immemorial. As they laughed and chatted on their success, the women showing their fangs (chipped with rocks as a show of strength), and the men slapping each other on the back, I could barely remember seeing such happiness elsewhere.

The Congo Basin may still be raw and atavistic—great adventures there are still possible—but it is no “heart of darkness” (a title which for Conrad lay not in the location itself, but rather mankind’s ability to exploit and vilify others). What separates it from other places is its independence. It requires protection, yes, but has no need, and few provisions, for any prying visitors; it is not a prize to be conquered. Most incredibly, it remains the home of peoples who have not yet latched themselves to tourism; people who sustain themselves almost wholly from an expanse of forest and the waters that for others can only be the basis of wonder and amazement. And yet, after all the sorrow and misery that colonialism brought to the Congo Basin, the people remain sincere and earnest, and willing to show others the best of their land.

A lone kayaker glides underneath a hazy sky.

One night, as the Ngalessa drifted northward, from beneath the awning on the ship’s upper deck, I watched a cloud bank clump and darken. Finally, with an incision of lightning, the downpour came, brief but fierce. The sun returned, low in the sky but still warm, and the scent of damp earth rose up. A patter of drumming reached us from somewhere, before being swallowed by the forest. The dinner bell rang, and I thought I never want this trip to end.

Researchers might have identified the oldest male orca ever recorded after testing for radioactive traces of atomic bombs in the teeth of whales stranded in Scotland.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nuclear fallout has potentially revealed the oldest male orca ever recorded, scientists have found.

The radioactive residue, a result of bomb testing in previous decades, was preserved in the teeth of orcas (Orcinus orca) and sperm whales (Physeter macrocephalus) that washed up over the years in Scotland, according to a recent study.

"It gives us what we call a kind of bomb pulse," study first author Kieran Tierney, a research scientist at the Scottish Universities Environmental Research Centre, told Live Science.

Male orcas are thought to have a maximum lifespan of around 50 to 60 years. However, in the recent study, published Oct. 1 in the journal Frontiers in Marine Science, the radiocarbon signature identified in one stranded male suggested he had lived to more than 65 years old.

The research team noted that the radiocarbon data doesn't provide a precise age. However, that doesn't mean the estimate is implausible.

Maximum ages are notoriously difficult to measure in nature — researchers can't track every animal to see which individual lives longest in all species — and there isn't an extensive worldwide record of orca longevity.

"The age estimates we have from life history studies are only a few decades old and researchers have only looked at limited numbers of individuals from a few orca populations," said Erich Hoyt, co-chair of the IUCN Important Marine Mammal Area Specialist Group and author of "Orca: The Whale Called Killer" (Firefly Books, 2019). "It would not surprise me if male killer whales were sometimes living to age 65 and beyond," Hoyt, who was not involved in the study, told Live Science in an email.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Orcas and sperm whales have banded growth layers in their teeth, which researchers believe form every year, like the rings in a tree trunk. To test this idea and learn more about the animals washing up in Scotland, the authors of the new study examined teeth from three orcas stranded between 1995 and 2016, and from two sperm whales stranded in the 1990s.

Researchers studied the tooth of an iconic male sperm whale named Moby, which stranded in 1997.

Atomic weapons testing, particularly during the middle of the 20th century, unleashed vast quantities of radioactive material, including radiocarbon, which subsequently entered the marine environment and is preserved in the teeth of cetaceans like sperm whales and orcas. Radiocarbon exists naturally in the atmosphere, but the detonation of these bombs significantly spiked environmental levels of this radioactive isotope, so by measuring levels of this compound, researchers could identify whether animals lived through the testing era.

Banded layers in the sperm whale teeth matched the atomic data, with the two whales estimated to have died in their 20s and 40s, respectively, suggesting that the layers formed annually at least in early- to mid-life. However, while the tooth layers and atomic age matched for one of the orcas — estimating the animal was in its early 20s — the other male's data didn't match at all, according to the study.

The oddball orca, named KW2, stranded in Uist, an island in western Scotland in 2015. The tooth analysis suggested that KW2 lived into his 50s, but the radiocarbon analysis suggested he was at least 65 when he died. Tierney speculated that either a cluster of layers appeared in the tooth as a single year, or new layers stopped forming in later years.

"We think that the tooth effectively ran out of space to put down any more layers," Tierney said.

The banded layers and atomic data also didn't match for the study's only female orca, named Lulu. In Lulu's case, she didn't have a clear bomb pulse signal, making comparisons difficult. The tooth layers suggested she was in her 30s when she died, while her radiocarbon signal was indicative of historic nuclear plant discharges in the Irish Sea in the latter half of the 20th century, which were carried to the Scottish west coast.

By looking at stable isotopes of carbon and nitrogen in the tooth samples, the researchers identified traces of what the animals might have eaten. Lulu appears to have had a higher proportion of marine mammals in her diet than the males, which seemed to eat more fish, according to the study.

Orcas' diets vary across different populations, and Lulu's is likely tied to her community. She was part of Scotland's West Coast Community — a genetically distinct orca population on the brink of extinction — before she stranded in 2016. The West Coast Community is known to prey on other marine mammals.

Lulu was famous for being the last known female in the West Coast Community. The population hasn't produced any calves in the decades researchers have studied it. Now down to just two surviving males, the remaining bulls are expected to be the last of their kind.

While the West Coast Community's living bulls weren't part of the new study, they are thought to be more than 50 years old. This longevity, combined with the estimated age of KW2, raises tantalizing questions for future orca research.

Tierney noted that until now, orca studies have mostly focused on populations off the Pacific coast of North America. There, males have a mama's boy reputation; they're typically observed spending their entire lives with their mothers, with life expectancy dropping significantly after their mothers die. But if male orcas are living longer lives off Scotland, and the West Coast Community's bulls are getting by without their mothers' support, then it's possible they could be more independent than their North American Pacific counterparts.

"It looks like the killer whales around our shores maybe do something a little bit different," Tierney said.

Tierney, K. M., McGill, R. A. R., Brownlow, A., Sayle, K. L., Tripney, B. G., Dunbar, E., Newton, J., Terrapon, M., Doeschate, M. T. I. T., Davison, N. J., Timmons, Z., & Kitchener, A. C. (2026). Integrating radiocarbon and stable isotopes in odontocete teeth to reveal life histories. Frontiers in Marine Science, 13. https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1934180

Patrick Pester is the trending news writer at Live Science. His work has appeared on other science websites, such as BBC Science Focus and Scientific American. Patrick retrained as a journalist after spending his early career working in zoos and wildlife conservation. He was awarded the Master's Excellence Scholarship to study at Cardiff University where he completed a master's degree in international journalism. #6262. Thune will lead Republicans through the minority

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., leaves a meeting in the Capitol on Tuesday, before his election as incoming minority leader later in the day. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.

The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.

“Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for,” Thune told reporters, referring to the midterms. “But I think it’s important that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us.”

While he and the rest of the leadership slate sailed through the conference contests by voice vote, it wasn’t without drama.

Before the leadership elections began in the Old Supreme Court Chamber early Tuesday morning, the conference held a meeting at the request of a group of GOP five senators, led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.

The conversation, which several senators described as “frank,” ended up pushing back the leadership elections by a few hours. But they were not postponed to another day as some had hoped.

“This has never been anything against John Thune,” said Johnson, as he made good on his commitment to leave the room early if the conference proceeded with its election. “What I didn’t agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position.”

“Part of the issue here is who wants the job? God bless him for serving,” Johnson added.

The conference conversation Tuesday morning turned into an “open-mic” with both conservatives and those who lost their elections speaking, according to senators.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told reporters, “To rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”

But no contender to Thune emerged despite the angst, and a motion to proceed to the election, introduced by Thune’s fellow South Dakotan Sen. Mike Rounds, was accepted.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters who rejected Republicans last week were reacting to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living, not to how Senate leaders were running the conference.

“I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem,” Paul said.

Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., was reelected to his position, as was the chairman of the Senate Republican Conference, Tom Cotton of Arkansas. Sen. James Lankford of Oklahoma was again selected as vice chair of the conference, while Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia was reelected as Republican Policy Committee chair.

“Our first step is to make sure the American people know that we heard what they said, and the American people’s priorities are our priorities. That’s the way we regain their trust,” Barrasso said afterward.

Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio got the nod to chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee, meaning he will helm the campaign arm as the party looks ahead to the uncertain waters of 2028.

Moreno said, “I was in the retail automobile business, so when you don’t listen to your customers, your customers punish you. I think we have to own it, and I think we have to learn from it.”

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said on Monday evening, “What we as a conference right now need is honesty. We need focus. We need to try to reach a consensus on what we need to change.”

Kennedy was among those pushing to delay the leadership elections and told reporters on Tuesday he voted present instead of yes on whether to proceed to them.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who ran for GOP leader twice — once in 2022 against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and in 2024 against Thune — declined to run again to challenge Thune. But in a Dear Colleague letter on Monday, he detailed what he’d like to see in the lame-duck session before Democrats take power, including confirming every nominee President Donald Trump has sent to the Senate, funding the government without an omnibus, banning stock trading, passing the permitting bill that is advancing this week in the Senate, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, balancing the budget and pushing through a sweeping voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act.

Senate Republicans on Tuesday also voted on a resolution on their path forward that was spurred by a motion from Scott, aides said.

“It is the sense of the GOP Conference that we will maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3,” the resolution reads in part.

That long list of goals highlights the expectations Thune has faced as leader, where he led one-third of Republicans’ trifecta in Washington. In the next Congress, Democrats will hold the majority in both chambers of Congress after their larger-than-expected wins, while Trump finishes out his term as president.

Thune said he told his conference: “As I look back on the last couple of years, my question is, what would you have me do differently?”

“Given the constraints we had to deal with, all the stuff that was coming at us on a daily basis, a narrow margin in the House, the White House, the Democrats over here who were obstructing two long government shutdowns — I think we came out of it as well as could have been expected, and got a lot of stuff done,” Thune told reporters.

“If you believe the exit polls, it was the war, it was the economy, it was inflation, it was fuel prices,” Thune added. “So no, I wasn’t apologizing for anything that we did. And I think on the political side, I don’t know what else I could have done.”

#6261. The 11 Most Beautiful Beaches in the Caribbean

Picking the most beautiful beaches in the Caribbean is an exercise in splitting hairs. Nearly every island has a stretch of powdery sand and improbably blue water, and after a while, the “nice sand, nice water” trope stops registering at all. We’re talking beauty in the transcendental sense—the kind of beauty that makes you feel something. Maybe it’s a crescent of sand more pink than you thought could happen in nature. Maybe it’s a labyrinth of granite boulders spilling into the sea. Or maybe it’s a beach bar so perfectly placed it feels as much a part of the landscape as the sand. Plenty of beaches are picturesque. These are the ones, if you ask us, that are beautiful.

Barbuda is the quieter, more elusive sister to Antigua, but Princess Diana Beach is the reason many visitors make a detour here. The long stretch of blush-pink sand is framed by low vegetation and blissfully few signs of life. There is, almost puzzlingly, a Nobu, which brings a welcome blip of civilization in the form of Japanese-Peruvian cooking, cocktails, and a beach club with cabanas. (Nobu Beach Inn is set to debut in 2027, too.) Book lunch there and a beach transfer in advance—many of the top resorts on Antigua offer this as a day excursion from the other island.

Grace Bay is famous for good reason: roughly three miles of powdery white sand and shockingly clear waters make even the most airbrushed postcards look inadequate. An offshore reef keeps the waters agreeably calm for swimming (especially with kids), too. This is one of the Caribbean’s most polished beach destinations, with a concentration of luxury resorts, watersports operators and restaurants that make a choose-your-own adventure beach day a pretty seamless affair. Public access points are plentiful and free, so you needn’t be staying at one of the grand hotels to enjoy the view. (Although you should.)

The kind of place that castaway dreams are made of, Little Bay is a tiny crescent of sand tucked beneath towering limestone cliffs. No beach club, no cabanas, no infrastructure, no fuss. It’s accessible by boat from neighboring Crocus Bay, or, if you’re feeling adventurous, by rope down the rock face. Bring water, a picnic and all your gear—there’s fantastic snorkeling here.

A mile-long horseshoe of white sand with clear, shallow water, Flamenco Beach is more than worth the ferry over from mainland Puerto Rico. It also has an unusual bit of history: two abandoned United States military tanks, left behind after the Navy used Culebra for training exercises, now sit near the shore, covered in colorful graffiti. We aren’t usually proponents of littering, but the counterpoint of natural beauty with human history is part of what makes this beach so unforgettable.

Definitely the most photographed beach in the U.S. Virgin Islands and probably the most photographed beach in the Caribbean, Trunk Bay never disappoints. From the access road, you see a sweep of white sand stretching out, with impossibly turquoise waters and a small offshore cay that seems placed for composition. It’s part of Virgin Islands National Park, so the infrastructure covers all the stuff you need—snack bar, restrooms, showers and snorkel rentals. The main attraction is the underwater snorkeling trail, where submerged markers introduce visitors to the coral reef and its inhabitants.

If you want swanky French beach clubs, head over to Saint-Jean, because Saline is St. Barth’s at its most elemental. The sand is broad and soft, the dunes rolling, and the sea open, with no beach clubs or hotels or influencers interrupting your view. Getting there requires a short walk over the dunes from the parking lot, which helps preserve the feeling that you’re leaving the chi-chi side of the island behind.

There are beautiful beaches, and then there are the Baths, a landscape so distinctive it feels like you’ve left the Caribbean, and perhaps earth entirely. The beach is home to a collection of enormous granite boulders, some as large as houses, all tumbled together to create something totally unique. Between them are hidden grottoes, tidal pools and narrow passages—making this as much a playground as it is a beach. Bring sturdy water shoes and expect to do some scrambling.

The longest beach on its island, this elegant crescent sits directly on the Tropic of Cancer. It’s relatively remote and unspoiled by Bahamian standards, making it a true bucket list destination for beach snobs. It’s about a 30-minute drive from George Town on Great Exuma (where the airport is), across the bridge to Little Exuma. There are no proper facilities, so pack what you need. There are Aman, Rosewood and Bulgari resorts debuting here in the years to come—so visit now for serious “I've been coming here since” bragging rights.

A hidden gem by any standard, Sandy Island is a miniature, uninhabited coral cay located just off the west coast of Carriacou, Grenada’s sister island. There are no hotels or roads, and the whole appeal is the rugged simplicity of arriving by boat, dropping anchor and spending an afternoon doing basically nothing except enjoying the elements. The island is part of a protected marine park, making it a fantastic spot for snorkeling with colorful reef fish, turtles and octopi.

The rest of the world is finally catching up with what the diving scene has known for years—No Name Beach is one of the most pristine, stunning stretches of sand anywhere in the Caribbean. It’s located on the tiny island of Klein Bonaire (“Little Bonaire”) just offshore of mainland Bonaire, and is part of Bonaire National Marine Park, meaning development is off the table. There aren’t any restaurants, bathrooms, or beach bars, but there are water taxis from Kralendijk. Bring food and water, your own snorkel gear, and prepare to be blown away by the untouched Caribbean at its finest.

While Bávaro Beach proper is about 5 miles long, it connects seamlessly with adjoining beaches Arena Blanca and Arena Gorda—so, depending on who’s counting, actually comes in at closer to 30 miles of uninterrupted shoreline. This is the beach that initially spurred Punta Cana’s resort boom, with coconut palms fringing the white sand, a barrier reef keeping the waters tranquil, and enough space for everyone to stretch out and (pretty much) never feel crowded. If you head toward El Cortecito or Los Corales, you’ll find beach bars where the party never stops. On a beach this beautiful, why would it?

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6259. 21 Best Places to Visit in December in the USA

We’ll never forget the first time we visited New York City in December. We’d seen it in movies, but standing there, seeing the Rockefeller Center tree all lit up for the first time, with skaters below and festive music in the air… it was pure magic.

But December travel isn’t just about snow and Santa. We’ve also spent the holidays escaping to the warmth, trading snow boots for flip-flops.

In fact, we’ve been to almost all 50 states and spent a lot of winters trying to find the most fun destinations and best weather. We’ve done so many road trips in the USA and flown almost everywhere, trying to find the best places to either escape the snow or enjoy the winter, you would think we are obsessed. And we want to share all of that knowledge with you.

If you’re looking for the perfect winter getaway, you have a clear choice: either lean into the winter magic or escape it completely. Are you dreaming of a warm-weather escape with sunshine and sand, or a storybook Christmas town that looks like a real-life snow globe?

Based on all those experiences, we’ve put together this list of our favourite places to visit. Whether you’re looking for a festive city, a snowy mountain, or a sunny beach, we’ll help you find the perfect spot.

Here is a quick look at some of the best places for a December getaway in the USA, from festive winter wonderlands to sunny escapes.

December is a month of pure magic and festive energy. It’s the perfect time to use up that last bit of vacation time for the year. The biggest draw is the distinct choice it offers: You can either dive head-first into a winter wonderland, complete with snow and holiday markets, or you can completely escape the cold weather and find yourself on a sunny beach. It’s a month of festive celebrations, incredible decorations, and finding the perfect atmosphere to end the year.

If you’re anything like us, sometimes the best gift in December is a break from the cold. Trust us, we know after living in Toronto, Canada. Those winters are brutal. These are our favourite spots to find sunshine and warm weather, where you can trade your winter coat for a light jacket or even a swimsuit.

We love the laid-back, quirky vibe of Key West, and it’s even more special in December. We have a great memory of biking around the island, seeing the historic inns draped in holiday lights, and then ending the day at Mallory Square for the sunset celebration. It’s a perfect escape from the cold.

Why Visit in December: This is the perfect time to visit. The summer humidity is gone, the weather is sunny and warm (often in the high 70s), and the risk of hurricanes is very low. The whole island is in a festive spirit, with unique events like the “Bight Before Christmas” boat parade.

Where to Stay: We recommend finding a guesthouse or inn in the historic Old Town to be close to the action.

We once went to a holiday luau in Ka’anapali, and it’s an experience we’ll never forget. You’re eating kalua pork and sipping a mai tai, watching a beautiful hula performance… and then Santa Claus arrives on an outrigger canoe. It was the perfect, uniquely Hawaiian way to get into the festive spirit.

Why Visit in December: You get tropical weather, festive holiday luaus, and it’s the official start of the humpback whale watching season. Be aware that this is a popular time, especially around Christmas, so prices can be high and you’ll need to book in advance.

Where to Stay: Look to the resorts in Wailea or Ka’anapali for a classic Maui experience.

We’ll always remember snorkeling the underwater trail at Trunk Bay in St. John. The water was so calm and clear, and seeing all the colourful fish felt a world away from the snow back home. That’s the magic of a Caribbean trip in December, and the USVI makes it so easy for American travelers.

Why Visit in December: It’s the start of the dry season, with fantastic weather and warm, clear water. You get a full-on tropical, warm-weather Christmas experience, all without needing a passport.

Where to Stay: You can choose from large resorts in St. Thomas or more eco-friendly villas and lodges in St. John.

We were not prepared for how magical St. Augustine is in December. We took one of the Old Town trolley tours at night, and seeing the entire historic city, from the old Spanish architecture to the palm trees, draped in millions of white lights… it was breathtaking. It’s a holiday light display unlike any other.

Why Visit in December: The famous “Nights of Lights” festival. The entire city is illuminated, and the mild Florida weather is perfect for walking around and enjoying the atmosphere. It’s one of the most festive and warm places you can visit.

Where to Stay: We recommend a historic inn or bed & breakfast in the downtown district to be within walking distance of all the lights.

While Maui is our go-to for a resort escape, Honolulu is where you go for a vibrant, city-meets-beach holiday. We loved seeing the massive Santa surfing with his reindeer in the fountain at the Iolani Palace. The whole city has this amazing “Mele Kalikimaka” (Merry Christmas) spirit.

Why Visit in December: It’s the perfect blend of warm beach weather, world-class shopping, and festive displays. It’s also a significant month for history, with the memorial events at Pearl Harbor.

Where to Stay: Waikiki has a huge range of hotels, from historic beachfront properties to modern high-rises.

If your idea of a winter getaway is to truly get away from everything, the crowds, the noise, the stress, then South Padre is a perfect choice. We spent a week there, and our days consisted of long, quiet walks on the beach. It was a total reset and the perfect way to escape the winter blues.

Why Visit in December: The weather is mild, and the crowds are gone. It’s one of the warmest places in Texas and offers a simple, relaxing beach vacation without the high prices or holiday chaos of other destinations.

Where to Stay: You’ll find many beachfront condos and hotels offering great off-season rates.

We thought we knew desert holiday lights, but the “Las Noches de las Luminarias” at the Desert Botanical Garden in Phoenix is on another level. Walking the garden paths lit by thousands of hand-lit luminaria bags, with musicians playing, was a top-tier holiday experience.

Why Visit in December: You get two trips in one: perfect, sunny weather for outdoor adventures like hiking during the day, and stunning, sophisticated holiday light displays at night.

Where to Stay: Choose from upscale resorts in Scottsdale or stylish hotels in downtown Phoenix.

Sometimes, the warm weather destinations just won’t cut it, especially if you are looking for that winter wonderland feel. So, this section is for travellers who want to dive head-first into the holiday spirit. These are the cities and towns that go all-out for December, with millions of lights, Christmas markets, and an atmosphere of pure magic.

We’ve visited NYC many times, but there’s a specific energy in December. We grabbed hot chocolates and walked through the Bryant Park Winter Village, watching the ice skaters zip around the rink under the lights of the surrounding skyscrapers. It felt like being in the opening scene of a holiday movie. There is nothing like New York City at Christmas.

Why Visit in December: It is the quintessential American Christmas destination. From the iconic tree to the world-famous window displays, the entire city is on a different level of festive.

Where to Stay: Midtown is convenient for seeing the main holiday sights, but we also love the West Village for its cosy, neighbourhood feel.

We’d heard Leavenworth was a “Christmas Town,” but we weren’t prepared for the reality. We visited during the Village of Lights festival, and walking through the snow-covered Bavarian-style village while every single building was covered in over half a million lights… it’s not an exaggeration. It’s the closest we’ve ever felt to being inside a real-life snow globe.

Why Visit in December: The entire town transforms into a “Hallmark movie” Christmas village. It’s a full-immersion holiday experience with carolers, festive food, and incredible decorations.

Where to Stay: Book a Bavarian-style lodge or inn right in the village. You must book many months in advance for December.

We love Asheville, but visiting in December is all about the Biltmore Estate. We took the candlelight evening tour, and seeing the main banquet hall with its 35-foot tree, fireplaces roaring, and carolers singing… it felt like we’d stepped back in time into a Gilded Age Christmas party.

Why Visit in December: Christmas at Biltmore is one of the most iconic holiday events in the country. The city itself is a cosy mountain retreat, and the Blue Ridge Mountains are just beautiful with a dusting of snow.

Where to Stay: You can stay on the Biltmore Estate for the full experience or choose a boutique hotel downtown.

Here are the remaining destinations for the “Best Christmas Towns & Festive Cities” section, all written with unique, December-focused content.

We’ve visited a lot of Christmas markets, but visiting the one in Bethlehem, known as “Christmas City USA”, just felt right. We sipped hot cider and browsed the stalls in the old quarter, and you can feel the city’s 250+ years of Christmas tradition. The whole place is lit by the glow of a giant Moravian star on the hillside.

Why Visit in December: This is Christmas City USA. It was nicknamed this on Christmas Eve, 1741. It offers one of the most authentic and historic holiday experiences in the country, blending its Moravian heritage with a European-style Christkindlmarkt.

Where to Stay: Look for a hotel or inn in the historic downtown area to be close to the festivities.

Walking into Solvang in December felt like we’d been transported to a Danish village during its Julefest celebration. We spent the day exploring the half-timbered buildings, windmills, and bakeries, all decorated for the holidays. It’s such a unique and charming way to experience a winter getaway in the middle of California.

Why Visit in December: The town’s month-long “Julefest” (Yule-fest) celebration is in full swing. It’s a one-of-a-kind Danish-style Christmas with parades, markets, and, of course, delicious European pastries.

Where to Stay: Choose one of the charming Danish-themed inns right in the village to be in the middle of the Julefest activities.

We had to see the “Christmas Capital of Texas” for ourselves, and it did not disappoint. The entire historic Main Street is transformed. We loved seeing the vintage railroad, which becomes the “North Pole Express” for the month. They take the “Christmas Capital” title seriously; there are over 1,400 events in 40 days.

Why Visit in December: It is the officially designated “Christmas Capital of Texas”. The sheer number of festive events, light displays, and activities is staggering, making it a top-tier destination for families and holiday lovers.

Where to Stay: The Gaylord Texan Resort is an attraction in itself, or you can stay near the Historic Main Street to be close to the events.

A New Orleans Christmas is an experience all its own. We did a “Reveillon Dinner,” a modern take on a Creole holiday tradition, and it was one of the most memorable meals we’ve ever had. Afterwards, we walked to Jackson Square to see the St. Louis Cathedral all lit up while carolers sang.

Why Visit in December: You get to experience unique Creole Christmas traditions you won’t find anywhere else. The weather is mild, the food is incredible, and the city’s lobbies (like at The Roosevelt) have some of the most elegant decorations we’ve seen.

Where to Stay: We recommend a hotel in the French Quarter to be in the middle of the action and see the decorated lobbies.

We went to Natchitoches (pronounced Nak-a-tish) specifically for its Christmas Festival, and it was a total joy. It’s one of the oldest and biggest in the country. The whole city, which is the oldest in Louisiana, lights up with over 300,000 lights along the Cane River, and the weekly fireworks shows are fantastic.

Why Visit in December: It hosts one of the oldest and most celebrated holiday festivals in the US, running for six weeks. It’s a classic, Southern Christmas experience in a beautiful historic district.

Where to Stay: Book a room at a historic bed & breakfast in the downtown area.

Visiting Colonial Williamsburg in December felt like walking through a living history Christmas card. We joined a candlelight tour, and seeing the historic buildings lit by real candles in the windows, with carolers in period costumes and the smell of woodsmoke in the air… it was absolutely magical.

Why Visit in December: You get to experience a traditional, 18th-century “Colonial Christmas”. The decorations are all-natural (no plastic lights), and the atmosphere is incredibly authentic and charming.

Where to Stay: Stay in one of the historic Colonial Houses or a tavern right in the restored area for the full immersive experience.

Here is the final category of destinations. This section is all about embracing the snow and finding that perfect winter wonderland.

For many, holiday season travel is all about finding that perfect, snowy scene. These are the places to go for world-class skiing, cosy lodges, and that magical feeling of a true winter escape.

We’ll always remember our first “après-ski” in Aspen. We had spent the day on the mountain hitting fresh powder whenever we got the chance, and as the sun went down, the sky lit up with this incredible pink and orange light they call “Aspenglow.” Sitting by a fire, enjoying a glass of Christmas cheer, and watching the snow fall on the historic town, it just felt like the peak of a luxury winter trip.

Why Visit in December: It’s one of the world’s most famous upscale ski destinations, and the town is just as much an attraction as the mountains. The festive atmosphere, high-end shops, and restaurants are all decked out for the holidays.

Where to Stay: Aspen is known for its luxury hotels and ski-in/ski-out resorts.

One of our favourite things about Park City is its history. We loved skiing down to the historic Main Street, popping off our skis, and walking straight into a saloon that’s been there since the silver mining days. It feels like a real Western town, not just a ski resort.

Why Visit in December: It’s a historic mountain town with two world-class ski resorts (Park City and Deer Valley). The historic Main Street is incredibly charming, and the “Snow Globe Stroll” features life-sized snow globes you can walk through.

Where to Stay: You can find ski-in/ski-out hotels or stay at an inn on the historic Main Street.

Jackson Hole in December is just dramatic. We took a sleigh ride through the National Elk Refuge, and seeing thousands of elk gathered against the backdrop of the snow-covered Teton mountains… it was a powerful and wild winter experience we’ve never forgotten.

Why Visit in December: It’s the perfect mix of rugged “cowboy Christmas” charm and some of the most challenging ski terrain in North America. The town square, with its famous antler arches, is beautifully lit for the holidays.

Where to Stay: Stay at a slopeside resort in Teton Village or in a hotel in the town of Jackson.

We love Whitefish because it feels like a real, down-to-earth ski town. We spent a day snowshoeing in nearby Glacier National Park, enjoying the total silence and incredible snowy landscapes, and then came back to town for a casual dinner. It’s all the beauty, without the glitz. Just what we were looking for in a winter vacation.

Why Visit in December: It’s a laid-back, charming mountain town with a top-rated ski resort and stunning scenery. It’s also right next to Glacier National Park, which is a spectacular place to explore in the winter.

Where to Stay: You can find lodges on the mountain or stay in one of the friendly inns in downtown Whitefish.

This was a trip purely for the fun of it, and it was 100% worth it. You drive down streets named “Santa Claus Lane” and “St. Nicholas Drive,” the streetlights are shaped like candy canes, and you can visit the Santa Claus House and see his reindeer. It’s a surreal and joyful experience.

Why Visit in December: It’s the ultimate Christmas fantasy come to life. The entire town is Christmas-themed, 365 days a year, but it’s most magical in December with real snow on the ground and the added bonus of possibly seeing the Northern Lights.

Where to Stay: North Pole is very small; most visitors stay in the nearby city of Fairbanks, which has a wide range of hotels.

For the best warm weather, your top choices are Southern Florida (like Key West), Hawaii (like Maui and Honolulu), and the desert Southwest (like Phoenix and Palm Springs). The U.S. Virgin Islands are also a fantastic passport-free tropical option.

Leavenworth, Washington, is often considered the ultimate “Christmas town” as it looks just like a Bavarian snow globe. Other top choices include Bethlehem, PA (known as “Christmas City USA”), Solvang, CA (for a Danish-style Julefest), and Grapevine, TX (the “Christmas Capital of Texas”).

Yes, but it depends on the park. It’s the perfect time to visit desert parks like Death Valley, Everglades, and Big Bend, where summer heat is unbearable. However, many mountain parks like Glacier, Yellowstone, and parts of Yosemite are mostly inaccessible due to heavy snow and road closures.

You are almost guaranteed to find snow in the mountain towns of the Rockies, like Aspen, CO, Park City, UT, and Jackson Hole, WY. You’ll also find snow in the Cascade Mountains (like Leavenworth, WA), Alaska, and the mountains around Lake Tahoe.

December is a magical month to travel. Whether you’re chasing the sun, seeking out that perfect snowy scene, or looking for a town that’s full of holiday magic, the US has the perfect spot for you.

We hope this list, based on our own winter travels, helps you plan your next getaway. Save this on Pinterest for your holiday planning! Where is your favourite place to go in December?

#6258. Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

FCC nominee Danielle Thumann Severs waits to testify during her confirmation hearing with the Senate Commerce Committee on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump's Republican nominee to the Federal Communications Commission faced opposition Tuesday from Senate Democrats who fear the commission could be controlled exclusively by Republicans under Chairman Brendan Carr, who they vowed to investigate in the next Congress.

Appearing before the Senate Commerce Committee, nominee Danielle Thumann Severs limited her commitments to independence from Carr, including on regulating broadcasters based on their content decisions.

Much of the hearing focused on Carr and his threats to use the FCC to punish broadcasters he disagrees with.

Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., said that he expects Carr will not last long in his position once Democrats take control of Congress in the new year.

“Mr. Carr, if you're listening now, know you're going to be in this body once a month, if not more, and in the House of Representatives as well, answering questions … so we can get to the bottom of the nonsense and the cover-ups that have been taking place,” Luján said.

The nomination of Thumann Severs, who currently serves as senior counsel to Carr, has led to consternation among Democrats due to continued vacancies at the FCC. The five-member commission is intended to have three members of the president’s party, including the chair, and two in the minority.

Currently Carr serves alongside fellow Republican Olivia Trusty and Democrat Anna M. Gomez, whose term expired earlier this year. Gomez may continue to serve through next year under the law if a replacement is not nominated and confirmed.

Democrats are concerned that if Thumann Severs were to be confirmed, the commission’s three Republican members could constitute a quorum on their own, allowing Trump to fire Gomez.

Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., said Senate precedent is to move pairs of one Democratic and one Republican nominee for the FCC and that he “strongly” believed the Thumann Severs nomination should have been paired with a renomination of Gomez in order to continue having “both parties at the table.”

“A bipartisan FCC is essential to avoid things like large-scale media consolidation [and] I think also, more fundamentally, to protect a free and diverse press [that] serves everyone,” Hickenlooper said.

In addition to urging Trump to renominate Gomez, Democrats underlined the need for a second Democratic member of the commission.

Hickenlooper highlighted Thumann Severs’ close work with Carr, who Democrats and some Republicans have been critical of for comments about using the FCC’s public interest standard against television stations airing programming Carr disagrees with.

Thumann Severs’ work at the FCC currently focuses on the Wireline, Public Safety and Homeland Security, and Consumer and Governmental Affairs bureaus, rather than the Media Bureau.

Committee Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, has also been critical of Carr’s comments. On Tuesday, he listed the FCC’s request for ABC-owned stations to submit early license renewals alongside earlier incidents in which he said Democrats encouraged the weaponization of the FCC against conservative voices.

“The First Amendment places important limits on the government’s ability to regulate speech,” Cruz said. “The FCC possesses significant regulatory authority over communications, so there is always a risk that it could weaponize its authority against Americans with whom it disagrees.”

Thumann Severs committed to Cruz that she would base licensing decisions on “the law and the record” and not use the FCC’s authority to “pressure or punish” broadcasters for protected speech.

However, when Sen. Edward J. Markey, D-Mass., questioned Thumann Severs on whether the FCC could punish broadcasters the president disagreed with, Thumann Severs repeated one of Carr’s arguments in discussing the FCC’s role.

“Broadcasters are subject to public interest obligations as part of the public trustee model in exchange for the licenses that they hold,” she said. “As part of those public interest obligations, they are subject to many different rules and requirements, and the FCC is charged with enforcing and investigating the public interest standard against broadcasters.”

Under repeated questions from Markey about Carr’s previous remarks, Thumann Severs said she would base her decisions “in the facts and the law and the record.”

Luján also asked Thumann Severs to name issues where she had disagreed with Carr or Trump. While she said her decisions would be her own, she declined to name any examples of disagreement.

In addition to questions about Carr, Democrats asked the nominee about the FCC’s E-Rate program, which provides low-cost connectivity for schools and libraries, and the Universal Service Fund, which funds the E-Rate program and other programs.

Thumann Severs said that she believes the E-Rate program has been successful and that the FCC has a statutory obligation to provide some kind of discounted service to schools and libraries. But she was less forthcoming on whether the FCC could shut down the program as it currently exists without congressional approval or whether the program should be restricted only to rural areas.

Late last month, Democratic members of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, led by Communications and Technology Subcommittee ranking member Doris Matsui, D-Calif., sent a letter to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and Cruz urging Gomez’s renomination with any move to confirm a Republican nominee.

“Commissioner Gomez has shown the experience and judgment to continue that work,” the members wrote. “We therefore ask that the Senate pair any new Republican nominee with her renomination to a full term, consistent with the bipartisan design Congress built into this agency.”

On Monday, the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights also sent a letter to committee leadership urging a delay on the hearing and any vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination until Gomez can be renominated.

“Independent agencies should not be extensions of presidential will: their leaders should exercise independent judgement based on their expertise and statutory mandates,” the group wrote.

Cruz did not indicate Tuesday when the committee might vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination, and no markup has yet been announced by the committee of hers' and those of three others for two posts at NASA and one at the Transportation Department who also testified.

Microsoft has doubled down on its Majorana 2 quantum computing platform despite pushback from the physics community, with DARPA researchers now set to evaluate the bold claims.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Microsoft scientists have doubled down on their controversial Majorana 2 quantum computing platform after encountering pushback for saying its "topological qubits" were powered by an enigmatic subatomic particle. In August of 2025, they said they would field a scalable, fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2033 — years ahead of schedule.

Now, after opening a new lab at the University of Maryland and partnering with the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) to conduct hardware validation, Microsoft has moved up this timeline to 2029.

The company's confidence is based on research suggesting that Majorana 2 represents a generational breakthrough in quantum computing. Scientists first announced that they had created this new qubit in a study published in the journal Nature in February 2025. Then, they followed up by announcing the Majorana 2 platform in a preprint study published this past June.

If verified, the prototype quantum processor would give Microsoft a commanding lead in the race to build a fault-tolerant, universal quantum computer, given that scientists said it can maintain a quantum state for much longer than alternative platforms. But some experts in the quantum physics community dispute the company's claims, suggesting that the qubit modality is highly experimental and had never been demonstrated in a working quantum computer prior to Microsoft's 2025 announcement.

Microsoft started its quantum computing program in 2005 after mathematician Michael Freedman convinced company leadership that conventional quantum architectures would eventually hit a brick wall. He advocated for a radical new approach to quantum computing based on a mathematical concept known as topological quantum field theory (TQFT). TQFT is a branch of theoretical physics and mathematics in which physical observables do not depend on local geometry (such as distances, curvature or angles) of space-time but rather on global topology.

Essentially, in TQFT, local geometry can change without disrupting qubits because its topology remains invariant. This feature of the theory is very attractive to hardware developers because it could yield qubits that are extremely resilient to disturbances such as atmospheric noise and perturbation. By contrast, conventional modalities, such as superconducting qubits, are perturbed pretty easily.

Microsoft subsequently built the first Majorana platform, named after theoretical physicist Ettore Majorana —who in 1937 hypothesized the existence of particles that act as their own antiparticles — to explore the use of TQFT in quantum computing.

If Microsoft's internal data holds up against DARPA's scrutiny, Freedman's theoretical bet may finally be paying off. According to internal research, Majorana 2 creates qubits that last between 20 seconds and a minute. By contrast, conventional qubits tend to last only microseconds.

In 2018, a research team that included Microsoft research scientist Roman Lutchyn published a study in the journal Nature Reviews Materials in which they claimed to have observed compelling evidence of Majorana "zero modes" — ostensibly demonstrating the existence of the theoretical Majorana quasiparticle.

However, when the data was released to reviewers in 2019, several noteworthy physicists raised objections centered on allegations of data trimming, confirmation bias and the potential misidentification of trivial electrical noise as exotic physics. That study was retracted in 2021, after the authors conceded that some of their methodology may have been flawed.

In the new study from June, Microsoft's claims were even bolder. The new study’s authors wrote that they observed physics indicating qubits built with the Majorana platform could last "orders of magnitude longer than typical qubit operation times."

The study was received with skepticism by many of the same critics of the 2018 research paper. The most common criticism, based on those that have been published, is that Microsoft researchers didn't operate a working qubit but instead tracked how long an electron state sits undisturbed before a stray charge flips its parity. The critics noted that measuring an electron's parity state isn't analogous to measuring a qubit's reliability.

Alex Khan, vice president of quantum research and development at physics acceleration firm BQP and a fellow at the University of Maryland QLab, dismissed much of the ballyhoo surrounding the Majorana research papers, comparing nascent quantum computing efforts such as Microsoft's to the Wright brothers' early airplane trials: There were only a few people there, and the aircraft went just a short distance. "And you could have had a lot of people sitting there saying, 'You know, this is never going to really do anything’,'" Khan, who wasn't involved in the Majorana 2 research, told Live Science.

When it comes to quantum computing breakthroughs, he took a more utilitarian view. "I've used a lot of quantum computers, but in order for me to use a quantum computer, it needs to be available," he said. "My most important thing is, can I have access to the computer? What kind of algorithms can I run on it? What can I test or what can I benchmark? What kind of capability will this provide? And does it begin to show some of the quantum advantage that's coming out of the quantum computer versus a simulator?"

Determining whether Microsoft or its critics are correct isn't as simple as running the team's experiments on another system. Microsoft is building Majorana 2 from scratch, one engineering feat at a time, Zulfi Alam, corporate vice president of Azure Quantum at Microsoft, told Live Science in an interview.

"The secret sauce is that we build our devices atom by atom, and that reduces disorder dramatically," Alam said.

Despite the back-and-forth between Microsoft and its critics, the question of whether the company has leapfrogged its competitors on the journey to build fault-tolerant, useful machines remains.

But with the topological qubits, they might know how to read the topological state, but then the question is, what are they reading? Also, is it able to store quantum information? Is it able to build a quantum state?

The U.S. government might be able to validate Microsoft's claims. The company will be included in DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative, which seeks to determine whether it's possible to build an industrially useful quantum computer by 2033. From now until 2029, the government will evaluate Majorana and Microsoft’s timeline to establish a framework for testing quantum computing claims.

In support of this endeavor, Microsoft is building a quantum computing lab at the University of Maryland so DARPA researchers can conduct their own hands-on evaluation of the hardware.

Khan described the partnership as "exciting," adding that he hopes DARPA can help determine the system's capabilities. "The physics is already known now," he said. "But with the topological qubits, they might know how to read the topological state, but then the question is, what are they reading? Also, is it able to store quantum information? Is it able to build a quantum state?"

If DARPA validates the biggest Majorana 2 claims, not only will Microsoft be vindicated, but the QBI team will have demonstrated their capabilities at the furthest frontiers of quantum computing research.

Alam said Microsoft is looking forward to the challenge. He described the shift in focus from theoretical science to "productizing" results as a focusing mechanism. DARPA has a team of about 50 engineers who are looking at the results and operating the machine at the University of Maryland, he noted.

"We have this deliverable for DARPA, and every six months or so, we have these massive deliverable dumps that we are giving to them," Alam said. "They know everything about our program."

Essentially, Microsoft's claims indicate that Majorana 2 solves most of quantum computing's biggest bottlenecks.

Designing reliable qubits is often cited as quantum computing's greatest challenge — and to solve problems at the edges of cryptography, chemistry and physics, we'll need quantum computers capable of fielding millions of qubits.

The first bottleneck is hardware. Scaling current systems such as those developed by IBM, Google and other quantum hardware labs requires scaling infrastructure in lockstep. Superconducting and spin qubits, for example, both need dedicated analog microwave lines for each physical qubit. This equates to millions of physical cables per computer.

If Majorana 2 works as Microsoft scientists claim, the cable problem goes away because its qubits can be controlled digitally via an integrated processor core that needs only a few connecting wires.

The next bottleneck that Majorana 2 solves is the massive qubit counts required to conduct useful calculations. Majorana 2 purportedly produces exponentially more reliable qubits than other platforms do, which promises a dramatic reduction in the number of error-correcting qubits needed to run a stable quantum computing system.

As Alam put it: "Our own internal teams thought we would need 16 million qubits to look at Shor's algorithm.” This is in reference to a commonly used encryption algorithm that it’s believed would take a classical computer years to crack while a sufficiently powerful quantum system is hypothesized to reduce that time to months or even hours.

"Since then," he added, "we have been able to publicly refine our estimates and think that we need more like 600,000 to 400,000 qubits."

Joseph Kearney, chief strategy officer and post-quantum cryptographer at Quantum Future in the U.K. who was not involved in the research, said that, if verified, Microsoft's Majorana 2 would revolutionize the field of quantum computing and shorten the timelines for quantum advantage in complex fields of study by years.

"If Microsoft had genuinely solved error correction, the 2035 deadline would no longer be credible,” he told Live Science in an email. "A breakthrough of this kind would remove our warning period, the clock is already running. Data intercepted today can be decrypted in the future, and Microsoft's claims, if they hold, would bring that future considerably closer than most organizations have planned for."

#6255. How a Screen-Free Retreat in South Africa’s Cederberg Rewired My Nervous System

As the sun dropped behind craggy peaks, the heat-baked sandstone dissolved into a deep twilight, and the silence thickened until the valley became a dark amphitheater. I had come to Bliss & Stars, an off-grid retreat perched above the Doring River deep in South Africa's Cederberg, for Orion's Odyssey, a program timed to the new moon, when the sky is at its darkest. As we neared midnight, the Milky Way's galactic core rose above the ridge, so dense and richly textured, it looked like the luminous, flowing reflection of the river below.

My phone had lost signal hours earlier, somewhere on the winding, vertiginous drive into this private reserve of over 3,300 acres. Initially, I had found that confronting, until I made peace with what I stood to gain. The eye needs around 20 minutes of true darkness to adjust, and a single glance at a bright screen largely undoes it. Without a signal, I had no reason to look down at it. It was just a camera.

Cradled by ancient rock, Weaver’s Nest is a villa for two above the Doring River.

That encompassing darkness is what brought Heine Rasmussen, an astronomy and nature guide and science communicator, and his wife Daria, a meditation teacher and somatic practitioner, here. In 2018, they left behind the security of corporate life in Copenhagen for a quest to find the least light-polluted skies. After searching around the world, they found them in the Cederberg, just over four hours north of Cape Town.

They acquired the virtually untouched land in 2019, and first had to construct a rudimentary access road before they could start building the lodge. Everything came in by pickup truck and trailer, and was carried by hand for the last stretch. The chalets were wedged between boulders or into the rock face above the river. More recently, the couple added a villa, bringing the total to six units that can accomodate no more than 10 guests.

On these monthly, stargazing-centered retreats, the nights belong to Heine. After dinner each evening, we gathered on a circular, open-air viewing deck in front of the observatory, where mattresses were laid out so we could lie flat and look straight up. One night Heine led us on what he calls "a little mental space walk," a star meditation designed to unground rather than ground us, during which he recounted the history of the universe. With our eyes closed, we breathed the night in through the nose and out through the mouth while he invited the city's stress to leave with each exhalation, until gravity seemed to loosen its grip and our arms and legs felt as if they might float. Falling asleep, he assured us, was perfectly fine.

After a night of stargazing, morning breathwork and yoga with Daria help put life into perspective.

The Cederberg's sandstone boulders have been sculpted by wind and water over aeons.

At the 20-inch telescope, one of the largest privately owned in South Africa, he taught us without jargon, finding a nebula and talking our small group through it while we took turns peering into the eyepiece. Guests here range from billionaires seeking quiet to people who come for free on the lodge's bursary program, and all of them arrive curious, looking for purpose, or simply to disconnect from the world they’ve left behind.

Heine's first subject: time. Moonlight, he told us, reaches us about a second after leaving the moon; sunlight about eight minutes after leaving the sun. The two pale patches in the southern sky, the Magellanic Clouds, are satellite galaxies of our own, and their light set out more than 160,000 years ago, when our species was young and still almost entirely in Africa. From there he moved to the iron in our blood and the calcium in our bones, forged in stars that exploded before our sun ever existed. I had heard the stardust line many times in other remote locales but never within the context of physics, explained step by step, or woven into a meditation under a sky like this one.

Daria took care of the mornings, which began with a thick, warm ceremonial cacao, readying the nervous system for what was to follow. I missed my regular wake-up coffee, the richness of the chocolatey cacao not compensating for the familiar kick of caffeine. From there, we headed to our yoga mats in an open-air studio where Daria led us in somatic breathwork, referencing the enormity of the night sky. Her view is that star-studded skies like those the Cederberg reliably delivers do not make daily concerns disappear; they merely change their size, put them into perspective. Much of what she imparts during the morning breathwork sessions is about making room to allow yourself to feel that. Daria works with the stress the body becomes so good at absorbing—shallow breaths and a clenched jaw, in my case. From hysterical laughter to sobs of grief, more surfaced for our small circle than any of us had bargained for.

The Cederberg has some of the darkest skies on earth.

After brunch, we hiked narrow paths where Cape mountain leopard tracks were pressed into the sand and raptors like Verreaux's eagles and rock kestrels caught thermals overhead. We scrambled over the orange sandstone rock, carved into fantastical shapes piled like giant, irregular building blocks, before washing off the dust and dry heat in the Doring River, the water surprisingly cool even though it was the end of summer. In the overhangs we marveled at San rock paintings between 2,000 and 5,000 years old, a collection of sites which Heine and Daria are still discovering on their land. There are more than 2,500 known rock art sites in the wider Cederberg, and whenever I see them I can't help thinking that the people who left their mark here once stood in this same silence, under much the same stars.

Every plant-based meal is consciously plated to nourish body, mind, and spirit.

With so much of the day spent on the move, in silence or alone, meals at the long wooden table in the lodge's open-plan kitchen became the social high point. With caffeine, refined sugar, meat, and alcohol off the menu, dining still felt indulgent despite being based on vegetables, fruit, and whole grains. Daria has little patience for the guilt and pressure so often associated with clean-eating dogma; in the retreat's cookbook, Eat, Thrive, Repeat, she writes about reaching the point where "appetite becomes information rather than judgment." In practice, that meant buddha bowls, ancient grain salads, roasted vegetables, and sweet treats at brunch like beetroot flapjacks with a miso caramel of dates and coconut oil.

One night, after hiking into the sunset and a surprise dinner in a cave, Heine gave an informal introduction to one of his passions, astrophotography. I learned how to hold a shutter open long enough to gather light the eye cannot. I stood still in the pitch black with a torch under my chin and came away with a portrait of myself against thousands of stars, the camera collecting photons that had been traveling for centuries, some for millennia, before they reached its sensor.

As you fall asleep, the night sky is framed in floor-to-ceiling glass.

On the final night, the telescope and the table worked in tandem. Dinner with Stars ran to six courses, eaten between turns at the eyepiece, and, read in order, the menu told the life story of the universe much as Heine had been telling it to us since we arrived—from Big Bang, a baked carrot dish, through to The White Dwarf, a wild strawberry dessert named for the small, dense ember a star like our sun leaves behind when it dies. The carbon on my fork was made inside stars that died before our sun existed, scattered into space, swept into the cloud of gas and dust that became our solar system, and pulled from the air, eventually, by the carrots on my plate.

Because it was summer and we had to wait for the sky to turn inky black, nights ended well past midnight. Back in my chalet, on a bed stuffed with horsehair, seaweed, and coconut fiber, I sipped from a flask filled with locally grown rooibos sweetened with wildflower honey before drifting off to sleep. The chalet's floor-to-ceiling windows face east over the river and are free of curtains to encourage waking with the morning light—a gentle but powerful way to reset one's circadian rhythm. When I opened my eyes in the small hours, the night sky filled the glass. I had never seen it framed like that.

Running year-round except July in South Africa's Cederberg, Bliss & Stars hosts intimate, all-inclusive retreats in six off-grid units sleeping a maximum of 10 guests.
