#6188. Review: United Airlines 737 MAX 8 Economy Class Newark To Nuuk, Greenland

My United Airlines flight from Newark to Nuuk, Greenland featured a friendly crew, two meal services, and a spectacular approach onboard a Boeing 737 MAX 8 in economy class. Economy Plus was perfectly comfortable for the four-hour daytime journey, though the flight became much fuller than I had expected thanks to a large contingent of United employees taking advantage of their travel benefits.

Greenland had been on my bucket list for years, and United’s nonstop service from Newark offered an opportunity to finally visit. I was heading back to Germany to pick up my children after their summer visit with family and decided to take a rather scenic route via Nuuk and Copenhagen.

I had already traveled from Palm Springs through San Francisco and Denver to reach Newark. By the time I boarded this flight, I was tired…but very excited about what lay ahead.

I booked the entire United itinerary from Palm Springs to Nuuk using 40,000 Air Canada Aeroplan points, plus $5.60 in government taxes and the CAD39 partner booking fee.

A cash ticket for the itinerary was about $1,600, so I was pleased to use miles instead. The premium cabin on the Greenland flight, marketed as Premium Plus, was sold out when I booked (and I don’t mean no saver partner award space, but sold out completely).

My overnight flight from Denver arrived at the A Gates, and the Nuuk flight would depart from the same terminal.

There was a United Club nearby, but I wanted a shower and barista-made coffee, so I took the airside shuttle bus to Terminal C and visited the United Club near gate C123. I wrote separately about that visit. There was no wait for a shower, and although I would have preferred hotter water and stronger pressure, it was refreshing to clean up after the redeye.

An illy double-shot cappuccino helped too. I had breakfast, got some work done, and then returned by bus to the A Gates about 30 minutes before boarding.

This turned out to be a much more energetic flight than I expected.

The night before departure, the flight appeared less than half full. By the time we pushed back a few minutes late, it was much closer to capacity, with a large number of United employees traveling on standby.

I initially had an Economy Plus row to myself, but two jovial United employees joined me. They were heading to Greenland for just one night. As I explained in my first impressions of the flight, several employees described arriving in Nuuk, exploring town, taking a twilight boat excursion, and visiting a bar before returning to the airport for the morning flight back to Newark.

That sounded absolutely exhausting to me, but I understood the appeal. If I had those travel benefits, I would certainly be tempted to use them on a route like this! There was certainly a festive atmosphere onboard, and I enjoyed hearing how others planned to spend their short time in Greenland.

Boarding was delayed 20 minutes, but it was finally time to step onboard.

I was warmly greeted by Craig, the purser, as I boarded. More on him below.

United’s 737 MAX 8 features 150 seats one economy class in a 3-3 configuration. Seats are Collins Meridian slimline seats and feature an adjustable headrest and seatback screens. Legroom is 30 inches (34 inches in Economy Plus), the seat is 17 inches wide, and seats recline two inches.

I selected a window seat on the left side of the aircraft in Economy Plus.

There are individual air nozzles onboard as well as seatback power (A/C under the seat and both USB-A and USB-C under the screen).

The window seat on the A side proved an excellent choice during our approach, though the best side will depend on which direction the aircraft lands, which will depend on the winds.

Despite a flight time of only about four hours, there were two services during the flight.

I had ordered United’s “balanced diet” special meal, which consisted of chicken pieces in tomato sauce accompanied by a side salad, bread roll, and “That’s It” fruit snack for dessert. It was not exactly gourmet, but it did the job and I had some club soda to drink with it.

The regular choices for passengers were pasta or beef. Is the diet meal worth ordering?

As we approached Nuuk, I received an Indian vegetarian wrap (other passengers received a pizza pocket). It was not necessary for such a short flight, but appreciated nevertheless. I enjoyed a cup of illy coffee as well.

United’s seatback screens feature a deep content of movies and TV shows with a handful of game and audio options. The same library of content was also available via streaming to your own device.

Complimentary earphones were provided, though you could pair your own device to these screens, which I did.

The flight featured Viasat Wi-Fi, available for purchase for $10 ($8 for MileagePlus members) and it worked well over the Atlantic.

United’s 737 MAX 8 has one lavatory in the front for premium cabin passengers and two in the back for economy class, which is not a great proportion.

The purser, Craig, was a highlight of the flight.

Apparently, he worked nearly every Nuuk flight that summer and has become something of an institution on the route. He was friendly, professional, and knowledgeable, making his way through the cabin and chatting with passengers.

We had a nice conversation about restaurant recommendations in Nuuk. I appreciated speaking with someone who knew the destination and could offer advice before I arrived. What a fun assignment to spend the summer flying to Greenland!

A good crew can make an ordinary flight enjoyable, and Craig helped make this unusual route feel even more special. Between the enthusiastic employee travelers and his warm welcome, the mood onboard was very pleasant.

I had chosen an “A” window seat on the port side, which gave me a northerly view during our final approach. Aircraft can arrive from the opposite direction depending on the wind, so the view will vary, but I was very happy with my choice.

As we descended below the clouds, tundra and floating ice came into view. Then the sun broke through, revealing the mountainous landscape around Nuuk.

I have flown over Greenland many times, looking down from cruising altitude and wondering what it would be like to visit. Seeing it from this perspective, knowing I would soon be on the ground, was quite different.

Some of the mountains still held snow, and the landscape looked rugged and sparsely populated. It was majestic.

I shared more photographs in my earlier post about the approach. My arrival in the Faroe Islands a couple of years earlier may have been even more scenic, but this was nevertheless a wonderful welcome to Greenland.

This is a flight where I would strongly recommend a window seat.

We landed at 7:08 pm local time under clear skies and taxied to a parking position outside the terminal.

Air Greenland-branded stairs were brought to the aircraft, and we walked down onto the apron. It was about 55ºF outside…crisp, clear, and beautiful.

After the long journey from Southern California, I was finally in Greenland.

Next came immigration, which turned out to be a story of its own.

> Read More: My Longest EES Immigration Wait Yet Was In Tiny Nuuk, Greenland

This was such a fun flight. Economy Plus was comfortable for the relatively short daytime journey, Craig provided excellent service, and the atmosphere onboard was cheerful…it almost felt like an inaugural flight. The approach into Nuuk was the highlight and made me very glad I had selected a window seat on the A side (though again, I was fortunate because the approaches change based on prevailing wind conditions).

Getting to Newark had required several flights and an overnight journey from Denver, but this final segment was a pleasure. I was thrilled to finally reach Greenland and appreciated being able to do so on United.

Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

Was the safety video dubbing in Danish or Greenlandic?

A 4+45 hour flight and you received two meals, well at least one plus a nice snack, yet on a 6 hour domestic transcon, you receive two passes of the Biscoff or pretzels. Just crazy. Now that the domestic airlines are making billions per quarter, you would think that one of them could start increasing service again, but I guess that will never happen.

#6187. Avianca Adds New U.S. Route

Colombian flag carrier Avianca is adding a new connection to the U.S. Northeast.

Starting Feb. 2, 2027, the airline will offer service between Barranquilla and New York-JFK.

Flights will operate four times weekly using Airbus A320-family aircraft, each with up to 180 seats.

“The launch of this nonstop route to New York reaffirms our commitment to [Barranquilla] and the entire Colombian Caribbean region,” Avianca President Gabriel Oliva said in a statement. “We want to continue connecting regions with major international markets, making travel easier, supporting tourism, and contributing to Colombia’s economic development.”

Avianca currently serves JFK from Bogota, Cartagena, Medellín, Pereira, Colombia, Guatemala City, San Salvador, El Salvador, Quito, and Guayaquil. From Barranquilla, it flies to Miami, Bogota, Medellín, and Cali.

#6185. ICAO Hosts Air Transport Conference, Elects New Council Members

Last week, ICAO headquarters in Montréal hosted the Seventh Worldwide Air Transport Conference, where member states and industry stakeholders gathered to set global policy priorities on aviation economic regulation, infrastructure financing, resilience, consumer protection, and sustainable growth.

Over 1,500 delegates from 154 member states and organizations attended the week-long event 13 years after the Sixth Conference in 2013. They discussed high-level topics in commercial aviation: modernizing economic and legal frameworks, investing in infrastructure and skilled workforces, and ensuring that innovation keeps pace with rapidly changing technologies and global demands.

“Broad agreement was reached on the need for harmonized, risk-based, and proportionate economic regulation that facilitates the adoption of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, automation, sustainable aviation fuels, and advanced air mobility solutions,” ICAO said in a press release during the conference.

Participants agreed on the value of frameworks that support innovation and investment for economic development. They stressed this especially for smaller landlocked states, which depend heavily on air connectivity for growth.

The conference supported modernizing air navigation infrastructure in line with ICAO’s Global Air Navigation Plan. It also supported liberalizing air service agreements without making liberalization conditional on infrastructure development, since new air links fostered by more liberal agreements are seen as key to economic growth.

However, all initiatives should be flexible enough to address local circumstances and should not burden developing states. ICAO’s statement continued: “The conference also reaffirmed that international standards are key to building effective, market-enabling policies and avoiding fragmentation that could impede cross-border air services. Delegates pointed to ICAO’s Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) as a successful example of this approach.”

Participants were asked to express their views on consumer protection legislation that has become an integral part of the legal framework for all air operators.

At the Sixth Worldwide Air Transport Conference in March 2013, ICAO was asked to develop core principles on consumer protection. The final document, adopted by the ICAO Council in 2015, contains provisions on:

The report for the Seventh Conference invites states to modernize their consumer protection frameworks, keeping them evidence-based, proportionate, accessible, and responsive to the changing realities of commercial air transport. It also says legislation should establish clear responsibilities for carriers, intermediaries, and other providers regarding information, complaints, and disruption assistance.

ICAO is expected to review its core principles while preserving national and regional flexibility. It is also expected to assess whether existing policies adequately cover online intermediaries and other overlooked situations.

Many member states cautioned against the ICAO Air Passenger Handbook proposed by IATA, because producing and maintaining a single repository covering many different national laws would be too costly.

The conference asked ICAO to “examine the need for harmonized, risk-based guidance on the use of AI in aviation, including common terminology and meaningful human oversight.”

The rapid development of AI and its unknown effects on aviation operations is a topic member states will need to monitor. ICAO will coordinate and facilitate international exchange, while states will oversee implementation to ensure that the technologies adopted are secure, interoperable, and consistent with cybersecurity and data-protection objectives.

ICAO will handle AI within its existing structure, as the proposal to create an ad hoc unit was not supported.

During the final two days of the conference, ICAO held an extraordinary session of its assembly to elect the four additional council members required by the entry into force of the 2013 protocol amending the Convention on International Civil Aviation. The council is the organization’s permanent governing body, accountable to the assembly and responsible for setting priorities and implementing its directions. Its membership increased from 36 to 40, and there are no permanent seats.

Six candidates competed for the four new seats: Ethiopia, Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Oman, Thailand, and Turkey. In the vote on the final day, Kazakhstan and Thailand were not elected, and the other four states won seats.

The council now comprises Angola, Argentina, Australia, Belize, Brazil, Canada, China, Colombia, Cuba, Denmark, Ecuador, Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Ethiopia, France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Italy, Japan, Malaysia, Mali, Mexico, Morocco, Nigeria, Oman, Poland, Qatar, the Republic of Korea, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, South Africa, Spain, Switzerland, Turkey, Uganda, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, the U.S., and Uruguay.

The next elections will take place at the General Assembly in September 2028.

Quark Expeditions' Ultramarine sailing in the Arctic

#6180. Bipartisan process for picking GAO chief breaks down

Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept. 23. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.

Sources said Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who currently serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget. The White House submitted ethics paperwork on Ueland — required for nominations — to the GAO, according to a source.

Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Thursday posted notice of a committee hearing Nov. 19 to examine more than a dozen presidential nominees for executive and judicial offices, including “a nominee to be Comptroller General.”

The post identifies by name all of the nominees except the candidate for comptroller general. The post has been filled by an acting comptroller general, Orice Williams Brown, since Gene L. Dodaro completed his 15-year term at the end of last year.

The move by Paul to short-circuit the convening of a legislative commission to recommend candidates infuriated top Democrats, who excoriated the chairman in a joint statement Wednesday night. A special bipartisan, bicameral legislative commission is supposed to recommend at least three candidates for comptroller general to the president, according to statute.

Homeland Security Committee GOP staff solicited recommendations for a comptroller general from some Democratic congressional offices Wednesday afternoon, imposing a deadline of 8 a.m. Thursday, according to Democratic aides.

The president nominates the head of the GAO, the investigative arm of Congress, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

Paul pushed back on the criticism Thursday, saying, “Democrats have known about this for months and months and months.” He said the last time the special commission made recommendations for the office, when Barack Obama was president, “Democrats submitted their own list, Republicans submitted their own list. So they can complain all they want but they just need to make their list and submit it.”

In the past, however, the special commission convened, sought applications for the position, interviewed candidates and deliberated before sending recommendations to the president.

A 1980 law states that when there is a vacancy in the comptroller general position, “there is established a commission to recommend individuals to the President for appointment to the vacant office,” and that the commission must submit at least three names.

Under the statute, the commission includes the speaker, Senate majority and minority leaders, House majority and minority leaders, chairs and ranking members of the Senate Homeland Security and House Oversight and Government Reform committees, and the Senate president pro tempore.

In 1981, for example, after the law took effect, the two congressional leaders, Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill Jr., D-Mass., and Senate Majority Leader Howard H. Baker, R-Tenn., sent a letter to President Ronald Reagan saying the special commission had met and voted to recommend eight candidates to succeed Comptroller General Elmer Staats.

“The members of the Commission have taken their statutory responsibility seriously,” they wrote.

Reagan nominated Charles A. Bowsher, who was on the list, and he was confirmed.

After Bowsher’s term ended in 1996, the commission eventually formed, interviewed multiple candidates, and deliberated for several months. Republicans controlled both chambers, and Bill Clinton was president. The members of the commission could not reach agreement, and as a result, the Republicans on the committee submitted their list to Clinton, and the Democrats on the panel submitted theirs.

Clinton also had his own list. Clinton nominated David M. Walker, who was on all three lists, and he was confirmed by the Senate more than two years after Bowsher’s departure. Walker argued Thursday against short-circuiting the commission process.

“The position is of critical importance and the related statutory Commission process should not be circumvented," Walker said. "Doing so would undercut the credibility of the person and the effectiveness of the GAO.”

Walker resigned in March of 2008, when George W. Bush was still president. He appointed Dodaro as acting comptroller general when he left. The commission got going several months later, creating a website with application instructions and candidate questions.

Over the next two years, the commission interviewed some 20 candidates. Democrats and Republicans on the panel were unable to reach agreement, and Democrats, who had a majority on the commission, submitted their own list to Obama in 2010. Republicans followed up with their list.

“The Commission has been working in earnest on this undertaking for more than one year and has dedicated considerable time and effort to present you with highly qualified candidates for this important position,” then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., along with other Democratic leaders, wrote to Obama when they submitted the Democrats’ list.

The Democrats’ move drew a rebuke from Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who was ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the time.

Collins said in a statement she was “extremely disappointed” that Democrats “abruptly ended the selection process for the next Comptroller General without a bipartisan agreement” on the recommendations. “We have had several exceptionally qualified individuals apply to be the next leader of the GAO, and it should have been possible to come up with a consensus list.”

Obama nominated and the Senate confirmed Dodaro, who was one of four recommendations from the Democrats.

Mendocino, a small coastal town in northern California, has welcomed its first points property. The nearly 50-year-old Hill House hotel was renovated and reopened in June 2026 as Hill House at Trailborn Mendocino, Outdoor Collection by Marriott Bonvoy — making it the first and only member of a major hotel loyalty program in Mendocino proper. (The closest options are members of IHG One Rewards and Wyndham Rewards in neighboring Fort Bragg.)

The Mendocino Coast region is known for its charming small-town vibes, natural beauty and outdoor pursuits, so the Trailborn brand’s laidback nature lodge concept fits in here like a seal in nearby Mendocino Bay. I stayed three nights in late October to get a first look at the property (and the town, which is on TPG’s 2027 Where to Go list).

Nestled just a few minutes’ walk outside downtown Mendocino, Hill House at Trailborn Mendocino’s unassuming two-story buildings fit right in with the surrounding hotel scene. The design is inspired by nature — specifically, the redwood forests and tide pools of the surrounding Mendocino Coast — while still feeling modern and polished.

The grounds are bursting with native plants, many of them still in bloom when I visited in late October. Botanical art prints and zoological illustrations on the walls give a nod to the great outdoors, and curious guests can lose themselves in the lobby’s curiosity cabinet, a revamped relic of the original building. Visitors are encouraged to sign the guestbook with a stamp of a dried leaf or flower.

The hotel offers just 44 accommodations — relatively large for a Mendocino property — including 14 double queen rooms, 25 king rooms and 5 junior suites. Within each room type, travelers can choose to upgrade to features such as a balcony or deck, an ocean view or both.

My room, a spacious King Junior Suite Ocean View, felt like a relaxing retreat with its muted color palette of greens, browns and yellows and its cozy linen spa robes. After a day of exploring Mendocino, I enjoyed relaxing on the sofa, perusing the coffee table book Botanicum, and sampling locally made goodies from the snack basket and minibar (for a fee).

Trailborn Hill House has one on-site restaurant: Pizza Standard Time, a casual bar and diner offering mostly pizza, plus salads, charcuterie boards and small Italian bites like arancini. The fare was limited but tasty; my friend and I tried a pizza, salad, and local Husch chardonnay and were quite happy. It’s nice having a quick, casual meal available on-site in case you arrive late and tired from the drive, but it’s also just a few minutes’ walk to Mendocino if you want more options.

Like all Trailborn properties, this one offers a lobby convenience store called Hill House Wine & Grocer. Guests can purchase local drinks and snacks (mostly the kind you’d find on a charcuterie board), plus apparel, toys, candles with the property’s signature scent and other souvenirs.

The hotel also offered a small but delicious complimentary breakfast spread. As with everything else during my stay, the breakfast was high-quality yet unpretentious, with guests serving and bussing their own tables. Instead of having a designated breakfast area, guests can find a cozy spot to eat inside Pizza Standard Time or the attached Cabot Cove Detective Library, outside by one of the fire pits or back to their room.

However, this will change when Trailborn’s second Mendocino property, The Mendocino Hotel, opens in 2027. Instead of complimentary breakfast, Hill House plans to provide guests with a voucher to Moonwave, The Mendocino Hotel’s dining concept, which will serve “coastal comfort” food three meals a day plus drinks at the lobby bar.

If you didn’t realize you were in a small town, you will as soon as you interact with any of the hotel staff — everyone I spoke to, from front desk staff to custodians, was beyond friendly.

As for amenities, they align with the brand’s laid-back, outdoorsy style and with some of the things the Mendocino area is known for. You’ll find:

Located just a few minutes’ walk (or bike ride) from downtown Mendocino, Hill House at Trailborn puts guests in the heart of the town’s charming boutiques and varied dining and drinking scene. But you won’t get bored if you hang around the property, either.

Here are some of the on-site activities guests may want to try:

While Mendocino’s remoteness makes it a haven for crowd-weary travelers, it’s becoming easier than ever to reach thanks to recent roadwork funding and new direct flights to Charles M. Schulz–Sonoma County Airport (STS), including on Alaska Airlines, Delta and Southwest. That’s one reason Mendo made TPG’s 2027 Where to Go list.

But travelers can also fly into San Francisco International Airport (SFO), Oakland San Francisco Bay Airport (OAK) or Sacramento International Airport (SAC), which are a bit farther away but offer more flight options.

Depending on the airport you choose, you’ll need to rent a car and drive two to four hours to Mendocino.

Basic rooms start as low as $140 per night in the off-season, while my King Junior Suite Ocean View starts around $350 per night (though these prices can climb much higher on summer weekends). Award rates start at 48,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night, or you could redeem a 50,000-point free night certificate.

When booking, you’ll want to use one of the credit cards that earn the most points for Marriott stays, as well as one that possibly offers automatic Marriott Bonvoy elite status for value-added benefits. These include:

The information for the Marriott Bonvoy Bountiful card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Hill House has three wheelchair-accessible rooms, including two double queens and one king; these feature accessible tubs and, in some cases, roll-in showers. The property and its parking lot are also wheelchair accessible. For hearing-impaired guests, a portable kit can be installed in any room.

As a points traveler who loves Mendocino, I’m thrilled to see the town’s first points property not only opening but thriving. As a traveler who appreciates unique stays and has experienced some of the town’s charming independent properties, I’m also glad that Hill House at Trailborn Mendocino has brought enough character to fit seamlessly into the local scene.

It seems the Trailborn brand — and Marriott Bonvoy — is betting big on Mendocino. Hill House is one of two Mendocino properties purchased by The Trailborn brand. The second, the 150-year-old Mendocino Hotel, is undergoing renovation and slated to open in 2027.

#6177. Norse Atlantic Cancels All Flights, Will File For Bankruptcy

Just days after warning that its financial situation was “critical,” Norse Atlantic Airways appears to have reached the end of the line.

The low-cost carrier said Monday that its main Norwegian operating unit will file for bankruptcy. All flights were canceled, and ticket sales were discontinued.

Despite “extensive efforts,” the company was unable to secure financing to meet its short-term liquidity needs, officials said. The board of directors “concluded that there is no longer a basis for continued operations” for the Norwegian business.

A bankruptcy petition is expected to be filed Monday with Agder District Court in Norway.

Other parts of the company, including Norse Atlantic UK, could be restructured and continue operating, but no firm plans have been announced.

“We are deeply sorry for the impact this has on our passengers, employees, and partners,” CEO Eivind Roald said in a statement. “The board, management, and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the U.K. subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations.”

Norse Atlantic operated only long-haul international flights, connecting cities such as Oslo, New York, Stockholm, Rome, Cape Town, Orlando, Florida, and Phuket, Thailand. That business model became unsustainable as the war in Iran pushed jet fuel prices higher.

The carrier said earlier this year that it was contemplating a sale, but no partner was ever announced. On Wednesday, it warned that its financial situation was “critical,” and said short-term financing was needed immediately to keep operations going.

#6176. Trump’s ‘invasion’ asylum ban to face justices

The border wall is seen in 2021 stretching along the U.S.-Mexico border near Columbus, N.M. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.

The Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that held the president could not broadly deny asylum claims under federal law. The case is the latest high-profile fight over one of Trump’s signature domestic policies.

The administration argues in its petition for the justices to take the case that the president has broad authority over asylum claims, which includes shutting down the system entirely because he has decided he will not grant any.

“The proclamation thus lawfully suspends access to asylum, which is a purely discretionary benefit. The court of appeals’ insistence that aliens are entitled to file futile asylum applications elevates empty procedures over substance,” the petition says.

Trump issued the order on his first day in office, declaring an “invasion” on the southern border and using that as a reason to deny asylum claims by refugees who present themselves there. The order is still in place, preventing asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border while the lawsuit plays out.

In court filings asking the justices to take the case, the administration pointed to “dramatic” reductions in illegal border crossings, which freed up resources to combat human trafficking and other threats.

In Friday’s order, the justices agreed to hear arguments over the legality of Trump’s executive order as well as whether the lower-court judge could grant an order in favor of all asylum seekers rather than just the ones who brought the suit.

Immigration rights groups initially challenged the order and won a successful ruling from a federal judge in Washington. The administration later appealed to the D.C. Circuit, where it lost at a three-judge panel before it brought the case before the justices.

The D.C. Circuit held that although federal law provides a president discretion in denying asylum claims, he cannot do so categorically.

The ACLU and immigrant rights groups who brought the case defended the ruling in their own filing. The filing argues that Congress mandated the creation of the asylum system and the president “may not invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.”

Last term the justices ruled in favor of a separate policy dating to the first Trump administration that allowed officials to prevent asylum claims by stopping refugees from actually reaching the U.S. border.

A ruling in favor of the refugees could allow the administration to restart that policy and still deny asylum claims.

The case granted Friday is the latest high-profile immigration policy clash on the justices’ docket this term. Earlier this year the justices agreed to hear a challenge to the administration’s policy that most immigrants facing deportation should be detained without bond.

The justices will likely hear oral arguments and decide the case granted Friday before the end of the court’s term next June.

The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services.

#6175. Lawmakers Criticize FAA Deploying New “Untested” AI Tool Days Before Nationwide Grounding

A group of 24 Democratic lawmakers has criticized the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) for prematurely deploying a new artificial intelligence (AI) tool across US airspace. In a letter to FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford on Tuesday, the lawmakers accused the agency of expanding a largely untested system nationwide before completing its promised 90-day validation period.

The nationwide deployment of the Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories (SMART) system came just three days before a telecommunications failure brought US departures to a standstill. While the FAA has denied any connection between the two events, the controversy raises fresh questions about whether the Trump administration's ambitious air traffic control (ATC) modernization program is prioritizing the speed of implementation over adequate testing, safety oversight, and transparency.

Led by House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee Ranking Member Rick Larsen, the lawmakers allege that the FAA expanded the SMART system nationwide without notifying Congress in advance. The expansion came just 50 days after its initial deployment in the Washington area, despite the FAA previously outlining a 90-day validation period.

In their letter to Bedford, the lawmakers expressed frustration with the lack of supporting safety data.

“We have yet to receive any substantive information proving the system was properly validated before its nationwide expansion.”

Concerns surrounding SMART considerably predate the nationwide grounding. In September, the National Air Traffic Controllers Association (NATCA) told Flying Magazine that it had been excluded from the system's development, testing, and implementation. Lawmakers subsequently requested that the FAA suspend SMART operations and called for an independent Government Accountability Office (GAO) audit. More troublingly, the latest letter cites allegations that FAA employees who raised safety concerns about SMART's accelerated deployment may have faced retaliation.

SMART launches at three Washington-area airports

NATCA's exclusion from development and testing is reported

Lawmakers request suspension of SMART operations

Congressional request for an independent GAO audit

SMART expands to all 22 enroute control centers

24 House Democrats demand answers from FAA

FAA and DOT officials scheduled to testify before Congress

The lawmakers have presented the FAA with 13 questions, demanding details on its safety assessments, performance metrics, controller training, cybersecurity protections, and contingency plans if SMART experiences an outage. They also question why the agency prioritized deploying SMART over essential infrastructure upgrades, including radar replacements. Reuters reported that the FAA has declined to address the allegations publicly, saying it will respond directly to lawmakers.

Developed by Air Space Intelligence (ASI) under an $875 million, 12-year contract, SMART is designed to make the increasingly congested US airspace more efficient. The cloud-based technology consolidates approximately 200 data streams, encompassing weather forecasts, flight trajectories, airport capacity, and controller staffing. Its predictive capabilities allow aviation professionals to anticipate operational bottlenecks and identify alternative flight paths before disruptions materialize.

Importantly, SMART does not autonomously direct aircraft. FAA specialists at a dedicated center in Washington review its recommendations before forwarding them to the agency's Air Traffic Control System Command Center in Warrenton, Virginia. Human controllers retain ultimate operational authority. The technology is similar to ASI's Flyways AI platform, which Alaska Airlines began using in 2021 to help flight dispatchers optimize aircraft routing.

The potential commercial benefits are substantial, and United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, American Airlines, and Southwest Airlines have all expressed support for the initiative. According to the FAA, and as reported by Aerotime, SMART's initial deployment delivered measurable efficiency improvements, potentially translating into considerable fuel savings and fewer passenger disruptions when replicated nationally. However, lawmakers argue that evidence of improved operational efficiency cannot substitute for comprehensive safety validation.

There is little margin for error in air traffic control.

The concerns come amid the shock of the November 13 nationwide ground stop, which demonstrated the vulnerability of America's existing ATC infrastructure. The FAA's preliminary investigation identified a telecommunications failure, with excessive data traffic overwhelming legacy equipment following routine maintenance work. The resulting instability affected communications and radar feeds across much of the country. Both the FAA and ASI have explicitly denied that SMART contributed to the disruption.

Total flight cancellations on November 13

Cancellations across the wider disruption

The incident was the first nationwide ground stop since the January 2023 failure of the FAA's NOTAM system. A September 2026 GAO report highlighted significant shortcomings in the FAA's modernization cost estimates and scheduling. Previous research found that 105 of the agency's 138 ATC systems were either unsustainable or potentially unsustainable, illustrating the urgency of replacing aging infrastructure while maintaining the integrity of existing operations.

Congressional scrutiny is set to intensify next week, with Bedford expected to appear before a House panel on December 1 and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy scheduled to testify before the Senate on December 2. Duffy's request for approximately $50 billion in additional aviation infrastructure funding, including $600 million for strategic traffic flow management technologies such as SMART, already faces significant opposition. Securing that funding may increasingly depend on the FAA demonstrating that its accelerated modernization efforts are not compromising safety.

Contour Airlines is expanding its presence in the Southeast.

Contour officials said there is strong demand for Nashville service from Macon.

#6173. How Much Does A Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 Engine Cost?

Allora Empire Art | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Rolls-Royce does not publish list prices for the Trent 1000, so every figure quoted for the Dreamliner engine is an estimate, and the most commonly cited is about $20 million per engine. That number answers only part of the question, because transaction prices differ from list estimates and the expense that has defined this engine’s reputation arrives years after delivery in the form of shop visits and retrofit campaigns.

A better answer therefore separates three prices: what an engine is estimated to cost at list, what a documented order implies once its fine print is read, and what it costs to keep one flying. This article works through each, then examines how Rolls-Royce’s latest upgrade could change the ownership economics.

Simple Flying’s 2025 survey of commercial engines places the Trent 1000 at an estimated $20 million, which sits below the roughly $22 million it assigns to the rival GE GEnx and well below Rolls-Royce’s own Trent 7000 at $25 million and Trent XWB at $35 million. The Trent 1000 can reach 74,411 pounds of thrust (331 kN), and the Trent 7000’s thrust band falls within that limit as well, so thrust alone does not explain the price spread. SlashGear arrives at the same $20 million figure and describes an engine optimized for the Boeing 787, with a fan that produces about 85% of the engine’s total thrust.

These figures are best read as list-price approximations rather than transaction prices, since common estimates exclude discounts, bulk purchase pricing, and support contracts. For example, Singapore Airlines had an order for 62 GE9X engines with a list value of about $45 million per engine, including a 12-year service contract. For context, narrowbody engines are not necessarily cheaper once transactions replace estimates: Willis Lease Finance purchased 15 Pratt & Whitney PW1100 engines in 2024 for $363.9 million, about $24.3 million each, more than the Trent 1000 estimate.

The clearest official data point is a January 2018 announcement in which Rolls-Royce said lessor AerCap had ordered Trent 1000 engines to power 10 Boeing 787s, a deal valued at $450 million at list prices. Dividing by 20 engines yields $22.5 million apiece, the figure usually quoted, but the arithmetic depends on assumptions the announcement does not confirm: two engines per aircraft and no spares.

A footnote in the release adds a more significant caveat, since Rolls-Royce measures its order book at list prices and, for long-term aftermarket contracts, counts the revenue it expects to recognize within seven years of the announcement. The release does not say whether such revenue sits inside the $450 million, so the $22.5 million figure may blend hardware with service value and should be treated as an upper reference for the engine itself rather than a price tag. The footnote also cautions that an order’s stated value may not reflect future revenue.

Two other details bound the interpretation, since the order covered the TEN variant, which entered service in November 2017, and AerCap held options on five more aircraft outside the stated value. The TEN draws on Trent XWB and Advance technologies and helps the Dreamliner achieve 20% greater efficiency than the aircraft it replaces, according to Rolls-Royce. Rolls-Royce also notes that the Trent 1000 powered the first flight of every Dreamliner version, the 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10. Because list prices exclude negotiated discounts, the price AerCap actually paid is not disclosed in the announcement.

Tada Images | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Purchase price is only the entry fee, because Simple Flying reports that a single unscheduled shop visit can exceed $5 million once transport logistics, spare engine leasing, and teardown labor are counted. The same report says early Trent 1000s achieved time-on-wing intervals that were a fraction of the GEnx-1B benchmark of more than 20,000 operating hours before the first major shop visit, which made the interval the main driver of lifetime cost. Because the Trent 1000 is a three-shaft design built exclusively for the Dreamliner, its tooling, spare parts, and overhaul procedures are unique to it and are not shared with the GEnx fleet.

Many Rolls-Royce operators shield themselves from that volatility through TotalCare, a power-by-the-hour agreement in which the airline pays a fixed rate per flight hour and the manufacturer assumes the cost of shop visits. Such contracts convert an uncertain maintenance expense into a predictable one, though the engine’s true cost to the operator then becomes a recurring rate rather than a single purchase price. Because the fleet now spans several build standards, airlines and maintenance hubs must also manage parts inventories and tooling for each sub-generation, an overhead that TotalCare terms do not remove.

Rolls-Royce’s exposure under those agreements explains why durability failures hurt it directly: in 2019, the company said added repair costs would push a small number of its contracts into loss-making territory, which its finance chief put at around three. Those losses made up about half of an exceptional charge of about £1.4 billion expected that year.

The technical cause was corrosion-related fatigue cracking in the intermediate- and high-pressure turbine blades, which emerged within five years of the engine’s 2011 entry into service and eventually affected as many as 500 engines. Groundings peaked at close to 50 Dreamliners in 2018, and in April of that year the FAA cut extended-range twin-engine operating time for Package C aircraft from 330 minutes to 140, a restriction that complicated long trans-Pacific planning. Operators such as Air New Zealand and British Airways grounded aircraft for inspections, and several affected carriers leased older, less fuel-efficient jets to protect schedules, which added millions of dollars in operating expense.

The financial tally has grown with each update: by November 2019, Rolls-Royce put the cost of the Trent 1000 problems at £2.4 billion for 2017 through 2023, an additional £800 million, and said the TEN would need servicing every four years instead of five. Later accounts place the total above $3 billion, covering retrofits, engine modifications, and customer compensation.

The commercial damage extended beyond Rolls-Royce’s accounts, as GE secured roughly two-thirds of the in-service 787 fleet and recent widebody sales campaigns ordered 677 GEnx-powered aircraft against only 71 for the Trent 1000. Emirates President Tim Clark, citing instability in the Trent program, said in September 2019 that he would not commit to ordering 787s, an early sign that reliability concerns could cost sales as well as repair money.

The Trent XWB just keeps getting better and better.

Rolls-Royce’s answer is the Trent 1000 XE, delivered in two certified phases; the first, approved by the FAA in June 2025, introduced a high-pressure turbine blade with 40% more cooling, along with changes to the combustor, fuel spray nozzles, and controller software. Rolls-Royce says that package alone more than doubles the time on wing, and the second phase, certified in late 2025, redesigns the blade shroud and adds advanced coatings for roughly 30% more. Together, the phases are meant to triple time on wing relative to the TEN, and CEO Tufan Erginbilgiç has put the real-world figure as high as six years between shop visits for some customers. The confidence rests partly on the Trent 7000, which has flown with the same durability technology since 2022, and by mid-2026 the fleet using the new blades had accumulated almost three million engine flying hours.

Deployment is under way, since Lufthansa flew the first XE-equipped 787 in November 2025. The XE is now standard on new Trent-powered deliveries, and by early 2026, more than 50 in-service engines carried the improved blades, with a fleet-wide retrofit targeted for the end of 2027. Rolls-Royce committed to upgrading existing engines at no additional charge to airlines, and it added maintenance capacity in the UK, Germany, and Singapore worth roughly 100 more shop visits a year. LATAM Airlines has selected the XE for its 787s, a win Rolls-Royce credits to the durability gains.

The Trent 1000 work forms part of a £1 billion durability program that also covers the Trent 7000 and Trent XWB, and Rolls-Royce has raised its mid-term time-on-wing improvement target from 40% to 80% by 2027. Investors reacted by pushing Rolls-Royce shares sharply higher after the company raised its profit guidance on the back of the engine fixes.

Over the next two years, the price tag on a Trent 1000 will likely matter less than evidence of how long upgraded engines stay on wing. Once the fleet retrofit concludes, the industry will have its first fleet-scale record of shop visit intervals for the XE standard, and that record should do more than any list estimate to set how lessors and operators value the engine. Simple arithmetic shows why, since tripling the interval between visits would cut visits per flying hour to about a third, a change in lifetime economics that outweighs the small purchase price gap separating the Trent 1000 from its GE rival.

Two uncertainties remain, since the sources reviewed do not say whether the XE standard changes the purchase price of a new engine, and the headline interval claims apply to some customers rather than the whole fleet. Pricing is therefore likely to shift toward service contract terms, where Rolls-Royce can back its durability claims with guaranteed rates, and away from the hardware figure that dominates headlines. If the 2027 data confirm the promised gains, the engine’s share of new 787 orders will be the first place the market shows that it believes them.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6172. Conservative firebrand Lauren Boebert ousted in Colorado

Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., leaves the Capitol after a vote on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Colorado Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken conservative and Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for a fourth term to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy.

Laubacher was leading 48.8 percent to 47.9 percent, a margin of 3,441 votes, when The Associated Press called the race on Friday.

The red-hued 4th District, which spreads across eastern Colorado, was unexpectedly competitive this year, a sign of how deep into red turf Democrats were able to compete this year. Boebert had Donald Trump’s endorsement, but her relationship with the president has been strained at times after she began pressing for the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Laubacher proved to be a strong fundraiser, hauling in $13.7 million as of mid-October to Boebert’s $1.2 million.

Boebert has been one of the most visible and controversial members of the House GOP conference since she won an upset primary in the 3rd District over five-term incumbent Republican Scott Tipton in 2020.

A newcomer to electoral politics, she quickly positioned herself as a disruptor on Capitol Hill, heckling former President Joe Biden during his 2022 State of the Union address and tangling with a fellow GOP firebrand, former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia, on the House floor.

In 2023, Boebert was embroiled in an embarrassing incident in a Denver theater that was captured on surveillance video. She subsequently embarked on an apology tour.

Running for reelection the first time in the 3rd District, which is centered around Colorado’s rural Western Slope, Boebert barely won a closer-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Frisch in 2022. When Frisch announced he was trying again in 2024, Boebert switched to the 4th District, which had been considered far friendlier terrain for the GOP.

This year, Democrats won all of Colorado’s House seats, except in the 3rd District, which is held by Rep. Jeff Hurd.

Mary Ellen McIntire contributed to this report.
