#6159. Malaysia Airlines Orders Up To 16 Boeing 787-10s, Deliveries Start 2032

Malaysia Airlines has just placed a new aircraft order, as the airline will be adding a new wide body aircraft type to its fleet. This seems logical enough, even if the carrier’s long haul fleet seems rather diversified at this point.

Malaysia Airlines has placed its first-ever Dreamliner order, as the airline will be taking delivery of up to 16 Boeing 787-10s. This includes a firm order for 10 jets, plus options for six more, with deliveries expected between 2032 and 2035.

For context, the 787-10 is the largest variant of the Dreamliner. While it has the least range of any 787 variant, the per-seat economics are great, given how it’s “stretched.” While some airlines have started to use the 787-10 for high capacity regional routes, Malaysia Airlines is taking a different approach.

The oneworld carrier intends to use these planes to support its long haul fleet modernization and international expansion, including routes to Europe, along with destinations throughout Asia-Pacific. The airline points out how long haul demand to and from Southeast Asia has increased by more than 50% over the past decade.

Here’s how Malaysia Airlines Group CEO Nasaruddin Bakar describes this:

“The acquisition of the 787 Dreamliner represents a strategic investment in the future of Malaysia Aviation Group. As we look ahead to the next phase of growth, these aircraft will strengthen our ability to serve key international markets with greater capacity, efficiency and flexibility, while delivering the elevated travel experience our customers expect. Beyond fleet renewal, this investment reinforces our commitment to maintaining a modern, competitive airline that supports Malaysia’s connectivity and global aspirations.”

For context, Malaysia Airlines currently has a fleet of just over 90 aircraft, with another 75 aircraft on firm order. As it stands, Malaysia Airlines has:

Now the airline has the following planes on firm order:

A few things stand out here. First of all, it’s cool to see Malaysia Airlines growing again, after a rather rough… what, nearly 15 years? At this point the airline has enough planes on order to both replace its previous generation fleet, and expand. I’d expect the 16 A330ceos will be retired at some point in the coming years, and more than replaced by the A330neos that remain on order. Furthermore, the 737-800s will all be replaced by the 737 MAXs.

The 787-10 is an incredible plane in terms of economics, especially as Boeing has been able to make incremental range improvements, turning it into a true long haul aircraft.

At the same time, I can’t help but feel like it’s unusual how the airline has just seven A350s, with no more on order, and is now switching to the 787 for fleet renewal. Admittedly the A350 was ordered back in the day under a completely different management team, which also at one point thought the A380 was a good fit for the airline.

So I am curious how the carrier’s fleet evolves. Will the seven A350s stick around, or will they eventually just be replaced by 787-10s? Even with airspace restrictions and headwinds, it seems like all of Malaysia Airlines’ routes should be within range for the 787-10, though admittedly London (LHR) might be on the cusp, depending on how airspace closures evolve, how dense of a configuration the airline selects, etc.

The big challenge with the airline industry is that it’s never static, and decisions aren’t made in a vacuum. One management team makes one decision, and then a management team later on can’t just undo what the other management team did, without it being costly. So I get that they’re doing what they can…

Malaysia Airlines is the newest customer for the Boeing 787, as the airline has ordered up to 16 787-10s, including 10 firm orders and six options. The airline plans to use this for a long haul expansion to Europe, as well as for flights in Asia-Pacific.

It’s cool to see Malaysia Airlines continuing to grow, as the carrier has quite the order book at this point. I am curious if the airline keeps around the seven A350s in the long run, or how the airline manages its three wide body aircraft types.

What do you make of Malaysia Airlines’ Boeing 787-10 order?

#6158. The New Airbus A220 Coming In 2027

The Airbus A220 is currently preparing for a major upgrade, although the manufacturer is falling short of launching a new variant altogether. This year, new Airbus A220 deliveries will be outfitted with the manufacturer's Airspace interior, aligning the A220 with the interior feel of the A350, A330neo, and A320neo. Highlights include new upgraded extra-large overhead lockers, which will be around 20% lighter while offering more than 15% additional baggage capacity.

These aircraft will also feature 16-million-color LED lighting, allowing airlines to tailor their brand or flight phases. Airbus also plans on offering this unique interior as a retrofit option for existing Airbus A220 customers. Meanwhile, starting in 2027, a higher-density Airbus A220-300, one that features a 160-seat layout, will be offered, which provides operators with additional revenue and unit-cost gains without introducing a larger model to any given route.

However, the much-discussed Airbus A220-500 variant remains unannounced, and it does not look like Airbus has any plans to make any quick moves there as well. The manufacturer has looked to continue improving the profitability of the Airbus A220 family while also improving production rates, offering even more flexibility for operators. Let's analyze all the upcoming changes to the Airbus A220 family.

To contextualize the upcoming upgrades to this extremely popular aircraft program, it is important to begin by breaking down the Airbus A220's origins and discussing the aircraft's industrial footprint. The Airbus A220 began its life as a member of the Bombardier CSeries, a five-abreast narrowbody jet which was launched on July 13, 2008, with the intent of bridging the gap between regional jets and larger single-aisle aircraft.

It was first introduced to the market as the CS100, and it first took to the skies on September 16, 2013, before being certified by Transport Canada on December 18, 2015. The jet entered service with SWISS on July 15, 2016. The Bombardier CS300, which flew on February 27, 2015, would be certified on July 11, 2016, and it entered service on December 14 of that year with launch customer airBaltic.\

In July 2018, after Airbus took a majority stake in the company, it was quickly rebranded as the Airbus A220 and later organized as Airbus Canada Limited Partnership in June 2019. The aircraft program was now fully in the hands of manufacturing giant Airbus. The manufacturer's industrial capacity was expanded beyond Mirabel, Quebec, with a second final assembly line opened in Mobile, Alabama, in August 2019.

This allowed the manufacturer to avoid hefty import duties from US regulators. The manufacturer's ownership stake was increased to 75% in February 2020, with Bombardier electing to exit the program. The Airbus A220 remains the only commercial program managed by the manufacturer entirely outside of Europe. After entering service, the aircraft quickly established itself as offering strong dispatch reliability and improved passenger satisfaction over other models.

The Airbus A220 is powered by Pratt & Whitney PW1500G geared turbofan engines, and the aircraft offers a carbon-composite lightweight wing and an aluminum-lithium fuselage. Fly-by-wire controls and refined aerodynamics help deliver long legs and low-cost operations. Family weights range from 63 to 71 tonnes (139,000-156,000 lbs) of maximum takeoff weight (MTOW).

The aircraft family offers a range of 6,390-6,670 km (3,450-3,600 nautical miles), making it capable of serving almost all transcontinental niches in the United States and even longer-range lower-gauge routes within Europe. The 35 m (115 ft) Airbus A220-100 seats around 108-133 passengers, while the longer A220-300 seats a larger 130-160 passengers, depending on the specific configuration.

Airbus also launched the ACJ TwoTwenty business-jet variant, which was launched in late 2020. Delta remains the largest customer for the aircraft, and, globally, more than 1,100 Airbus A220s have been ordered, with over 500 delivered to date.

Globally, the fleet has surpassed 1.5 million flights and 2.7 million block hours, with the aircraft carrying more than 100 million passengers. The aircraft has also managed to maintain an exceptional safety reputation, with only one non-fatal smoke-related accident showing up on its rap sheet. It mainly competes with the Embraer E-Jet E2 family, holding a 55% share in this small-airliner niche, demonstrating the success and competitive value this program offers.

Airbus already operates several variants in its A220 series.

The A220 has slowly matured from being a promising upstart in the industry to becoming a core single-aisle workhorse for most carriers, especially with airlines wanting more revenue, lower unit costs, and a cabin that matches the rest of the manufacturer's portfolio. The five-abreast Airbus A220 already offers exceptional passenger comfort and impressive fuel burn, but bin space, lighting, and brand cohesion lag behind the newest Airbus models. Bringing the Airspace cabin to the aircraft helps close this gap.

Airlines today are extremely focused on premium and brand perception, and improving interiors is a key element of this overall strategy. From a commercial perspective, airlines need a low-risk way to add seats without adding a new aircraft type. The 160-seat Airbus A220-300 adds about ten more seats while providing more attractive costs per available seat mile, which ultimately proved useful for capacity-constrained layouts where upgauging to an A320neo would negatively impact profitability.

From a strategic perspective, Airbus needs to widen the A220's overall addressable market and strengthen the plane's business case before choosing to green-light a stretch to the Airbus A220-500. After all, the manufacturer wants to continue improving cabin appeal for legacy operators first.

Throughout this retrofitting and upgrade process, Airbus is mainly looking to pull two key levers. This year, new Airbus A220 deliveries will adopt the new Airbus Airspace cabin, a similar design that has been seen on Airbus A350, Airbus A330neo, and Airbus A320neo jets. Headlines are quick to discuss the 16-million-color LED lighting, which brand-matches the ambiance and circadian cues across different flight phases.

However, the Airspace kit also standardizes modern trim, surfaces, and touchpoints so that the aircraft will resemble any other Airbus model as closely as possible. Airbus is also quick to point out that it will be offering flexibility to operators, specifically when it comes to high-density Airbus A220-300 models. This ensures that its upgrades are not only providing optionality to future customers, but also letting existing operators improve their fleets.

The idea of stretching to the Airbus A220-500 also brings a lot to the table, as this model would upgauge the family and could potentially fill a capacity gap (albeit a small one) that exists in the Airbus commercial lineup. These upgrades are an extremely low-risk way to improve its product offering quickly.

Do Airbus or Embraer's narrow-bodied airlines dominate the short-haul and regional market?

From a financial perspective, the A220 upgrades represent a relatively low-risk lever being pulled by Airbus. For operators, these upgraded cabins will lift premium appeal, especially when it comes to corporate travelers who are interested in flying more modern aircraft. This will also result in more loyalty captured across the board.

Larger overhead bins are beneficial for operators, as they enable them to have lower gate-check-related costs and faster aircraft turns. Higher-capacity A220 variants can lower unit costs by spreading overall expenses out over more seats and adding capacity at slot-constrained airports and during peak leisure travel seasons.

Investing in these upgrades comes with low risks as aircraft downtimes are relatively low. This refresh supports overall pricing and will hopefully accelerate Airbus' order momentum: Delta, for example, is in the process of replacing its aging Boeing 717 fleet with advanced Airbus A220 models. This will improve learning-curve economics all along the way, ultimately pushing the program toward profitability before the A220-500 stretch.

Airbus is investing in the A220 to make it even more competitive. Here's what's new and what's coming in the future for the smallest Airbus.

At the end of the day, all of this means relatively little for passengers. The upgraded A220 cabins will likely provide a marginally more comfortable passenger experience, thanks to the cabin lighting being a little nicer, and it is also less likely with these new cabins that passengers will have to place their bags far away from where they currently are.

In the grand scheme of things, these are very marginal changes likely to have a small impact on your experience as a traveler. On the other hand, the higher-capacity variants of the aircraft will likely result in less available room per passenger, reducing comfort across the board. It will certainly be interesting to see if the high-capacity variant coming in 2027 will pave the way for a stretched A220-500.

The Norway-based long-haul budget airline officially ceased operations and filed for bankruptcy on Friday after failing to raise the cash necessary to keep flying.

The bankruptcy filing comes two days after Pakistan International Airlines, which contracts Norse to operate select flights, said on X that Norse had suspended operations "without prior notice."

Norse flew just one U.S. route at the time of its shut down: Orlando International Airport (MCO) to London's Gatwick Airport (LGW), schedules from aviation analytics firm Cirium show.

During the prime summer months, Norse also seasonally flew from New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) to Athens International Airport (ATH) in Greece, LGW and Rome's Fiumicino Leonardo da Vinci International Airport (FCO).

At its peak in 2024, Norse served five U.S. destinations, including Las Vegas's Harry Reid International Airport (LAS), Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), Miami International Airport (MIA), from gateways in Europe.

The collapse of Norse comes at a challenging time for airlines. Jet fuel is at historic highs, spiking after Iran war and other conflicts. Geopolitical tensions have closed significant swaths of airspace, including Russia and significant portions of the Middle East. And, high interest rates have pushed the cost of capital for any business to the highest levels in years.

Norse warned on Wednesday that its financial situation was "critical" and said its continued operation was "dependent on securing financing to meet its short-term liquidity needs."

Luis Gallego, the CEO of International Airlines Group that owns British Airways and Iberia, told the Financial Times in October that smaller airlines would struggle this winter due to the those financial headwinds.

Norse was one of the last airlines trying to make long-haul, low-cost work between the U.S. and Europe. Play Airlines, which attempted the same strategy via a connecting hub at Iceland's Keflavik International Airport (KEF), shut down in September 2025. And both Norse and Play were formed following the retrenchment and collapse of previous attempts; Norse from Norwegian Air's withdrawal from the market in 2021 and Play from the ashes of WOW Air that shut down in 2019.

Only independent French Bee and the budget arms of the larger European airline groups, including Discover, Level and Edelweiss Air, continue to offer lower-cost transatlantic flights.

Story updated with Norse confirmation of its shut down and subsequent bankruptcy filing.

#6155. SkyWest Pilots Do The Right Thing At SFO, Then Get Snapped At By ATC

With the number of close calls we see at airports nowadays, it’s great to see when pilots or air traffic controllers go above and beyond to be observant, and exhibit good situational awareness. So along those lines, here’s a case of a pilot paying close attention to ensure everyone’s safety, and then an air traffic controller being frustrated by that…

YouTube channel You can see ATC has the air traffic control audio and a visualization of an interaction that happened shortly before noon on November 21, 2026, at San Francisco International Airport (SFO).

In this interaction, a SkyWest Embraer E175 operating on behalf of American Eagle had just landed on runway 28L, after flying from Los Angeles (LAX). The pilots were switched to the ground frequency, and that’s when things quickly went downhill:

The SkyWest pilots then continued their taxi, and when they got to the gate, the conversation continued:

When you screw up, I suppose it’s human nature to get a bit defensive, and I think that’s exactly what happened here.

Credit to the SkyWest pilots for their situational awareness here. They were instructed to taxi in front of another plane, and another plane was instructed to give way to them, but never read back those instructions. The air traffic controller absolutely should have caught that, and as a pilot, they 100% did the correct thing by noticing the lack of a read back, and erring on the side of caution.

This isn’t just some theoretical risk, but ground collisions are the most common kinds of accidents involving commercial aircraft. Could the SkyWest pilots have said “we’re holding short because the other plane didn’t read back instructions?” Sure, but it seems like the time gap here was a matter of seconds, and they didn’t want to step on the radio calls of another pilot, in case they were going to read back.

What I think is really unprofessional is how the air traffic controller then responded to this:

The pilots of a SkyWest flight decided to hold short of a taxiway after they observed the plane that was supposed to give way to them not reading back the correct instructions. That was absolutely the right move, and the air traffic controller should’ve caught that.

When the pilots explained why they held short, the air traffic controller didn’t respond particularly well. Then when they asked for a phone number, she said the pilots would be talking to someone else, and she clearly wasn’t having it. But then she was also mad when the pilot explained very briefly what was going on, saying the conversation should happen off frequency… a conversation she wasn’t willing to have!

This is a clear situation where you have two very professional pilots, and one very unprofessional air traffic controller.

What do you make of this SFO ATC interaction?

#6153. 5 Mid-Sized US Airport Projects Quietly Adding Gates & Merging Security Checkpoints In 2026

Brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age. He became involved in the flight simulator and VATSIM communities, which sparked his interest in aviation and eventually led him to earn his private pilot license. Outside of work, he continues to build flight hours, explore new airports, and stay involved in the aviation community.

Billion-dollar terminal programs at Chicago, Los Angeles, and New York tend to dominate airport construction headlines, but some of the most practical upgrades in the country are happening one tier down. Medium-sized airports that grew quickly over the last decade are now dealing with the same problem: too few gates for the flights airlines want to add, and terminals split into separate wings that each need their own security checkpoint. For passengers, that layout often means picking the right checkpoint before knowing which gate is free, and for airlines, it limits where new service can go.

The five projects below take different routes to the same goal. Some add gates, others knock down the walls between concourses so a single checkpoint can feed every gate, and a few do both. Each has also hit a visible milestone in 2026, whether that is new gates opening to passengers, a finished concourse, a design contract, or steel rising on a replacement terminal, even though most of the work will not wrap up until 2028 or 2029.

Eppley Airfield (OMA) in Omaha is the furthest along of the projects on this list. In November 2026, passengers got their first look at the $950 million Build OMA Terminal Modernization Program, which the Omaha Airport Authority approved to nearly double the terminal's size. According to Travel Weekly, the building will grow from 375,000 square feet (34,839 square meters) to 646,000 square feet (60,015 square meters), and the expansion adds two gates for international flights along with a customs hall. Holder Construction is managing the work, which broke ground in February 2024 on a terminal that had not been modernized since the 1980s.

Four new gates, numbered A1, A1A, A1B and A2, opened on November 4, 2026. Airways Magazine reported that Delta Air Lines was using the new space in place of its previous south concourse gates, with passengers reaching the area through the existing south terminal and its current checkpoint, an arrangement that will only last until the rest of the building opens. Once finished, the unified concourse will connect the terminal areas that are separated today, and every departing passenger will clear a centralized TSA checkpoint in a new central pavilion that also houses a food court and shops.

The timeline beyond that is already set. Airways reports that the central pavilion and more of the concourse should open in early 2027, followed by new baggage and ticketing systems in mid-2027, and WOWT reported that the full program remains on time and on budget for completion in 2028. Steady demand is driving the work. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) data shows Eppley enplaned 2,565,135 passengers in 2025, a 0.70% dip from the prior year, but the airport still set a monthly record of 530,157 passengers in June 2026, according to WOWT. Construction stood at 60% complete in September 2026.

Spokane International Airport (GEG) technically sits in the FAA’s small hub category, with 2,106,307 enplanements in 2025, but it is the second-busiest airport in Washington and runs a terminal program on a medium-hub scale. Its Terminal Renovation and Expansion program, known as TREX, began with a $150 million expansion of Concourse C. The first part, Concourse C West, opened in May 2024 with three new gates and six new ticket counters. The second part, Concourse C East, replaced ground boarding with three new passenger boarding bridges at gates C1 through C3, and the airport announced the full Concourse C project complete on May 26, 2026.

That finished concourse sets up the larger second phase. Today, Spokane operates two siloed terminals, so passengers screen separately for the A and B concourses or for Concourse C. The new Central Hall will consolidate security screening for all airlines into one checkpoint and add a post-security hall connecting all three concourses. As the Spokesman-Review reports, the building will place baggage claim on the ground floor and security screening on the second. Utility relocation along the front curb began in May 2026 to clear the site.

The scope has grown considerably since planning began, both in floor area and in cost. A January 2023 filing with Washington’s Department of Enterprise Services described a 145,000-square-foot (13,471 square meters) Central Hall with an estimated maximum price of $152 million. The Journal of Business now puts the project at 255,000 square feet (23,690 square meters) and an estimated $335 million. Simple Flying has detailed how the hall will end repeat screening by 2030. Growth explains the larger footprint, since by then the airport expects roughly 6.2 million annual passengers, according to the Daily Journal of Commerce.

Gone are the days when only the largest airports got the big money improvements. Here are six regional airports that are investing billions.

The largest project here belongs to John Glenn Columbus International Airport (CMH). The CMH Next program is a roughly $2 billion replacement terminal, and WHIO noted it is the most expensive public works project ever undertaken in Franklin County. Columbus also leads this group in traffic by a wide margin, with 4,396,625 enplanements in 2025 according to the FAA, and the Columbus Regional Airport Authority reported nearly 9.4 million passengers across its airports that year. The existing terminal opened in 1958 and will be demolished once the new building is ready.

Unlike Omaha and Spokane, Columbus is not stitching older buildings together. Spectrum News reported that the approved plan includes a 36-gate terminal and a central marketplace with just one security checkpoint, replacing the three checkpoints the airport operates today. According to Construction Equipment Guide, those 36 gates are seven more than CMH currently uses, and two will handle international flights with on-site customs facilities. Gensler designed the building, which comes in at just over 1 million square feet (92,903 square meters) and adds 40% to 60% more waiting area at the gates, according to Archinect.

Progress in 2026 is mostly structural, with crews now working vertically on the terminal itself. Construction began in December 2024, focused first on a new elevated roadway, and the first steel beam for the building went up on August 8, 2025. Construction Equipment Guide reported in October 2026 that the authority now expects completion in January 2029. That date is deliberate, since Axios notes that the opening is timed to coincide with the airport’s 100th anniversary. Once the move happens, the old terminal site will become additional overnight parking for aircraft, letting airlines position more planes for early morning departures.

Richmond International Airport (RIC) is the newest medium hub on this list. The airport was classified as a small hub based on 2024 data, but FAA figures for 2025 list it as a medium hub after it enplaned 2,481,863 passengers, a 1.04% increase. That growth has put pressure on a terminal where passengers heading to the A and B concourses use two separate TSA checkpoints. The Capital Region Airport Commission, which runs the airport, describes the planned Consolidated Security Screening Checkpoint as among the most transformative projects in RIC’s history.

According to AviationPros, the project is estimated at about $253.1 million. It includes about 103,000 square feet (9,569 square meters) of new construction, renovation of 84,000 square feet (7,804 square meters) of existing space on the first and second floors, and roughly 29,000 square feet (2,694 square meters) of mezzanine. Richmond BizSense reports that the merged checkpoint will open with 10 screening lanes, with room to expand to 14, and that the work will also reshape the main atrium and add space for concessions beyond security.

The 2026 milestones at Richmond have focused on securing funding and finalizing the design. In May, the FAA awarded Richmond a $5.8 million grant toward construction, and Senator Mark Warner’s office noted that the rest will come from a mix of federal, state, airport and passenger facility charge revenue, along with bonds. On October 27, the commission approved design contracts that put a team led by architecture firm Gresham Smith officially in charge of the checkpoint, according to Richmond BizSense. Airport officials plan to build in phases to limit disruption, though travelers may see checkpoint locations shift during construction. A firm opening date has not yet been published.

Spokane Airport is investing millions in a new Central Hall to connect three concourses, consolidate security, and eliminate repeat screening by 2030.

Boise Airport (BOI) is the outlier on this list because its project focuses on gates rather than checkpoints. Traffic has quickly outgrown the current terminal. According to Engineering News-Record, passenger traffic has climbed 81% over the past decade, and FAA data shows 2,579,647 enplanements in 2025, up 4.21% from 2024. Boise was reclassified from a small hub to a medium hub after that growth, which added federal requirements for passenger services and airline competition plans. The airport also shares its airfield with the Idaho Air National Guard at Gowen Field.

In August 2025, the Boise City Council approved Hensel Phelps as construction manager and general contractor for the Concourse A and Terminal Improvements project. The city states that the contract carries a not-to-exceed amount of $700 million for work scheduled through 2029. Its centerpiece is Concourse A, which will add up to 10 new gates for future air service. The package also covers an expanded back-of-house baggage handling system, a new central utility plant, and two phases of improvements to passenger flow inside the existing terminal.

No local tax money is involved. KIVI reported that the project will be paid for with airport revenue and passenger facility charges, not local tax dollars. The broader BOI Upgrade program began in 2019, but the project stalled during the pandemic and was later redesigned to handle more passengers. Concourse A remains in design with Fentress Architects and Jacobs, and the airport states that construction is set to begin in 2026. Boise does not plan a checkpoint merger as part of this contract, so its case shows that some mid-sized airports need more gates first, while others need to simplify how passengers reach the gates they already have.

#6152. This week: Permitting bill hits Senate floor amid aviation funding fight

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

The lame-duck session continues as lawmakers look ahead to Thanksgiving and the funding deadline that arrives in December. The primary legislative business this week is the Senate's bipartisan permitting overhaul, but a late-breaking aviation funding fight and the Senate Democratic leadership contest are also commanding attention.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., and both men are accumulating supporters ahead of leadership votes that are currently scheduled for early December — though there's been an effort to move that up to this week.

Van Hollen has expressed disagreement with Schumer's participation in primaries.

​"I don't think it's the role of the Senate majority leader to get involved in open, contested Democratic primaries," Van Hollen said Sunday on CNN.

​Van Hollen has also said he wants to use all available tools to stop funding for the Iran war immediately, with a government funding deadline in December. That's going to be one of several flash points for December's funding discussions, as President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans try to use what leverage they have before Democrats take the gavels in the House and the Senate in January.

A new issue is the state of federal air traffic control after Friday's nationwide ground stop, with the Trump administration now seeking $50 billion to upgrade systems.

"I need additional money to do the additional work to keep the airspace safe," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Fox News Sunday.

Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, a senior appropriator who is in line to become majority whip, has suggested reallocating funds from the additional money the Trump administration and congressional Republicans allocated to Immigration and Customs Enforcement to address the challenges at the Federal Aviation Administration.

"There is a pot of 60 billion extra dollars on top of the regularly appropriated amount for ICE and we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA. We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars," Schatz posted on X.

"We can do all things, we don't have to do one versus the other," Duffy said in the Fox News Sunday interview. "I don't think that is the answer. The answer is let's do everything that's going to keep Americans safe, whether it's with immigration or it's with air travel."

Meanwhile on the Senate floor, the energy permitting overhaul bill faces a key test Monday evening​, with a vote scheduled to limit debate on a substitute amendment that represents the most recent version of the bill. Votes on a number of President Donald Trump's judicial nominations are also lined up this week.

On the other side of the Capitol, the House floor schedule i​ncludes several labor-related bills. ​One of the measures, introduced by Sen.-elect Kevin Hern, R-Okla.,​ would set standards for the way labor law applies to franchise operators.

New member orientation is also continuing, and committees in both the House and Senate will be holding hearings throughout the week as the outgoing Republican committee chairs aim to get through priority items on their agenda before the end of the Congress.

That includes a Tuesday morning Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing for Hung Cao, the nominee to be Navy secretary, who is currently the acting secretary. The Senate Judiciary Committee will be busy as well, as Chairman Charles E. Grassley, R-Iowa, looks to tee up more of Trump's judicial nominations for floor consideration.

#6151. Why JetBlue Is My Favorite Way To Fly Economy Across The Atlantic

I’ve flown back and forth across the Atlantic dozens of times in all cabins, including many times in economy. JetBlue definitely stands out as being my favorite, and dare I say it, the most premium of all the transatlantic economy flights I’ve experienced.

My most recent trip was from Europe to Boston (BOS) for the opening of JetBlue’s newest BlueHouse location. The airline covered my flights for the event, but had no input in this article. I’d like to share some of the reasons that JetBlue’s transatlantic experience impressed me so much.

Economy class meals can seem like quite the downgrade should one be accustomed to the elevated fare at the pointy end of the plane.

JetBlue currently partners with NYC-based Dig Inn for its transatlantic economy-class meals, and they’re far better than average. They also offer products from a range of interesting brands, rather than just your classic soda labels.

Here’s an example of the drinks menu on my flight from Amsterdam to Boston.

Meals are served in these stylish, reusable, matte-black sealed containers. I’d love to see more airlines do more to reduce their waste like this.

I was very happy with my choice of chicken pesto pasta salad as the main course, accompanied by sides of beet and carrot slaw and snap peas with feta. The fresh, flavorful, yet cold dishes were far better than many of the reheated slop I’ve been served in economy before.

I was equally impressed by the breakfast I had on the morning departure back from Boston to London Heathrow (LHR). I went for the Bubly sparkling water again, as I avoid coffee on a plane unless it’s served as espresso. The stuff they pour out of those vats is pretty much just glorified dirty water.

As far as pre-landing light meals go, this pizza thing was pretty good, too.

In addition to the main meal and pre-landing light bite, JetBlue keeps a well-stocked pantry at the back of the Airbus A321LR.

JetBlue has been offering fast, free, in-flight Wi-Fi for as long as I can remember. The same cannot be said for some full-service carriers, which still can’t guarantee a reliable, fast, and free connection on their transatlantic flights.

They’ve also added some fun tech features, like the ability to choose the elements for the main meal service via the IFE screen, even in economy. I think it has a more premium feel than being asked “chicken or beef?”

I’m not a frequent JetBlue flyer, so I couldn’t really make the most of the fun personalization features, such as the option to continue watching the movie where you left off on your last flight.

Being given anything more than the standard pillow and blanket in economy is a rare bonus. It had been so long since my last JetBlue flight in economy that I’d forgotten about the complimentary Snooze Kit.

I prefer to use my AirPods to earplugs, but I did make good use of the eye mask for a mid-flight nap.

I’ve flown over my fair share of narrow bodies on long-haul flights, and I genuinely don’t know why such a fuss is made about them being terrible.

JetBlue’s version of the aircraft has comfy seats, with standard Core (economy) seats having 32 inches of pitch. Another common complaint I hear is that there are fewer toilets. For a plane with far fewer passengers (only 114 in economy), fewer toilets kind of makes sense. I didn’t once find myself waiting in line to use the bathroom on either flight.

For what it’s worth, there are two lavatories for 114 economy passengers, so that’s one lavatory per 57 passengers. That’s a little lower than the industry standard, but not by much. For example, American’s standard 787-9s have five lavatories for 255 economy seats, so that’s a ratio of one lavatory per 51 passengers.

If you’ve only got the budget or the points for economy for your next trip to Europe, I couldn’t recommend JetBlue more. They now fly to eight cities in Europe, the planes are comfortable and modern, and the in-flight food and beverage is top of the game for economy.

What do you make of JetBlue’s transatlantic economy offering?

#6150. British Airways Visa Card Review: Is It Worth The $95 Annual Fee?

The British Airways Visa Signature® Card is one of Chase’s co-branded airline credit cards, and British Airways Club is certainly a popular frequent flyer program, given the overall value of the Avios ecosystem, plus the number of destinations in the United States that British Airways serves.

Who should be applying for the British Airways Visa, and under what circumstances is it worth spending money on it? Let’s take a look at what you need to know about this card, and what the best alternatives are.

Link: Learn more about the British Airways Visa Signature® Card

Before jumping into a closer look at every aspect of the British Airways Visa Card, here’s a high-level view of the card’s key features, perks, and fees:

Here are my thoughts on the biggest British Airways Visa Card pros and cons:

If you’re considering the British Airways Visa Signature Card, its welcome bonus, application rules, and annual fee are all probably top of mind. So let’s start by taking a look at these important details.

The British Airways Visa currently offers the following welcome bonus: Earn 75,000 Avios after you spend $5,000 on purchases within the first three months of account opening.

Based on my current points and miles valuations, which put Avios at 1.2 cents apiece, this current bonus is worth about $900. That’s a pretty solid welcome bonus, especially for a card with a moderate annual fee.

The British Airways Visa has a $95 annual fee. This is not waived for the first year, and there’s no additional fee to add authorized users.

British Airways’ credit card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s potentially a great card to use for purchases abroad.

The welcome bonus on the British Airways Visa isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have received a new cardmember bonus on the card in the past 24 months. You are eligible for this card if you’ve had the Iberia Visa Signature® Card and/or Aer Lingus Visa Signature® Card, despite the similarities between the cards.

Chase’s other general policies on card approvals apply as well, including the 5/24, whereby you generally won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more credit cards in the last 24 months.

The British Airways Visa Card has no foreign transaction fees, but does the rewards structure warrant putting spending on the card? It might, but only thanks to additional bonuses offered by the card, which incentivize spending.

The British Airways Visa doesn’t have terribly exciting bonus categories. You earn:

There are lots of great credit cards for airfare purchases and hotel purchases. This isn’t a card I would be putting much spending on unless you’re trying to earn a Travel Together Ticket, in which case it could definitely be worth it. More on that below.

British Airways Club is a transfer partner of Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Chase Ultimate Rewards, so it could make sense to put spending on a card earning one of those currencies if you want to earn Avios at an accelerated rate.

There are lots of great uses of British Airways Avios. British Airways Club has roughly distance based award pricing, and the program offers value in situations where other programs might not. Generally speaking, here’s where I see value with Avios:

British Airways is known for adding large taxes and surcharges to some of its own award flights, so this is worth keeping in mind.

Personally I find Avios to be one of the most useful frequent flyer programs for redeeming points, thanks to the number of redemptions this opens up.

Often one of the big challenges people have with points is figuring out how to pool them since you typically need enough points in a single account for a redemption. A cool feature of the British Airways Club program is that you can form household accounts. This allows you to pool the Avios you earn with up to six other people registered at the same address as you.

This is especially awesome in the context of a credit card welcome bonus, since you can pool a ton of Avios in a single account if you have two people get the card in a household, etc.

There are some benefits to the British Airways Visa Card that could alone justify having this card. For some people, it will be worth spending money on the card to unlock some perks, while for others just having the card and not spending money on it offers sufficient benefits. Let’s look at what those benefits are, and how they work.

One of the best benefits of the British Airways Signature Visa is that it offers a 10% discount on British Airways flights starting in the United States. To take advantage of this, just book through ba.com/chase10, and use your card to pay while using promotion code BACHASE10.

If you fly British Airways with any frequency, this could cover the annual fee over and over. See this post for everything you need to know about the British Airways Visa flight discount.

If you have the British Airways Visa Card and redeem Avios for a reward flight, you can receive up to $600 in statement credits annually. You can earn up to three statement credits, as follows:

There are some basic terms to be aware of:

British Airways now also offers Reward Flight Saver from the United States, allowing you to redeem more Avios and pay lower surcharges. Getting a further statement credit of up to $200 on that is pretty great.

One of the potentially great perks of the British Airways Visa is that you can earn a Travel Together Ticket when you spend $30,000 on the card in a calendar year.

This companion ticket will be deposited in your British Airways Club account four to six weeks after you’ve completed the required spending.

With this certificate, you can book a British Airways award ticket at the full cost of Avios (plus taxes, fees, and surcharges), and then for the second passenger you don’t have to pay any Avios, but rather just have to pay all the fees.

This also offers a lot of flexibility — you can also use the voucher as a solo traveler and get 50% off the Avios required for a ticket. Your ticket can originate anywhere in the world, and you can even travel on Aer Lingus or Iberia.

This can represent a fantastic deal for first and business class travel, given how much those tickets would otherwise cost. This isn’t for everyone, though it has the potential to represent a good value, and I know it’s a feature that many value.

See this post for everything you need to know about the British Airways Visa companion voucher.

As a Visa Signature card, the British Airways Visa comes with the following shopping and travel protection benefits:

You’ll want to review the card’s benefits guide for any exclusions and rules that apply.

The British Airways Visa Card has a solid welcome bonus, and that could be a legitimate motivator for picking up this card. However, personally this isn’t a card I would use for everyday spending, since you can earn British Airways Avios at a better rate with other American Express or Chase cards. It also lacks a few benefits that many other airline credit cards offer, including a free checked bag and priority boarding.

That said, I absolutely think this card is worth holding onto if you fly British Airways with any frequency because:

There are several Avios currencies, with three belonging to International Airlines Group (IAG) airlines — there’s British Airways, Aer Lingus, and Iberia. There are also two other US-based credit cards that directly earn Avios from these airlines. Specifically, we’re talking about the Iberia Visa Card (learn more) and Aer Lingus Visa Card (learn more).

Which of these cards should you select? They have a lot in common:

The differences mainly come in the form of the perks associated with just holding onto the cards, and also the perks associated with spending $30,000 on the cards in a calendar year:

Between shopping for gifts, planning holiday getaways and squeezing in activities with family, the last few months of the year can get expensive.

The Amex Platinum comes with a long list of benefits, but its $895 annual fee (see rates and fees) means I try and get as much value from the card as possible. Lululemon offers some of its biggest discounts during Black Friday and Cyber Monday, making the holidays a great time to stretch that $75 credit even further (almost as far as my favorite Lululemon Align leggings). I also have a little shopping trick to share. If I find something I want but I'm worried it'll sell out before the sales start, I can buy it ahead of time and keep an eye on the price. If it drops, I'll reach out to Lululemon's customer service to request a price adjustment.

Lululemon has a great price drop guarantee policy and will issue a gift card for the difference. Just make sure to pay attention to the details since price adjustments aren't guaranteed and Black Friday deals are often excluded. Still, it never hurts to ask.

#6148. The Airbus A350’s Unique Cabin Design That Sets It Apart From Others

The Airbus A350 has silently become one of the most recognizable long-haul aircraft in the skies today, but its most distinctive asset is likely not going to be its curved wingtips or ultra-efficient engines, but rather the aircraft's cabin itself. From the beginning, Airbus designed the A350's cross-section and interior architecture around overall passenger wellbeing, before wrapping that in the airline's 'Airspace' design language.

The aircraft features higher ceilings, wider sidewalls, and large overhead bins that all combine with low cabin noise, large windows, and advanced air management systems in order to create a noticeably calmer environment on long flights. Humidity and overall cabin pressure levels remain optimized to reduce jet lag and fatigue, while carefully engineered lighting schemes help allow passengers to adjust to new time zones.

Airlines, on the other hand, get a flexible interior shell that they can tune for all kinds of routes. As more carriers introduce refreshed Airbus A350 interiors and Airbus rolls out its New Production Standard with wider, longer cabins, the aircraft is increasingly beginning to set a benchmark for how a modern long-haul cabin should feel.

It also showcases why cabin design matters just as much as range or fuel burn for passengers and airlines alike. For many travellers, the first step onto an Airbus A350 instantly signals a different kind of widebody experience for passengers that an airline can market.

Originally launched as the Airbus XWB (which stands for 'eXtra-Wide-Body'), the A350 family was developed as a clean-sheet, long-range twin-engine aircraft designed to replace earlier four-engine types and to compete directly with the Boeing 787 and 777. Originally built from carbon-fibre reinforced plastic, the aircraft combines a lightweight fuselage with a high-aspect-ratio wing and Rolls-Royce Trent XWB engines.

These turbofans deliver double-digit fuel-burn and carbon emissions reductions over older widebodies. The family today spans the Airbus A350-900, the ultra-long-range Airbus A350-900ULR, and the stretched Airbus A350-1000, in addition to the forthcoming Airbus A350F freighter, giving airlines a common cockpit and systems across multiple mission profiles.

Typical three-class layouts seat roughly 300 to 380 passengers, with range figures comfortably exceeding 8,000 miles (12,875 km) on passenger variants. Airbus has continued to refine the platform using its New Production Standard, trimming weight across the board, and significantly improving take-off performance while unlocking extra usable cabin length and width.

The table above details some additional specifications for the Airbus A350, according to documents published by the European Union Aviation Safety Agency. Orders have now passed 1,600, with hundreds already in service and a growing backlog from both established network carriers and fast-growing new market entrants.

Operational data now shows that the global Airbus A350 fleet has flown well over a million sectors on more than a thousand routes, with an excellent safety record and strong overall dispatch reliability. For airlines, that translates into the ability to open thinner long-haul city pairs while upgauging older fleets on trunk routes and standardizing on a single modern widebody family.

What differentiates the Airbus A350 most from its rivals is its Airspace cabin architecture. The fuselage cross-section was shaped to maximize usable interior width between the sidewalls, giving designers more shoulder room at seated eye level than earlier Airbus types and many competing jet models.

That extra space can thus be spent on wider seats, broader aisles, larger armrests, or a mix of all three, depending on each airline's philosophy. An improved cabin experience offers a lot of comfort and versatility for passengers, allowing airlines to charge more for these kinds of premium seats.

High ceilings, carefully sculpted sidewalls, and large pivoting overhead bins create a sense of openness while still giving generous space for passengers to easily stow carry-on bags. The cabin is also engineered for comfort on a microscopic level, with higher humidity, lower effective cabin altitude, and very low noise levels that all help reduce fatigue on long-haul overnight sectors.

With the latest New Production Standard, Airbus has subtly widened and stretched the cabin envelope. This has freed up space for larger galleys, new crew-rest arrangements, and ultimately additional seating options without the requirement to fundamentally change the feel of the aircraft's interior.

Combined with flexible lighting, advanced connectivity, and a step-by-step modification approach, the Airbus A350 offers airlines an unusually adaptable canvas for everything from minimalist economy layouts to highly differentiated four-class flagship aircraft.

Discover why the Airbus A350 offers the ultimate passenger experience — quieter cabins, roomier seats, and comfort praised by flyers worldwide.

The Airbus A350's geometry and flight control systems make it an unusually strong platform for offering premium cabin service. The aircraft's wide, oval-shaped cross-section supports spacious 1-2-1 business-class layouts that offer long beds and large side consoles that do not feel squeezed, all while leaving room for generous aisles and direct aisle access at every seat.

Lower overall cabin noise, advanced filtration, and higher humidity, all alongside a lower effective cabin altitude, all enhance sleep quality and overall well-being. This aligns nicely with what high-yield passengers are looking to get out of overnight flights. The New Production Standard adds roughly four inches of extra usable cabin width.

SWISS is another airline that will use the aircraft to introduce new kinds of premium cabins, with the carrier debuting its new SWISS Senses four-class concept, which includes enclosed first-class suites and door-equipped business-class seats. These projects highlight how the Airbus A350 gives designers the room and range to build truly differentiated flagship products, turning the cabin into a competitive weapon on the world's longest and most lucrative routes.

The Airbus A350 is not a niche experiment but rather a core long-haul workhorse for dozens of major airlines. By the summer of 2026, around 730 Airbus A350s were in service worldwide with roughly 40 different operators. The largest fleets sit with Singapore Airlines, Qatar Airways, Cathay Pacific, Air France, and Delta, all of which use the type as a long-haul flagship on key intercontinental routes.

Airlines in China, including Air China and Sichuan Airlines, deploy the A350 on domestic trunk routes as well as for long-haul services to Europe and North America. This allows them to capitalize on the aircraft's exceptional versatility and efficiency. In Europe, carriers such as Lufthansa, Iberia, Finnair, SAS, and Turkish Airlines use the Airbus A350 to modernize aging Airbus A340 and Airbus A330 fleets.

In the Middle East and Africa, Qatar Airways and Ethiopian Airlines have embraced the type for global hub-and-spoke operations. Newer long-haul brands like STARLUX in Taiwan and upcoming operators such as IndiGo and Riyadh Air are also turning to the Airbus A350, underscoring its appeal from full-service legacies to ambitious challengers.

Freighter and corporate variants are joining the mix as well, with cargo specialists and VIP customers ordering the Airbus A350F and the private ACJ350 respectively. This will extend the family's presence beyond traditional passenger airlines into high-yield logistics spaces and ultra-long-range private or government operations.

The future of the Airbus A350 looks increasingly central to long-haul aviation. Airbus has logged more than 1,400 orders for the type across both passenger and freighter variants, with several hundred aircraft still to be delivered to both established and new kinds of carriers. In the coming years, airlines like IndiGo, Riyadh Air, and Qantas are set to introduce large Airbus A350 fleets, using the model to open new long-haul markets and replace older twin- and quad-engine aircraft.

Emirates is also rolling out its brand-new Airbus A350 models on a handful of routes. At the same time, a first wave of cabin retrofits for older models is already well underway, with early customers looking to densify layouts, shift space towards premium cabins, supporting Airbus' dedicated A350 upgrade services, and third-party retrofit programs.

The arrival of the Airbus A350F will pull the manufacturer deeper into the cargo market, all while ultra-long-range projects like Qantas' Project Sunrise show how far the platform can be stretched. New premium concepts such as the SWISS Senses, which debuted on the Airbus A350-900 before spreading to other aircraft types, reinforce the aircraft's role as a launchpad for next-generation cabins.

As environmental pressure continues to intensify, the aircraft's combination of composite structure, efficient engines, and SAF-ready systems positions the Airbus A350 as a key tool for airlines pursuing lower-carbon long-haul networks. They will be able to do so without sacrificing passenger appeal.

Taken together, the Airbus A350 is as much a story of cabin innovation as it is of engineering. Airbus gave airlines a wide canvas, which they wrapped in the branding and marketing of the company's Airspace concept. This interior offers extra space, low noise, and generous natural lighting. The manufacturer also refined this design with the New Production Standard and other retrofit options.

Airlines use the aircraft as a flexible canvas for everything from dense leisure layouts to ultra-luxurious ultra-long-haul flagships. Guests gain quieter rides, better air quality, larger bins, and comfortable seating, especially when it comes to the premium cabins. For airlines, strong economics and a future-proof cabin make the Airbus A350 a standout choice for next-generation long-haul fleets for years to come.

#6147. Biden: ‘Hard to take’ as Pelosi, Schumer turned on him in 2024

President Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug. 9, 2022. In his new memoir, Biden said he was disappointed when Pelosi and Schumer urged him to drop out of the presidential race in 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

In conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir. The consensus view, even among some who’d worked for the former president, was that if he did anything other than accept some responsibility for his role in Donald Trump’s return to the White House, they didn’t have much appetite to hear what he had to say about anything else.

Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.

But while his perspective on the climactic moment of his political career will be the most scrutinized portion of Biden’s new book, “Promise Me, America” seems primarily intended to offer the former president a platform he has otherwise not had since leaving office: to catalog what he sees as his historic achievements and offer his perspective on how he wrestled with the major issues of our time.

It’s often said that the only thing better than being president is being a former president. That has hardly been the case for Biden in the nearly 22 months since he left the White House, especially as he’s endured what his son Hunter has described as “debilitating” physical pain following a cancer diagnosis last March.

But where “Thanks, Obama” became a popular mantra nearly a decade ago for Democrats seeking to defend and celebrate the 44th president’s record in contrast with the first Trump administration, no such widespread nostalgia has emerged around Biden, as the party is loath to revisit the trauma of the summer of 2024.

The sheer length of his new book — more than 400 pages — seems an implicit acknowledgment that presenting a positive portrait of Biden’s single term in office is largely to be a solitary effort. Over 15 chapters, Biden offers sometimes mechanical descriptions of specific policies and their impact, but also new details of the sausage-making required to pass major initiatives like the Inflation Reduction Act. That legislation, he writes, was revived thanks in part to an Italian dinner hosted by Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo to make peace between West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin III and White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain.

Biden writes in sweeping terms about other accomplishments like responding to the COVID-19 crisis he inherited, calling his administration’s work “one of the most monumental achievements in public health history.” He repeatedly defends his frequent efforts to warn Americans about the need to safeguard our democracy even as critics in the press and his own party suggested he focus more on economic concerns.

Supporting Ukraine in its war against Russia gets the most extensive treatment of any single issue in the book, including a detailed account of Biden’s clandestine trip to Kyiv in February 2023. And the former Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman takes great effort to delve into the complexity of the U.S.-China relationship and his relationship with President Xi Jinping, while asserting that Taiwan “will likely be the most important foreign policy challenge in the world over the next generation.”

Recurring throughout the book are expressions of optimism that under his administration, Washington was beginning to work again like it was supposed to, that America’s global leadership was being restored through its alliances, and that he was tackling problems that previous presidents had sidestepped. And in offering this comprehensive presentation of his record, Biden also offers his primary rationale for running again.

“We had accomplished so much —  I wanted to finish the job. And yes: I believed I was the best person to do it,” he says. “I was the only person who had ever beaten Donald Trump. And I felt I was the best person to do it again.”

One of Biden’s top advisers put it to me a different way in the months leading up to his decision to seek another term. “He has been running for president for 50 years. And the idea that he would actually be president and stop running for president is almost laughably preposterous.”

The biggest question, of course, was his age, something Biden, who was 81 when he dropped out of the race, asserts he gave serious consideration.

“I knew better than anyone how old I was. I knew what I was —  and wasn’t —  capable of doing. I carefully monitored how I was meeting the demands of the job. And there is not a single example of me failing to handle my responsibilities,” he writes.

The June 27 debate, of course, created a very different perception, as Biden acknowledges that his flubbed comment that “we finally beat Medicare” was to become “Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job.” But he tries to argue it was no different than the poor showings of previous incumbent presidents, including President Barack Obama, in their first debates.

“The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate. As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me,” Biden writes.

He argues the response he was seeing from voters at his public events after the debate didn’t justify the panicked response of elected Democrats in Washington, and that public polling showed only minor slippage after the debate, until a steady drumbeat of elected Democrats publicly began calling for him to step aside.

Describing separate visits from former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., personally urging him to step aside, he says there was a “yawning gap between what I was seeing with Democratic voters and what I was hearing from the Democratic leadership in Washington.”

“I have to admit it was personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me,” Biden says. “I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have said it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race. Loyalty matters to me. If I give you my word, I stick with you. If I say I’m with you, I’m with you to the end.”

At one point, Biden seems to reflect some resentment that some of the Democrats who would ultimately call on him to drop out of the race had themselves been too afraid to challenge him in the first place, saying: “Anyone who was scared off from running has no business being president.” While there was a constant narrative about the weakness of his candidacy, Biden acknowledges, the lack of a serious challenger was in fact a sign of his strength.

“I had it on good authority that several big names in Democratic politics had looked at running. They held meetings and took polls and talked to donors and to potential staff. If they thought I was weak or vulnerable, they would have taken their shot. But they didn’t,” he writes.

Biden’s defiant tone, and his insistence that the lack of party unity was a greater threat to his continued candidacy than his own performance, may be dismissed by Democrats who don’t want to revisit this difficult chapter. But as Schumer and other Democratic leaders are now facing their own internal challenges, “Promise Me, America” may also serve as a cautionary note for an ambitious crop of potential candidates hoping to reclaim the presidency in 2028.

#6146. Norse Atlantic Collapses: Airline Cancels Flights, Strands Passengers

Back in August 2026, all-Boeing 787 airline Norse Atlantic Airways announced it was in a rough financial spot, and was pursuing a sale, merger, or other arrangement. Not a whole lot of progress was made in subsequent months, and just this morning, the airline announced that it was in a “critical” financial situation.

Well, it seems that it didn’t take long for things to get much worse, as the airline has seemingly canceled all flights just hours later, leaving travelers stranded.

Earlier today, Norse Atlantic provided an update on its financial situation and ongoing strategic review. There’s no point in paraphrasing this, so here’s the direct statement from the airline:

The Company’s financial situation is critical. It is dependent on securing financing to meet its short-term liquidity needs and to continue its operations. Norse, supported by its advisors, has explored various strategic alternatives and entertains discussions for a potential takeover. In parallel, the Board and management have diligently considered other available options, including ACMI contracts. Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution.

To state the obvious, this sounded really, really bad. When the company was publicly stating that its “financial situation is critical” and that it needed to secure financing to meet “short-term liquidity needs,” you knew things weren’t good. I expected we’d see something bad happen in the coming weeks, but it didn’t take that long.

Norse Atlantic has canceled its own scheduled flights effective immediately. On top of that, the airline was leasing two jets to Pakistan International Airlines, and those flights were also canceled with very little notice, “due to an unexpected operational suspension” by Norse Atlantic. Travelers were literally checking in at the airport when they realized the airline was grounded.

Due to an unexpected operational suspension by our wet-lease partner Norse Air without prior notice, tonight’s PK786 (London–Islamabad) & PK710 (Manchester–Lahore) are cancelled.We deeply regret the disruption. Efforts have been made to mitigate the impact, and from tomorrow,…

So while the company hasn’t formally announced that it’s liquidating, it’s clear that operations are at least suspended, and we’ll see how this all plays out.

The airline industry can be a funny business, and there’s no clearer example of that than Norse Atlantic Airways. The airline launched in 2022, with the goal of operating long haul, low cost flights, particularly across the Atlantic.

That wasn’t exactly a unique business model, because this was exactly what Norwegian did, before it discontinued long haul flights in 2021. Not only was the idea sort of copied, but Norse Atlantic had some executives from Norwegian, and even picked up the planes that Norwegian previously flew.

But as is all too common in the airline industry, clearly they thought it would be different this time around… it wasn’t. So in 2024 we saw the airline update its business model, making the focus less about operating regularly scheduled commercial flights, and more about leasing out aircraft, all while reducing its fleet.

The company got a lifeline when IndiGo decided to lease some Norse Atlantic 787s to dabble in long haul flying, ahead of the airline taking delivery of its own Airbus A350s. However, between all the airspace closures, high oil costs, and generally declining performance at IndiGo as the airline increasingly moved away from its core strengths, the airline recently decided to scrap that experiment, and stop leasing planes from Norse Atlantic.

Since then, opportunities for Norse Atlantic have been limited. The airline did manage to lease a couple of Dreamliners to the “new” Pakistan International Airlines, but for an airline with 12 planes, that hardly pays the bills.

Norse Atlantic did still operate some of its own flights, but in a very limited capacity. The airline had some flights from Europe to Thailand, South Africa, and the United States, but most were seasonal, and they were a fraction of what they previously were. Clearly they just didn’t have enough money to “keep the lights on” anymore.

I am curious to see what comes next for Norse Atlantic’s 787s. The airline doesn’t own them, but instead, they’ll presumably return to their leasing companies. I can’t help but point out that Southwest Airlines wants to start long haul flights. The airline had been considering a Boeing 787 order, and was possibly even looking at ways to get planes faster than from a direct order (which requires waiting for years).

Could these dozen Norse Atlantic 787s somehow end up at Southwest? The interiors would just need some updates (assuming the airline wants to offer business class), but talk about a quick way to grow a decent sized fleet.

This morning, Norse Atlantic released a statement admitting that its “financial situation is critical,” and that the company’s future is “dependent on securing financing to meet short-term liquidity needs.” That wasn’t exactly a great sign, but little did we know that the company would collapse just hours later, as the airline has now ceased all flying, including on a wet lease basis.

Financial issues at the company started when… well, it launched. Norse Atlantic was just a direct replica of Norwegian, which had failed. When the airline realized that the long haul, low cost business model doesn’t really work, they tried to pivot to wet leasing. And while there’s some demand for that, it’s also not a 100% consistent business in terms of demand.

I feel horribly for all the frontline employees at Norse Atlantic who put their best foot forward. May they find good opportunities at other airlines.

What do you make of Norse Atlantic’s seeming collapse?

#6145. Not Again: Cargo Jet Overruns Miami Airport Runway (This Time A FedEx MD-11)

Miami International Airport (MIA) is having a bad luck streak when it comes to cargo planes being able to stay on the runway, but at least this time around there were no fatalities. Still, yikes…

At 8:25PM on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, a FedEx McDonnell Douglas MD-11 overran the runway at Miami Airport, leading the airport to be shut down for an extended period of time.

The 34-year-old MD-11 with the registration code N605FE had just performed flight FX910 from Memphis (MEM), and was coming in to land on runway 26R, which is 9,355 feet (2,851 meters) long. That’s a solidly long runway, for what it’s worth.

However, the plane wasn’t able to stop before the end of the runway, and seemed to exit the paved surface at a speed of around 50 knots, and came to a stop around 320 meters (1,000 feet) past the end of the runway, right by the airport perimeter fence.

🚨 USA | FEDEX CARGO PLANE OVERRUNS RUNWAY AT #MIAMI AIRPORT!MD-11 arriving from Memphis skidded into the grass beyond Runway 26R, triggering an FAA ground stop.2 crew members are safe. No deaths or injuries.#FlaPanthers #Survivor51 #ไฟไหม้ pic.twitter.com/kTM48GkeGf

WATCH: FedEx cargo plane in the grass after overshooting runway at Miami International Airport pic.twitter.com/t4DPQwUb0m

Fortunately there were no serious injuries. There’s video footage showing stairs being pulled up to the plane, and the pilots walking off with their bags. There’s always the classic aviation adage that “any landing you can walk away from is a good one,” and if that’s the case, I guess this was a good landing.

Footage showing the FedEx Express MD-11F after it overran the runway at Miami International Airport tonight. As a result of the incident, a ground stop was issued. pic.twitter.com/ldraejGQ4v

This accident ended up causing a ground stop of nearly two hours at the airport. That’s not exactly ideal timing, given what a busy travel day yesterday was, ahead of Thanksgiving. Operations did eventually resume, but with delays averaging over three hours.

🚨 迈阿密国际机场关闭！今晚，一架联邦快递（FedEx）货运飞机在迈阿密国际机场（MIA）冲出跑道，机场目前已实施地面停飞令（Ground Stop）。根据空中交通管制（ATC）的录音，飞机冲出跑道后，管制员通知其他飞行员，机场“刚刚关闭”。这是今年迈阿密国际机场发生的第二起货运飞机冲出跑道事故。…

Of course the concept of a plane overrunning a runway at Miami Airport is fresh on people’s minds, given the September 6 accident we saw with a 21 Air (Amazon Air) Boeing 767-300 that overran runway 30. Tragically that accident claimed five lives, as the plane ran through the perimeter fence, and killed motorists. What we’ve found out about the piloting of that flight since the accident, and just how recklessly the captain was flying the plane, is astounding.

We’ll have to wait for a full investigation to know what happened (the NTSB typically releases a preliminary report within a month), but in terms of circumstances and possible contributing factors, there are a couple of things we know.

First, there’s footage showing the plane’s approach, and it makes it pretty clear that the plane touched down extremely late.

JUST IN: FedEx cargo plane overruns the runway at Miami International Airport. Flights halted pic.twitter.com/PFFH0TNpe1

A recreation of the approach based on flight tracking data shows just how late the plane touched down, and the big question is why the pilots didn’t perform a go around.

🚨 BREAKING: FedEx FDX910, an MD-11F registered N605FE, went off the end of runway 26R landing at Miami International from Memphis at about 8:28 PM local, Nov 25. Tower sent the next arrival around and ground control closed the airport. No injuries reported so far. pic.twitter.com/IhRUGEVR97

It’s also worth pointing out that weather in the region was really bad at the time of the accident. Anna Giaritelli, a reputable aviation journalist with good sources, quotes a Miami air traffic controller, who told her that “this was absolutely the most dangerous operation I’ve seen,” as much of the traffic approaching Miami had run into a “black hole of weather.”

A Miami air traffic controller sent me this chilling text minutes before the FedEx incident in MIA tonight(Controller was not on duty while texting me.) pic.twitter.com/Fvy7vb7xuP

It doesn’t seem like conditions at Miami Airport as such were that awful (compared to reports of severe turbulence in the region), but I imagine the bad weather could’ve contributed to a sense of “get-there-itis” for the pilots.

While this is of course unfortunate, the great news here is the lack of injuries or fatalities. The plane ended up coming to a stop just feet from the airport’s perimeter fence, and if it had crashed through that, the outcome could’ve been completely different, with fatalities among motorists.

It also has to be acknowledged that the pilots seemingly turned the plane a little bit left off the end of the runway, to avoid the localizer antenna. So at least the overrun was handled as well as it could be.

Based on the preliminary information we have so far, DEI does not appear to be a factor in this accident. 😉

A FedEx MD-11 overran the runway at Miami Airport last night, and ended up in the grass just short of the airport perimeter fence. Fortunately there were no major injuries, and the pilots managed to walk off the plane. This had major operational impacts for the airport, as a ground stop was issued, delaying lots of travelers.

Unlike the 21 Air Boeing 767 accident we saw in September, there were no fatalities this time around. Either way, two cargo planes going off Miami runways in under three months is not great.

What do you make of this FedEx MD-11 accident in Miami?

It's that time of year again: Your last chance to plan your final flights or mattress runs of 2026 in order to snag last-minute elite status for next year.

If you hold Marriott Bonvoy elite status and aren't going to requalify for your status tier this year, there's good news: The program is extending its “soft landing” policy into 2027. With this policy, if you fail to requalify for your current status this year, you will only drop one tier from March 2027 until February 2028.

Related: Marriott elite status: What it is and how to earn it

Based on the program's elite-status policies, the Marriott Bonvoy status you earned in 2025 will expire at the end of February 2027 unless you requalify for your current level or higher in 2026. But what if you don't meet the threshold for the same or higher status?

That's where Marriott's generous soft landing policy comes in. Whether you qualify for a level far below your current status or don't qualify for status at all in 2026, you'll only drop one status tier in 2027.

According to Marriott's website, members who don't requalify for status will see their new, lower tier take effect in early March 2027, and they can enjoy this status through February 2028. Meanwhile, if you requalify for your existing tier or a higher tier, you will also hold this status through February 2028.

This soft landing policy, which Marriott has offered for years, is a win-win: It provides valuable benefits to elite members who weren't able to requalify for status, while giving them a reason to stay loyal to Marriott and perhaps try again for status next year.

Related: The complete guide to earning Marriott elite status with credit cards

Marriott Bonvoy elite status offers some excellent perks, such as room upgrades, late checkout and even lounge access. Thankfully, with this soft landing policy, mid- and upper-tier elite members who don’t requalify this year won’t be left empty-handed. You can still enjoy the benefits of the next-lower tier from March 2027 to February 2028.

For example, with Titanium Elite status, expiring Ambassador Elite members will enjoy many of the same perks of their current status, including complimentary breakfast at most brands, suite upgrades at check-in, 75% bonus points earned on stays and a status match to United MileagePlus Premier Silver status.

You should see your new Marriott status and updated expiration in early March.
