#6141. The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek Will Pay You To Redeem Points Over Peak Dates… But Why?

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is incentivizing people to redeem points at the property for stays over some pretty peak dates, which you don’t often see, as flagged by View from the Wing. This has the potential to be a good deal, but beyond that, I think the more interesting part of this story is the topic of why the hotel would offer something like this, since this is pretty rare.

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is offering 15,000 points back per night when you redeem over some peak dates, for a total of up to 90,000 points back (which you’d get if redeeming for six nights). To cover the basics:

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is a ski-in, ski-out property in Colorado, and it’s one I’ve reviewed before. For what it’s worth, the hotel is currently charging 55,000 World of Hyatt points per night over the dates eligible for this promotion.

Based on my valuation of 1.4 cents per World of Hyatt point, that means a redemption will cost you the equivalent of $770 per night. Meanwhile cash rates are running double as much, and that’s before taxes are factored in.

Understandably, I think a lot of people might be confused as to why the Park Hyatt Beaver Creek would be incentivizing award redemptions in this way. If the hotel wants to fill rooms, why only offer bonus points for points stays, and not for cash stays? That’s especially true when you consider redeeming points is already a good value compared to the cash rate.

The explanation here is probably pretty simple, if you understand the economics at play. I’ve written in the past about how hotels are reimbursed for award stays. Keep in mind that the loyalty program centrally (rather than the individual hotel) sets the cost for redemptions, based on their internal costs associated with redemptions. The way it generally works is as follows:

How does this all factor into the Park Hyatt Beaver Creek’s promotion? I suspect a few factors are at play here:

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is offering 15,000 points per night for award redemption over peak holiday dates. So while the standard rate is 55,000 points per night, you’d end up paying 40,000 points per night, which is quite the deal compared to the cash rate.

Given that some hotels treat points guests as second class guests who are staying for “free,” I think the goal here is pretty clear. Hotels are reimbursed for award stays based on overall occupancy levels, and presumably the hotel hopes that a promotion like this will get it to the occupancy level needed to trigger the highest reimbursement rate.

What do you make of this Park Hyatt Beaver Creek promotion?

#6139. Gabe Evans announces 2028 comeback bid from Boebert’s district

Rep. Gabe Evans, here arriving at the Capitol in July for a House Republican Conference meeting, lost his bid for a second term representing Colorado's 8th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Colorado Rep. Gabe Evans, who lost reelection earlier this month, announced Monday a 2028 run from the neighboring district of fellow defeated Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert.

“Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls' sports and locker rooms, protect our water, and make energy affordable,” Evans said in a statement.

His announcement comes less than two weeks after he lost his bid for a second term representing the battleground 8th District in the Denver area. While the race had been considered one of the most competitive in the country, Democratic former state Rep. Manny Rutinel secured victory by 15 points.

As part of House Democrats’ massive midterm gains, they flipped three seats in Colorado. Boebert narrowly lost her reelection bid in the 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, while Republican Rep. Jeff Crank lost in the 5th District.

Evans’ statement cited his ties to the 4th District, which encompasses the eastern part of the state and extends into the Denver metro area.

“From Loveland to Lamar, I’m ready to keep fighting in the 4th District, where I grew up, and where my family has lived since 1976,” he said.

The district has a deep history of voting Republican. Boebert won by 11 points in 2024 while Donald Trump carried the district by 18 points.

Evans is far from the first member of Congress to switch to a district seen as more favorable to his party. Boebert herself shifted from Colorado's more competitive 3rd District to run for the heavily conservative 4th in 2024.

The 4th District will likely be a top target for Republicans in 2028, and Evans’ campaign sought to portray him as a clear front-runner in what could become a crowded GOP primary.

“Gabe Evans will enter 2027 and the race for Colorado’s 4th Congressional District with $300,000 in campaign funds and name recognition that no first-time candidate in the district could match,” his campaign said in the statement. “Combined with his record as an Army aviator, police officer, rancher, and member of Congress, that gives him a head start in money, name recognition, and credibility before the field takes shape.”

A former state legislator and Denver-area police officer, Evans also served 12 years in the Army. He was first elected to the House in 2024, unseating Democrat Yadira Caraveo, and currently sits on the Energy and Commerce and Homeland Security committees.

Laubacher, a Navy veteran who will take office on Jan. 3, is the first Democrat elected to represent the 4th District since Betsy Markey won her lone term in 2008. In response to Evans’ announcement, Laubacher’s campaign said she would be “focused on making Washington deliver” for district residents.

“There’s real work to do: ending the war in Iran that Gabe Evans voted six times to continue, lowering the cost of groceries and fertilizer that his eight votes for the tariffs helped drive up, and protecting the rural hospitals across the 4th district he voted to gut,” Laubacher spokesperson Taylor Gillespie said in a statement.

#6138. Two American Airlines 737s Collide On Taxiway At Reagan National, One Loses Winglet

Two American Airlines Boeing 737-800s collided while lining up on a taxiway at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA) on Friday evening, with images of the aftermath showing one jet had its winglet torn off. Moments after the collision, a pilot told air traffic control (ATC) that the aircraft had moved "slightly over the hold short line" and had "swapped paint" with the American jet next to it.

The mishap occurred at around 5:10 PM local time near Runway 19 and involved American Flight 638 to Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) and American Flight 2152 to Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD). It is the second time in less than 20 months that two American-branded aircraft have collided while waiting to depart from DCA, following a similar wingtip collision in April 2025.

Flight tracking data shows that both 737s had taxied out and were lining up waiting to enter Runway 19, with Flight 2152 lined up behind Flight 638. When the controller instructed Flight 638 to hold short of the runway, one of its pilots reported that they had collided with a fellow American 737, before stating that they were unsure whether the two aircraft were still attached.

A pilot onboard Flight 2152 then confirmed, "Oh yeah, we got clipped," before stating that the two 737s had separated. Debris was then reported, with a pilot stating that a "whole winglet" had been torn off and was on the ground. Airport operations subsequently recovered the winglet, and both aircraft taxied back to their gates for inspection. An inbound Envoy Air aircraft was also ordered by ATC to go-around immediately after the incident.

In a statement to Simple Flying, American said that "the wingtips of both Boeing 737-800s made contact," and that both planes had been taken out of service for maintenance inspections. The airline added that passengers on both flights would depart later on Friday evening. Tracking data shows that Flight 2152 left at around 11:00 PM, while Flight 638 departed at 11:20 PM, representing a delay of around six hours for both flights. An American spokesperson said,

"While taxiing for departure at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA), an American Airlines aircraft made contact with another American aircraft."

Hold short lines consist of four yellow lines painted across a taxiway before it meets a runway, and are there to prevent potentially dangerous runway incursions. Two solid lines are on the taxiway side, while two dashed lines are on the runway side. Pilots must stop before the solid lines unless ATC has cleared them to enter the runway.

The taxiway leading to DCA's Runway 19 is wide enough to accommodate two aircraft lined up side-by-side, an arrangement attempted by both jets on Friday. The 737-800 has a wingspan of 117 feet 5 inches (35.8 meters) including winglets, and pilots are expected to maintain situational awareness to ensure sufficient clearance from other aircraft.

The Federal Aviation Administration has confirmed it is investigating the incident, while the extent of the damage will determine whether the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) also becomes involved. Under the NTSB's definitions, an incident without serious injuries is only classified as an accident if an aircraft sustains "substantial damage." Notably, this category specifically excludes damage to wingtips.

Winglets can really cut fuel consumption and costs, but engineers have to carefully weigh down sides.

Friday's incident is the latest in a series of ground collisions at major US airports in recent weeks. On November 14, a UPS Airlines Boeing 767 freighter and a Copa Airlines Boeing 737-800 collided at Miami International Airport (MIA) after the cargo jet taxied past the point where it had been instructed to give way.

On October 6, a Delta Air Lines Airbus A350 clipped the horizontal stabilizer of an Air Canada Boeing 777 being towed at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), leaving its winglet lodged in the 777's tail. Friday's collision also has similarities to an incident at DCA in April 2025, when two American Eagle regional jets clipped wings while waiting to depart, one of which had several members of Congress on board.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Seems to happen so often these days, it's hardly news.

Wyndham Rewards recently revised its fixed award chart, expanding from three to four redemption tiers.

The 15,000- and 30,000-point tiers remain, while free nights now start at 5,000 points instead of 7,500. Wyndham also added a 45,000-point tier for a select number of its highest-tier hotels and redistributed thousands of properties across all four tiers.

The new top tier is 50% higher than the former 30,000-point maximum, a devaluation in anyone's book. However, the new astonishingly low 5,000-point tier was what caught my attention. What exactly do you get for so few Wyndham Rewards points?

As someone who can't resist a great deal, I checked into one of these hotels to find out whether it was an amazing new sweet spot or a night I would rather forget.

Related: Wyndham Rewards guide: How to earn and redeem points, elite status and more

On a recent visit to Kansas and Missouri, I checked the Wyndham Rewards website and saw that the area had several properties for just 5,000 points per night.

I chose the Super 8 by Wyndham Riverside/Kansas City, mainly for its proximity to the beautiful new Kansas City International Airport (MCI). The next morning, I was flying to Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) before continuing to Europe in a lie-flat seat for less than the price of a cup of coffee.

At the time of booking, the hotel had a 2.8-out-of-5 score based on 84 ratings on Wyndham's website, which did not fill me with confidence. However, the Wyndham Rewards member rate for my night was $96.21 including taxes and fees. Redeeming 5,000 points therefore gave me 1.92 cents per Wyndham point, about 3.5 times TPG's November 2026 valuation of 0.55 cents per Wyndham point.

Related: It’s easy to earn Wyndham Diamond status — here’s how and why you should care

I took a Lyft from downtown Kansas City, Missouri, to Riverside, a small suburb on the north bank of the Missouri River. First impressions of the property were that it was pretty remote, with nothing really nearby other than the Argosy Casino.

There was plenty of parking, and the 48 rooms were spread across a two-story motor-inn-style building.

While the property was less than 20 years old and was renovated in 2010, the rather garish lime-green lobby looked ready for another refresh.

I was quickly helped by a very friendly attendant, who I believe was the franchisee, and his wife, who also greeted me warmly.

There were several property rules listed on the counter with normal restrictions on smoking and pets in rooms.

What raised an eyebrow was the rule that visitors were allowed in guest rooms for only 60 minutes maximum, which made me wonder what kind of visitors might be passing through the doors and for what purpose in one-hour blocks.

The attendant thanked me for being a Wyndham Rewards member and quickly handed me my room key. So far, the experience had been better than the 2.8-out-of-5 rating suggested, but the room would be the biggest test.

I nervously opened the door to find a comfortable room with a king-size bed, plenty of pillows, a large flat-screen TV, a minifridge and a workspace.

Like the lobby, I doubt this decor will win any design awards, but it was clean, quiet and comfortable, and everything worked.

The separate bathroom had a tub/shower combo and a spotless toilet with several towels for me to choose from.

If I had one complaint about the room, it was that the showerhead was pulling away from the bathroom wall, but it still provided a steady flow of hot water.

The property was light on other amenities: There was no fitness center, swimming pool, bar or restaurant. However, the Argosy Casino was a few minutes' walk away, so there was plenty to keep me occupied for the evening.

After a good night's uninterrupted sleep, all guests even received a complimentary breakfast, with toast, cereals, juice and coffee available.

This is a great deal for a 5,000 point redemption with no resort fee.

Related: How I earned 24,500 points from $180 in hotel stays

The staff bid me a friendly farewell when I checked out, and I was on my way to the airport after a comfortable, peaceful and stress-free stay.

Wyndham Rewards are easy to earn, as they transfer at a 1:1 rate from the following transferable rewards:

But the best transfer option is for anyone with Wells Fargo Rewards points. This is because rather than transferring at a 1:1 rate, they transfer at a much more generous 1:2 rate. This means you would only need 2,500 Wells Fargo points to book a 5,000-point Wyndham Rewards hotel night, and Wells Fargo points can be transferred in any increments, unlike the strict 1,000-point increments of most transferable rewards.

Given that Wyndham Rewards properties offering 5,000-point nights regularly sell these nights for around $100 cash, this is an easy way to get around 4 cents per Wells Fargo point, more than twice TPG's valuation of Wells Fargo Rewards points.

Barclays also offers four Wyndham Rewards branded credit cards. Depending on the card and, in some cases, when it was opened, eligible cardholders receive a 10%, 20%, or 25% discount on free-night redemptions. That reduces a standard 5,000-point night to 4,500, 4,000 or 3,750 points, respectively.

Wyndham's new 5,000-point redemptions will not put you in a luxury hotel, but this stay was terrific value for money and delivered a clean, quiet room, a comfortable bed and a simple breakfast before an early flight.

The decor was dated, and the loose showerhead fixture needed attention. Even so, the friendly service and uninterrupted night's sleep were far better than the hotel's 2.8-out-of-5 rating had led me to expect. For a one-night stay near an airport, I would give it 4 out of 5.

Redeeming 5,000 Wyndham Rewards points instead of paying the nearly $100 member rate will give you 2 cents' worth per point. Even better, a traveler transferring from Wells Fargo Rewards would need just 2,500 points for the same award — I can't think of a more valuable way to use Wells Fargo points.

I would happily stay at a property like this again for just 5,000 Wyndham Rewards points per night.

#6136. Global Entry Renewal: My Step-By-Step Experience, Cost, And Timeline

Global Entry is an incredibly useful program for anyone who travels internationally with any frequency. I’ve had Global Entry for nearly 15 years now. Several weeks ago, I received an email reminding me that I was within six months of my Global Entry expiring, so I just went through the process of renewing it.

In this post, I’d like to outline the process of renewing a Global Entry membership, since it’s something that frequent travelers have to do periodically. I’ll include a step-by-step guide, the cost, and the timeline. I’ve separately written about how to apply for Global Entry.

For those not familiar, Global Entry is a US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) program that allows expedited clearance for pre-approved, low-risk travelers upon arrival in the United States (or at CBP Preclearance facilities). With this program, approved members can enter the United States using their biometric data at virtually all international airports.

The exact way that biometric data is verified varies by airport. It used to be that you’d have to go up to one of the Global Entry kiosks and answer a few questions. Then they updated the technology, and you just had to stand in front of one of those kiosks for a few seconds. Now many airports just have a camera in the Global Entry lane that automatically verifies your identity as you walk through. It’s pretty awesome.

You do still typically have to walk past an immigration officer and verify that you don’t have anything to declare. You can then proceed to the baggage claim area and exit (unless you’re selected for additional screening).

Over the years, Global Entry has probably saved me dozens of hours. Back in the day I’d be stressed when landing back in the United States, wondering if I’d be stuck in an hour-long immigration queue. Nowadays I can just breeze right through.

Before I share a step-by-step guide of my Global Entry renewal experience, let me share some basics about the timeline, how much it costs, etc.

Global Entry is valid for roughly five years after you’re approved. The reason I say “roughly” is because it’s valid for five years from your next birthday. In other words, if your birthday is December 1, and you apply January 1, 2027, your membership would be valid through December 1, 2032.

If you strategically apply for Global Entry, you can get it for almost six years with one membership. Just apply shortly after your birthday.

Generally speaking you’ll get an email six months before your Global Entry expires informing you of the upcoming expiration. If you want to look for it in your email, that usually comes from [email protected].

Alternatively you can log into your Trusted Traveler Program dashboard, and go to the section that lists your program status. You’ll see the expiration date listed there.

You can apply to have your Global Entry renewed up to a year before the expiration date. There’s no penalty for renewing early, in the sense that it will still be valid for five years from when your membership currently expires, and not five years from when you’re approved. So you might as well renew early.

You won’t want to let your membership lapse, since the process is more complicated for a lapsed membership. Be sure to apply for renewal well before your Global Entry is set to expire.

There is a grace period for Global Entry renewal, as long as you submit your renewal application before your membership expires. Specifically, there’s a grace period of up to 24 months, which is super long. Back in the day, the grace period was only six months, but that has been increased considerably over time.

If you do submit your application but aren’t approved before the expiration, you’ll continue to be able to use Global Entry the same way as before during that period.

It costs $120 for adults to renew Global Entry (Global Entry is free for kids under the age of 18). Fortunately, many credit cards offer a fee credit toward Global Entry renewal. Note that in all cases, you can use your credit for anyone — so if you have extra credits, you can use them for friends and family to renew their Global Entry.

When you first apply for Global Entry you have to be interviewed, either in-person or virtually. Do you need to be interviewed when you renew? It depends:

While only tangentially related, what happens if you have to renew your passport before your Global Entry expires? The good news is that it’s a really easy process.

You just have to log into your account on the Trusted Traveler Programs website and update your passport number there. Your Global Entry will then continue to apply with the new passport up until the Global Entry expiration date. See this post for more details on how that works.

On November 15, 2026, I submitted my application to renew Global Entry. My current membership expires on April 20, 2027, though as long as the application is submitted before then, there’s a grace period of two years.

To renew your Global Entry membership, you’ll want to go to the Trusted Traveler Programs website, and click “LOG IN” at the top right under the “Returning GE/NEXUS/SENTRI/FAST Member/Applicants” heading.

Note that back in 2017 the government migrated from the Global Online Enrollment System (GOES). So if you don’t yet have a new Trusted Traveler Programs profile, you’ll have to set that up first, which is a quick process (though at this point I imagine that virtually everyone has transitioned).

Once logged in you’ll see your current Global Entry membership, and underneath that you should see a “Renew Membership” option listed, assuming you’re within the renewal period.

There you’ll be able to select the program you want to apply for or renew, which in this case would be Global Entry.

Essentially the Global Entry renewal application contains all the information you submitted the last time around, so you just have to confirm that it’s correct, and update any outdated information.

This includes reviewing your personal information, documents, driver’s license, address, employment info, travel history, and more.

You do have to upload a copy of your passport during the process (assuming your passport number changed since your last application, which will likely be the case half of the time for adults, since passports are usually valid for 10 years, while Global Entry is valid for five or so years).

The only slightly complicated part of this process is having to update your travel history, as you have to list all of the countries that you’ve been to since the last time that you applied. So yeah, that can take a second, if you’re a frequent traveler.

At some points the process of reviewing info isn’t very intuitive, as you have to click a lot of unnecessary buttons confirming that nothing has changed. But it’s pretty self explanatory. I’d say the whole process up until this point took me about 15 minutes, and that includes having to recall all the countries from the past five years (which is quite a few).

To finish off the process you just have to certify that all of the information that you’re providing is accurate, and then you have to pay.

When you pay, make sure you use a credit card that has a Global Entry fee credit, assuming you have one.

I used my Amex Business Platinum, and the fee reimbursed within two days.

As mentioned above, I submitted the Global Entry renewal application on November 15, 2026. Then on November 25, 2026 — 10 days later — I received an email indicating that there had been an application status change on the renewal. The email came from [email protected] with the subject line “TTP Application Status Change.”

The email as such doesn’t tell you a whole lot, so you have to log into your account again to see the status. There I found out that the application was approved, meaning that there was no need to take part in an interview.

Experiences seem to be mixed as to whether an interview is required for renewals. For example, during my last renewal, I did need to get an interview, while during my renewal before that, I didn’t need to get an interview.

The good news is that if you do need to be interviewed, you can typically just do so when you return from an international trip. When I did it, it took less than a minute.

I just went through the process of renewing Global Entry, and it was pretty easy. You basically just have to confirm that all the information during your last application is still accurate, add all the countries you’ve been to since then, and pay a fee.

This time around, the application was processed in 10 days, and there was a full approval, so no interview was required. However, don’t be surprised if you do need an interview, as that happened to me during my last renewal.

Hopefully this is useful for anyone else who has a Global Entry renewal coming up soon.

Both our Nexus cards have pictures that are 15 years old (from our original application/interview). One thing I didn't remember from before is when the card(s) came you have to go back online & activate it with the "CVV" on the card.

I travel internationally with quite some frequency and this subscription is about as useful to me as a chocolate teapot because, despite its misleading brand name, it only works in one country and I have limited need or desire to visit that country...and even if I did travel there more often, they might have ended up rejecting my application because I don't have the 'right' nationality, travel history, regime-friendly Facebook posts or whatever.

I was renewed in 48 hours without the detailed questions cited here. Very impressed by their service.

I renewed back in September. Took maybe 24 hours to get the notice saying I was approved again. I do find it funny that my photo remains of 25-year-old me, taken in 2011 at LAX. I haven't had to re-interview since, and 41 year old me definitely doesn't look like the skinnier, full head of hair, 25 year old me.

#6135. How Many Crew Members Does It Take To Fly A B-1 Lancer?

The B-1 Lancer remains an integral part of the US Air Force’s long-range bombing capability. While the process of phasing out the supersonic variable-sweep-wing heavy bomber is underway, the aircraft is set for at least a decade more of service. This is especially true as the Air Force awaits the moment it can drop the Lancer from its ranks with absolute certainty that it will not leave a weaker fleet overall.

Reaching such a moment was always going to be tough, though. The Lancer is highly versatile, capable of carrying the largest payload of conventional weapons among any jet in the US Air Force to target precision or non-precision targets on various missions. No doubt, that is hard to replicate. It also explains why operating such an aircraft takes a whole team of crewmembers.

In total, it requires four personnel onboard to split the workload of operating the B-1 Lancer. Two pilots — an aircraft commander and co-pilot — sit up front and handle the task of getting the high-speed bomber to target, often over hours-long missions. Two personnel located behind them in the aft crew station are then responsible for managing the jet’s weapons systems.

But each crewmember’s task is complementary to another's, and their jobs are interlinked in practice. By design, the Lancer boasts multi-mission capabilities that Boeing — the primary contractor for the program since acquiring Rockwell International in 1996 — notes can be applied anywhere in the world. That means managing the Lancer’s variable wing sweeps, carrying out air-to-air refueling, and even flying low-level at high speed across variable terrain, to name a few, all before deploying weapons. That, naturally, takes a team.

While the pilots divvy up tasks like handling the Lancer and carrying out standard communications, the rear-seat weapons systems officers — or combat systems officers, as the Air Force calls them — directly offer aid in several ways. The offensive systems officer (OSO) is responsible for navigation, as well as primarily operating the plane’s Lockheed Martin targeting system known as a Sniper Pod, for instance. Including a defensive systems officer (DSO) who monitors threats and might deploy countermeasures, the rear-seaters also assist during low-flying by calling out altimeter readings, for example. Each weapons systems officer is trained to do the other's jobs too, and can communicate with ground forces to coordinate strikes. Again, it takes a crew to fly the Lancer, and that is partly down to its extensive capabilities.

Alongside the B-52 Stratofortress and B-2 Spirit, the B-1 Lancer is one of three bomber types the US Air Force uses today. Accordingly, each has a specific role. The B-52 is the heaviest of the trio and the backbone of the fleet by number in service. Conversely, the stealth B-2 is designed to penetrate air defenses. Each of these can be equipped with nuclear, as well as conventional weapons. While the B-1 only carries conventional payloads, it is arguably the most versatile.

Indeed, the B-1 trumps its counterparts in range and service ceiling, as detailed below in figures from the Washington DC-based industry publication The National Interest. Notably, it is the quickest of the three, being the only one capable of surpassing supersonic speeds. It also boasts the highest maximum payload, at roughly 75,000 pounds (34,000 kg) compared with the B-52’s approximate 70,000 pounds (31,500 kg) and the B-2’s maximum 40,000 pounds (18,100 kg).

US Air Force bombers, from The National Interest:

~79 feet swept / ~137 feet extended (24/41.8 meters)

1,620-3,780 nautical miles (3,000-7,000 km)

~70,000 pounds (31,500 kg) of mixed ordnance, including conventional bombs, precision-guided munitions, stand-off weapons, and nuclear weapons

~75,000 pounds (34,000 kg) of conventional weapons

Up to 40,000 pounds (18,100 kg) of conventional and nuclear precision munitions

Developed in the 1970s, the B-1 was initially slated to replace the B-52. Some to-and-fro saw the program canceled in 1977; however, it was reinstated under the Reagan administration, at which point improvements were made and the B-1B variant we know today emerged. As the Air Force writes: “[Its] capabilities, when combined with its substantial payload, excellent radar targeting system, long loiter time, and survivability, make the B-1B a key element of any joint or composite strike force.”

The B-52 stays relevant thanks to its low operating costs, its plentiful remaining flight hours, and the ability to use stand-off munitions.

In any case, getting a B-1 Lancer off the ground takes far more than just its four-strong flight crew. Behind the scenes, everything from refueling to major fixes can pile on the human hours required to keep just one of the jets in service.

The 28th Maintenance Group, responsible for servicing B-1s at Ellsworth Air Force Base, South Dakota, and one of the jet’s two primary stations, is said to encompass some 1,500 professionals, for reference. This is split into four squadrons, each supplying personnel for specific work — be it loading and supporting mission operations, servicing munitions, managing overall fleet utilization and health, or carrying out heavy repairs.

While a flight crew rested, ate, checked out equipment, received several briefings, and so on before a mission during Operation Enduring Freedom in Afghanistan, ground-based maintenance crews regularly spent five or more hours preparing each B-1, per the Air Force. That is, the entire aircraft was analyzed to be cleared to fly by a crew chief. Upon each B-1’s return, about 10 maintenance specialists would meet the flight crew for a briefing on the plane’s performance, before an intelligence officer sat down with those onboard to go over the mission details. While substantial, the large-scale effort required for each B-1 flight is similarly mirrored by its counterparts.

As the largest US bomber in operation today, the B-52 Stratofortress also requires the largest aircrew. No doubt that's also down to its roots dating back to the 1950s, and to older technology that relies on several specialist operators. In contrast, the B-2 Spirit is operated with a smaller, more conventional crew than both the B-52 and B-1.

For the B-52, five personnel go on each mission, including an aircraft commander, co-pilot, and electronic warfare officer—all seated on the upper deck—alongside a radar navigator and a navigator located downstairs. Add in those on the ground and the number needed per flight balloons once again. The 5th Mission Support Group — one of five groups assigned to support B-52 operations from Minot Air Force Base, North Dakota — has 1,600 military and civilian members alone, for instance, though it also serves the 91st Missile Wing.

Just two crew members are needed to operate the far more modern B-2, developed in the 1980s and first delivered in 1993. This includes a pilot and mission commander. They are also joined by numerous people on the ground, with the 509th Bomb Wing at Whiteman Air Force Base, Missouri, again encompassing several groups dedicated to supporting B-2 operations at one of two sites that primarily house the bomber.

Such a two-strong crew makeup, like that of the B-2 Spirit, is on course to become increasingly common across the US Air Force’s bomber fleet. With the Northrop Grumman B-21 Raider set to start arriving with the military from next year, existing B-2s and B-1 Lancers will make way.

This process has already begun, in fact. In 2021, it was announced that 17 B-1s would be retired, leaving an active fleet of 45. “Due to the wear and tear placed on the B-1 fleet over the past two decades, maintaining these bombers would cost tens of millions of dollars per aircraft to get back to status quo,” then Air Force Global Strike Command head Timothy Ray said at the time. “And that’s just to fix the problems we know about.”

Northrop Grumman B-21 Raider specifications, from The Defense Post:

Those that are left are expected to be retained into the 2030s to ensure time for the new B-21 fleet to be delivered and incorporated. Given that plans are for the Air Force to acquire at least 100 of the new stealth bombers, extensive training of flight and maintenance crews will be needed, of course.

Either way, that means the B-1 Lancer’s days are somewhat numbered, along with its unique four-person aircrew requirement. As to when the B-1 will ultimately be phased out, time will tell. Plans previously called for this to happen in the early 2030s. Now it is expected to be closer to the end of the decade.

In the meantime, funds are still being poured into sustaining and modernizing what is left of the fleet. Back in 2019, Boeing secured a $14.2 billion contract to test and modify weapons systems on both B-1 Lancers and B-52 Stratofortresses.

#6134. White House budget aide Ueland slated to head GAO

Eric Ueland, No. 2 official at the White House Office of Management and Budget, arrives for his confirmation hearing in the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on April 3, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump on Monday nominated Eric Ueland, deputy director for management in the White House budget office, to be the next comptroller general to lead the Government Accountability Office.

The nomination fills in the blanks after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., had scheduled a Nov. 19 hearing to examine more than a dozen of Trump’s nominees for executive and judicial positions but without identifying who the comptroller general candidate would be. Ueland's name has since been added to the hearing agenda.

The move sets up an unprecedented scenario where a top official of the Office of Management and Budget, a White House office that has tangled with the Government Accountability Office since Trump’s first term, is put forward as the next head of the legislative agency.

The GAO, a congressional watchdog with some 3,000 employees, has repeatedly accused the administration of violating the 1974 budget law by withholding or "impounding" enacted, appropriated funds. In September, for example, the GAO said Trump’s cancellation of $810 million in spending without the approval of Congress through a so-called pocket rescission was illegal.

White House Budget Director Russ Vought was quick to respond on X, writing that GAO “has become hyper partisan and ... they make their legal assessments based on whether Democrats are in the White House.” The administration has dismissed GAO opinions, arguing the agency has no authority over the executive branch because it is part of the legislative branch.

Democrats immediately denounced Ueland's nomination, saying it promised to further inflame tensions between the executive and legislative branches over the power of the purse.

“It would be lunacy for the Senate to hand a 15-year term leading Congress’ nonpartisan watchdog to a Russ Vought acolyte who spends his days plotting new ways for this administration to defy Congress," said Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., who is likely to chair the panel next year.

"Ueland orchestrated the president’s destructive mass firing campaign, is presiding over the razing of USAID, and is the last person who should be leading GAO," Murray said in a statement.

Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., ranking member of the Homeland Security committee, urged all senators to oppose the Ueland nomination, saying it would provide “further power to the Executive Branch at a time when independent oversight from Congress is needed more than ever.”

Peters also reiterated his previous criticism of Republicans for skipping bipartisan deliberations by a special 10-member legislative commission that is charged under statute with recommending candidates to the president for nomination.

“All three times the Commission process has occurred in the past, the president has selected a nominee with bipartisan support,” Peters said.

In a sign of potential trouble for the nomination, a few Republicans expressed qualms about Ueland and what critics described as a rushed process for picking a GAO chief.

"I'm not a fan," said retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who faulted Ueland's boss for not providing proof of the cost savings claimed by Trump's Department of Government Efficiency, known as DOGE.

"To me, there's a lack of discipline or business experience in there to answer that simple question, or the reason they don't answer it is they don't have an answer," Tillis said. "Both are bad."

While Tillis stopped short of promising to oppose Ueland, he said the nomination "deserves individual consideration" instead of being taken up in a group with several other nominees.

And Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, "has concerns that the nomination is too partisan, particularly given how independent and long-term the appointment of the Comptroller General is," a spokesman said in a statement.

Ueland has served as deputy director for management at the White House budget office since last year following his confirmation by the Senate on a party line 52-45 vote. He also has been performing the duties of the OMB controller since September 2025, according to his LinkedIn profile.

An expert on legislative procedure and strategy, Ueland has worked in a wide range of administrative and policy-oriented positions in the executive branch — including at OMB, the State Department and White House — and before that in the Senate.

He served as director of legislative affairs for Trump in his first term, as well as the State Department undersecretary for civilian security, democracy and human rights, and director of the department’s Office of U.S. Foreign Assistance, among other positions.

Before that, he was the Senate Budget Committee’s GOP staff director under then-Chairman Michael B. Enzi, R-Wyo., for four years through the end of 2017.

Earlier, he worked as chief of staff to then-Senate GOP Whip Don Nickles of Oklahoma and then-Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist of Tennessee.

Ueland, who has a bachelor’s degree in history from the University of San Francisco, lacks the financial background of recent past comptrollers. He has, however, gone deep in the weeds with numbers at OMB and the Senate Budget Committee, and has extensive experience as an administrator.

Former comptroller Charles A. Bowsher was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson and assistant secretary of the Navy for financial management before President Ronald Reagan tapped him to lead the GAO in 1981.

David M. Walker, his successor, was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson, assistant secretary of labor in the Employee Benefits Security Administration, and deputy executive director of the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation before his nomination by President Bill Clinton.

Gene L. Dodaro, whose 15-year term ended last year, had a bachelor’s degree in accounting and had worked at GAO for some 35 years before President Barack Obama nominated him to succeed Walker.

When Dodaro left, he designated Orice Williams Brown, who was GAO’s chief operating officer, as acting comptroller.

Before Trump nominated Ueland, the six Republican members of the legislative commission sent a letter to the White House last week recommending three candidates for the position — Ueland, Brian C. DeBusk and Roland Foster, according to sources.

DeBusk is president and CEO of DeRoyal Industries, a privately held medical equipment manufacturer. He served on the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission from 2016 to 2022 after being appointed by Dodaro. Foster is a longtime GOP aide currently serving as senior adviser to retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa.

#6132. Hyatt Credit Cards Compared: Is The Personal Or Business Card Better?

Chase and Hyatt have a pretty straightforward co-brand card portfolio, as there’s one personal card and one business card. Specifically, I’m talking about the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card.

In this post, I’d like to compare the two cards, and talk about which is better. First let’s cover the details of both products, and then I’ll share my take on which is worth applying for. This is an especially good time to pick them up, given the current welcome offers.

Link: Learn more about the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Credit Card

To start, let’s cover the details of Hyatt’s two co-branded credit cards. Below is a chart with the basics, and I’ll go into a bit more detail below.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) is Hyatt’s personal credit card, with a $95 annual fee. Hyatt’s personal credit card offers a variety of perks, including the following:

The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (learn more) is Hyatt’s business credit card, with a $199 annual fee. Hyatt’s business credit card offers many benefits, including the following:

If you’re considering applying for a Hyatt credit card and would be eligible for a business or personal card, which should you apply for?

The first thing to understand is that the World of Hyatt Card and World of Hyatt Business Card aren’t mutually exclusive. You could apply for both cards, and also earn the welcome bonus on each. So in some ways, it’s worth assessing the value of the cards independently, since you don’t actually have to decide between them.

If you ask me, the World of Hyatt Card is a slam dunk if you stay at Hyatts with any frequency. The card has a reasonable annual fee, and it’s worth holding onto even if you don’t spend a dime on it.

The annual free night award alone more than justifies the annual fee, and the five nights toward elite status with no spending requirement is a great perk as well. On top of that, I think there’s merit to spending $15,000 on the card per year, to earn a second annual free night award, plus to earn an additional six elite nights toward status.

The math on the World of Hyatt Business Card isn’t quite as straightforward. The card has a different welcome bonus than on the personal card, so there’s merit to picking up the card for that. But beyond that, the main reason you’ll want to get this card is because it offers the best rate of return on spending in terms of earning elite nights.

With the business card, you can earn one elite night for every $2,000 spent, while with the personal card, you can get one elite night for every $2,500 spent (though the increments for earning elite nights differ).

So my best consolidated advice would be that the World of Hyatt Card is more valuable and is easier to justify, and is the best for the first $15,000 in spending annually. Beyond that, though, the World of Hyatt Business Card is best for helping to earn Hyatt status, especially if you’re a big spender. Furthermore, it can be worth picking up the card in part for the huge bonus.

Hyatt has both a personal and business co-branded credit cards. The products are totally different, and there’s potentially merit to both. The World of Hyatt Card is much easier to justify — the card has a lower annual fee, offers an annual free night award, provides five nights toward status without a spending requirement, and more.

That being said, you don’t have to decide between the two cards, and there’s also merit to getting the World of Hyatt Business Card. The card has a better welcome bonus, and has the potential to be more rewarding for spending.

What’s your take on the value proposition of Hyatt’s personal vs. business card?

Although the holiday season can be joyous, it can be an expensive time of year, with gifts, travel and gatherings putting extra pressure on your budget.

But with a little planning, you can make the most of your credit card rewards and benefits without overspending.

Here are five tips to help you save money and earn rewards like a pro this holiday season.

First, map out your holiday shopping plans and set a realistic budget for spending. Who are you shopping for? How much are you planning to spend on gifts? What other expenses should you factor into your holiday budget?

These are all good questions to help you set expectations and prevent impulse buys that can lead to overspending.

A spreadsheet is a great way to keep track of spending and budgeting. You can simply insert your budget into a premade template or write it down on paper. If you already know what you plan to buy, insert links to the sales pages so you know how much it will cost.

While adjusting and finalizing your budget, remember to factor in additional costs due to extra gatherings, like larger grocery and dining expenses.

One of the best things about rewards cards is that they often come with perks to help you save money.

Before making your holiday purchases, check whether your credit cards offer statement credits or other benefits that could help you save money.

For example, comes with an up to $75 quarterly statement credit (up to $300 annually) Lululemon credit that can be used at U.S. stores (excluding outlets) or online after enrollment. This is a great way to maximize purchases on clothing, yoga gear or other accessories.

Or, if you have a frequent jet-setter in your life, you can use a credit card’s Global Entry/TSA PreCheck credit to cover their application fee of up to $120.

Statement credits aren't the only card benefits worth checking before you shop. For an expensive electronic device or other high-value gift, purchase protection or extended warranty coverage are other useful perks.

We talk a lot about shopping portals during this time of year. That's because skipping them is essentially leaving money on the table.

By doing your online holiday shopping through a portal, you can earn bonus points or cash back at a massive number of online retailers. Most of the major U.S. airlines have shopping portals to help you earn additional miles on every eligible purchase, or you can use third-party portals such as Rakuten to earn cash back or Amex Membership Rewards or Bilt Points.

We suggest using a shopping portal aggregator like Cashback Monitor to find the best portal for each online purchase. That way, you don’t have to sift through each portal’s offers individually.

No matter where you shop, review any Amex Offers, Chase Offers or Citi Merchant Offers available on your cards. They vary by cardmember, and often stack with your card's standard rewards plus a shopping portal. Some require activation or enrollment before making a purchase.

Related: Everything you need to know about credit card merchant offers

We’re big fans of points and miles at The Points Guy — and for good reason. Points and miles can reduce the cost of future travel, but cash-back cards may be more useful if you want rewards to offset your holiday expenses directly.

A flat-rate cash-back card such as the (see rates and fees) is an easy way to earn rewards no matter where you shop since it offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase and another 1% cash back when you pay your bill. Redeeming those rewards as a statement credit helps reduce the size of January's bill.

The (see rates and fees) is another great option that earns at least 1.5% back on every purchase.

Paying your statement balance in full is generally best, but some rewards credit cards offer a 0% introductory annual percentage rate period on new purchases. That can give you time to pay for a planned expense without interest as long as you have a plan to pay it off completely before the introductory period ends.

Another option is to use one of the financing options some credit card issuers offer. Amex Plan It® and Chase Pay Over Time after purchase may allow eligible cardmembers to divide qualifying purchases of $100 or more into fixed monthly payments, generally with a fixed monthly fee instead of interest.

You’ll almost always save money using these programs compared to paying interest over time.

Related: Chase Pay Over Time and My Chase Loan: Should you opt in?

Holiday shopping doesn't have to derail your budget. By planning ahead, using the right rewards cards and taking advantage of statement credits and shopping portals, you can make your spending more rewarding without buying more than you can afford.

The key is to prioritize your budget over earning points, miles or cash back. After all, the value of those rewards can quickly disappear if you're carrying a balance and paying interest.

#6130. New aviation funding request hits Senate turbulence

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov. 10. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.

Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.

“I got to obviously see the explanation behind it, or sort of laying out the numbers why it's necessary,” Thune said of the $50 billion, which jumped from $30 billion a day earlier.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters he was unimpressed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s request and that he wanted to see a breakdown of how the department would use the funds.

“They got to give us an update,” Tillis said. “I mean, the $50 billion request — I thought that was $30 billion. So people have got to explain to me, really, even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion that Duffy mentioned the other day.”

Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., similarly said legislators would need “more detail” on the request but said “obviously there needs to be more” funding for the modernization efforts.

Hoeven serves on the Senate Transportation-HUD Appropriations Subcommittee, which rolled out a fiscal 2027 spending bill Monday that would increase the FAA’s annual allocation to facilities and equipment by $500 million, a nearly 13 percent boost.

Duffy is slotted to attend the Senate GOP conference lunch on Tuesday, where he is likely to be peppered with such requests for specifics. Meanwhile, FAA staff are expected to brief House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee aides on Tuesday, after that meeting got pushed on Monday.

The Senate’s go-slow approach is in contrast to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who said over the weekend that he would add the $50 billion request to a year-end legislative package.

The White House’s call for additional funds ballooned last week in the aftermath of the nationwide ground stop that created confusion and concern at airports around the country. The Federal Aviation Administration said Sunday that the unusual move was made “out of an abundance of caution” after legacy equipment became flooded with data during routine upgrades.

The FAA’s initial investigation tied the data flooding to work being done at a radar site in Texas and a radio communications site in Arkansas by contractor L3Harris Technologies.

Speaking on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Duffy said the server thought to have caused the flooding was taken to the L3Harris lab in Florida where FAA personnel are working with the FBI to analyze the router that likely caused the system instability.

Still, as administration officials attempt to understand the system errors that led to the ground stop, Duffy has used the moment as justification to lobby for additional funds.

“In this old telecom network, I do have money to switch over from the old copper wires to fiber and we’re 70 percent completed with that mission, but we need a brand new architecture for our telecom and aviation,” Duffy said on CNBC Monday. “This can happen quickly to build a new state of the art telecom network, it’s just that it has to be funded.”

A day before the incident, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought wrote to congressional appropriators, formally asking for $30.1 billion in added funds for the modernization effort, in line with a bill introduced by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., in late September. That ask inexplicably jumped up to $50 billion by Friday night in the aftermath of the ground stop.

On Monday, Thune noted the prior request for approximately $30 billion, which he said included “some other stuff” as well.

Schmitt’s bill and the White House request would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $7.2 billion for a “common automation platform and a common controller workstation,” and $2 billion for cloud computing and telecommunications infrastructure.

Another $10 billion would go toward airport improvement projects, including $2 billion to “construct, replace, and improve terminal air traffic control facilities, including activities using digital tower technologies.”

The request includes $10 billion for a terminal modernization or reconstruction pilot program for certain midsized airports.

Thune said Monday that he tallied about $12 billion in the new request specifically for air traffic control related issues, likely a reference to the $10.1 billion plus the $2 billion for terminal facilities.

“I think there's more we need to figure out, and obviously I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the number one priority, but also we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we're using taxpayer dollars wisely and well,” Thune said. “We’ll hear him out.”

Meanwhile, Democrats kept up the drumbeat of criticism, both for the airspace management that led to the ground stop and the rollout of the new funding request.

“So typical of this incompetent administration — they have money, they don’t use it and then they come back and say ‘give us more money,'” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., said on the floor.

Savannah Behrmann and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#6129. Royal Air Maroc Business Class Boeing 737 Review: Good For A Short Hop

To kick off the return portion of our Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, we flew Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 737-800 business class on the 45-minute flight from Malaga (AGP) to Casablanca (CMN).

I must admit, Royal Air Maroc has a really solid short haul product. While there’s no Wi-Fi or seat back entertainment, I appreciate that the airline has “proper” business class seats, the inflight meal service was outright generous for such a short flight, and I also appreciated the dedicated business class bus upon arrival.

Admittedly the flight attendant serving us didn’t have much personality, and the cabin wasn’t in great condition. But still, those are hardly huge issues. For that matter, it has to be acknowledged how the airlines of northern Africa really lower the bar when it comes to the quality of the inflight experience (hi, Air Algerie!), so on a relative basis, this was rather excellent.

Ford and I booked an itinerary on Royal Air Maroc all the way from Malaga to Miami via Casablanca. The reason was because the airline offered the best schedule that would get us home the same day after our Orient Express Sailing Yachts cruise.

Royal Air Maroc often makes only one business class seat available, so I had to get a bit creative to make this work. I ended up booking one ticket using 57,500 American AAdvantage miles plus $85.72 in taxes & fees, while the other ticket was booked with cash, at the cost of $1,620, with the following itinerary:

10/09 AT989 Malaga to Casablanca departing 2:15PM arriving 1:30PM10/09 AT204 Casablanca to Miami departing 3:00PM arriving 7:45PM

Obviously paying cash for a ticket wasn’t ideal, but that still ended up being less out of pocket than flying British Airways business class through London on awards, factoring in the carrier surcharges.

We arrived at Malaga Airport at around 11:30AM, plenty early for our 2:15PM flight. We headed through security and then cleared passport control… only then did I realize that the non-Schengen lounge is currently closed, so we had no lounge option there.

I guess we could’ve exited passport control again to access the lounge in the Schengen area of the terminal, but we figured that wasn’t worth it, so we just decided to grab a seat. I have to say, the non-Schengen portion of the Malaga Airport had quite the scene. Virtually every other flight departing around the same time was on Jet2, and it was definitely a “festive” spirit in the terminal. Based on the passengers, you’d think the airport had banned close-toed shoes.

Boarding for our flight was scheduled for 1:30PM, 45 minutes before departure, from gate B16. Sure enough, that’s exactly when boarding started, with business class passengers being invited to board first.

We boarded the Royal Air Maroc Boeing 737-800 through the forward door, and then turned right into the business class cabin. Royal Air Maroc’s 737s have 12 business class seats, spread across three rows, in a 2-2 configuration.

Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class seats are particularly spacious, as they boast 43″ of pitch and 21″ of width, with 6″ of recline. So this is significantly more spacious than what you’d find in domestic first class within the United States, where pitch is more commonly around 37-38″ — an extra 5-6″ is definitely noticeable!

These seats have little foot bars that fold down from the seat in front, for extra support while inflight. These were also old style seats, in terms of having large, deep, leather pockets on the seat back.

The tray table folded out from the side of the seat, and had to be flipped over to be fully extended. It was a bit flimsy, as the cabin definitely felt a bit past its prime.

There was a center console where drinks could be placed during the flight, along with additional little drink trays that could be extended, acting as “wings” to the center console.

On the front side of the center console were the AC charging outlets, which were the extent of the charging options there — there were no USB-A or USB-C charging options.

There were also little channel and volume controls, along with a headphone jack, for tuning into the inflight entertainment.

Perhaps the most modern part of the cabin was the overhead consoles, which had the more modern Boeing overhead lights and air nozzles.

While the cabin definitely felt tired and wasn’t in great shape, the comfort was otherwise great, when compared to what you’ll otherwise find in the region. I mean, my previous two regional flights on airlines from northern Africa were on junky wet leased planes, so this was luxurious by comparison.

Unfortunately this Royal Air Maroc 737 didn’t have any sort of Wi-Fi or streaming entertainment. Instead, there were monitors that folded down from the overhead consoles, which had some programming during the flight — on this flight, there were cartoons.

So the entertainment situation was disappointing, but of course on a flight of this length, it wasn’t an issue. But if I were on a three or four hour flight on one of these 737s, I’d of course have a different impression.

During boarding, the crew came around with pre-departure drinks, including the choice of water or lemon mint juice, and we got one of each. They were served in proper glassware — I love the branding!

One thing I have to mention is that the cabin was insanely hot during boarding — I imagine the APU wasn’t working, or something, so we were sweating our you-know-whats off.

Airlines of northern Africa are always a bit funny when it comes to safety. At 1:55PM the safety video was screened, while the door was still open, and before all passengers had boarded.

At 2:05PM the main cabin door closed, with seven of the 12 business class seats occupied. At 2:10PM we began our pushback, and at 2:15PM we began our taxi. There were zero security checks during the taxi out, and a couple of people in business class had their seats reclined.

The captain sure was a good multi-tasker, or at least so I assume — he made his welcome aboard announcement while also taxiing us out and making some turns (at least I assume that at Royal Air Maroc taxiing is a captain-only function, but maybe that’s not the case?).

It was just a quick taxi out to runway 13, where we were second in line for takeoff, behind a Ryanair 737. We were cleared for takeoff at 2:20PM, with some nice views on the climb out.

The seatbelt sign was turned off just five minutes after takeoff, at which point the crew sprung into action, starting by closing the curtain between the cabin and the galley.

After takeoff, the crew distributed some warm towels, which had a nice scent to them.

A few minutes later, the inflight meal was brought out. For a flight of this length, I was impressed. The main dish had some prawns, burrata, and veggies. Then there was a cheese plate, a slice of cake, and a piece of bread. Unlike on Air Algerie, a little thought was also put into presentation.

The crew passed through with water, while other drinks had to specifically be requested. I asked for a cup of tea, which was also promptly served. By the time I finished my snack, we were already well into our descent.

For a flight of this length, this kind of snack is really tough to beat.

Just before landing, I checked out the business class lavatory on the Royal Air Maroc 737. It was a pretty standard previous generation 737 lavatory, and had definitely seen better days. Among other things, the toilet seat just wouldn’t stay up unless you held it open the entire time.

There were no special amenities, other than Royal Air Maroc branded hand lotion.

The lead flight attendant on this flight was a nice older guy. We didn’t interact with him much, but he seemed generally charming. For example, I saw him kindly bring some toys to a kid seated in business class, and engage nicely with him.

The primary flight attendant working in business class was a younger lady. She wasn’t rude, but had zero outward personality. She didn’t smile, and if we exchanged five words, that would’ve been a lot. But at least she was efficient and on top of things, and compared to Air Algerie, she was basically a Singapore Airlines flight attendant.

At 1:50PM Casablanca time (there was a one-hour time change from Malaga, so this was 30 minutes after takeoff), the seatbelt sign was turned on, as we were well into our descent to Casablanca. At that point the pre-landing announcement was made, but again, there was nothing in the way of safety checks, and the person seated in front of me even still had a glass at their seat.

The views on the approach were lovely — Morocco really is a beautiful country.

We ended up landing at Casablanca Airport at 1:05PM, on runway 35L.

From there we had a short five-minute taxi to our arrival stand, where we’d have to get on a bus to get to the terminal.

On the plus side, this gave us a great view of the 737 we had just flown, which was in the special oneworld livery.

As we deplaned, the lead flight attendant and captain kindly bid farewell to everyone. The airline did have a special bus for business class passengers, which is at least a nice aspect of the passenger experience, as it shows some effort.

It was a roughly five-minute ride to the terminal, then we cleared security, and then we boarded our Royal Air Maroc 787 business class flight to Miami a short while later.

I had a pleasant flight in Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class. For a 45-minute flight, it sure is nice to get real business class seats and a proper, tasty snack. The flight also operated on schedule, so I really have no complaints, especially when you consider the typical airline experience in the northern part of Africa.

To be fair, though, the cabin was definitely a bit tired, and the lack of Wi-Fi and streaming entertainment would prove more frustrating on a longer journey. Furthermore, the primary flight attendant working business class just didn’t have any personality.

What do you make of Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class?

#6128. Trump's birthright citizenship restrictions struck down again by DC federal judge he called 'hater'

Fox News legal editor Kerri Urbahn analyzes President Trump's new executive orders targeting birth tourism and birthright citizenship, plus the legal battle with the ACLU and a Texas hospital settlement. Urbahn discusses the constitutional battles ahead.

A DC federal judge, previously dubbed by President Donald Trump as an "anti- Trump Hater," blocked Trump's second attempt to restrict birthright citizenship in a Wednesday ruling.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper, who was recently in Trump's crosshairs after ruling against efforts to shut down the Kennedy Center for renovations and add Trump's name to the cultural institution, issued a 67-page ruling striking down an August executive order that barred U.S. -born children whose parents are suspected terrorists or gang members, or children born through surrogacy to foreign parents, from citizenship eligibility.

Cooper's ruling comes months after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's initial executive order, signed on his first day back in office. The order attempted to deny birthright citizenship to U.S.-born children whose mothers were in the country illegally or temporarily and whose fathers were neither U.S. citizens nor green card holders.

WHITE HOUSE RIPS ‘ACTIVIST’ BIDEN JUDGE WHO UPENDED TRUMP BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP ORDER

Demonstrators hold up an anti-Trump sign outside the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, DC, on June 27, 2025, after the justices curbed nationwide injunctions in a case stemming from President Donald Trump's initial bid to end birthright citizenship. (ALEX WROBLEWSKI/AFP via Getty Images)

"As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the President cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws," Cooper ruled.

Trump's second executive order was already partially blocked on Sept. 2 by U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman in Maryland, whose injunction protected U.S.-born children of mothers who were in the country illegally or temporarily and whose fathers were neither U.S. citizens nor lawful permanent residents.

Cooper's ruling expanded protections beyond that class to include additional children born to certain foreign government and international organization employees, parents deemed "alien enemies" by the administration and foreign parents who used commercial surrogacy services in the U.S.

"The merits in this case are clear-cut. The Supreme Court has twice confirmed that all children born in this country are U.S. citizens, save only for the small handful who are not subject to U.S. law," Cooper wrote.

In addition to the Supreme Court's June ruling in Trump v. Barbara, Cooper referred to the high court's ruling in United States v. Wong Kim Ark, which determined that a man born to Chinese immigrants was a protected U.S. citizen under the 14th Amendment.

SEN ERIC SCHMITT SEEKS TO END BIRTH TOURISM, REVOKE CITIZENSHIP FOR BABIES OF FOREIGN DIPLOMATS

President Donald Trump speaks during a news conference in the James S. Brady Briefing Room at the White House in Washington, DC, on June 27, 2025, following a U.S. Supreme Court ruling on nationwide injunctions in litigation over his first birthright citizenship executive order. (Mehmet Eser/Middle East Images via AFP)

Cooper noted that Wong Kim Ark established narrow exceptions to birthright citizenship, including for children of foreign diplomats, children born aboard foreign public ships and children of enemy forces occupying American territory.

"While the Fourteenth Amendment may theoretically permit new exceptions beyond those listed in Wong Kim Ark, Congress has not authorized any such exceptions," Cooper wrote.

Cooper argued that membership in a terrorist organization alone does not satisfy the historical exception to birthright citizenship for children of enemy forces occupying U.S. territory. He criticized the Trump administration's contention that foreign invaders could occupy American territory without actually holding it as an "outside-the-box understanding" of what constitutes an occupation.

"To recap, a parent’s purported status as an alien enemy, standing alone, cannot strip a U.S.-born child of his right to birthright citizenship," Cooper wrote. "The alien-enemy exception, properly understood, applies only to children born to hostile enemy forces in temporarily occupied U.S. territory."

Cooper also rejected Trump's attempt to deny birthright citizenship to children born through commercial surrogacy arrangements involving foreign parents, finding that the circumstances of their birth do not exempt them from U.S. jurisdiction.

"Indeed, foreign parents choose surrogacy arrangements in the United States precisely to have the child be governed by U.S. law and have the surrogacy process ‘supervised by a court.," Cooper wrote.

TRUMP TO ASK SUPREME COURT TO REHEAR BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP CASE AFTER 'INSANE DECISION'

Demonstrators gather outside the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, DC, on May 15, 2025, in support of birthright citizenship during litigation over President Donald Trump's first executive order narrowing citizenship eligibility for children born on U.S. soil. (Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg via Getty)

He noted that, prior to Trump's second executive order, the State Department recognized the citizenship of children born on American soil regardless of whether they were born through surrogacy.

The Trump administration is expected to appeal the decision and request that the executive order be temporarily enforced while the litigation works its way through the courts, a process that could take months.

"This is just another ruling from an activist judge appointed by Obama attempting to thwart President Trump’s commonsense agenda," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "The birthright citizenship executive order is consistent with the holdings and analysis set forth by the Supreme Court."

The Justice Department could seek temporary relief from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit or seek intervention from the Supreme Court. Fox News Digital reached out to the Justice Department for comment.

OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE WITH TIES TO ANTI-TRUMP CONSPIRACY THEORY HIT WITH MISCONDUCT COMPLAINT

In addition to ruling against Trump's Kennedy Center renovation efforts, Cooper ruled that Trump's Department of Government Efficiency must turn over records requested in a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit.

Trump has called Cooper one of the "Radical Left Democrats."

Cooper is also married to Amy Jeffress, who was Biden’s personal lawyer in 2025 and previously did some work for the Jan. 6 committee.

Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.
